10008-the-mystery:
Stewart Edward White and Samuel Hopkins Adams wrote this 1907 sea mystery in two parts. Part one, The Sea Riddle, opens on desert seas with the Laughing Lass, a death ship, a second prize crew, a disappearance, and castaways.

Part two, The Brass Bound Chest, moves to the Barbary Coast, a graven image, and twelve repeating rifles, as the riddle's answer comes into view. White and Adams keep the sea adventure brisk and the puzzle fair. Readers get a double mystery: a ship that vanishes, and a chest that explains it.
10029-the-hunt-ball-mystery:
Sir William Magnay's 1918 mystery opens at a hunt ball, where an intruder, stained flowers, and a streak on a cuff set suspicion running. A guest goes missing, a room is locked, and the mystery of Clement Henshaw deepens while Gervase Henshaw refuses to believe it.

Kelson's perplexity grows as clues point in several directions at once, in the classic country-house manner. Magnay, author of The Mystery of the Unicorn, keeps the puzzle tight and the suspects polite. Mystery readers get a well-bred whodunit, where evening dress hides secrets and a ball becomes a crime scene.
10058-the-divine-office-a-study-of-the-r:
Reverend E. J. Quigley's 1920 study explains the Divine Office, the daily prayer of the Roman Breviary. Part one answers general questions: what the breviary is, a short history of divine praise, and the excellence of the Roman book beside others.

Later sections set out the breviary's contents, the church year and its parts, and the general rubrics. They add rules from moral theology for reciting it: intention, attention, and cases such as saying matins before finishing compline. Quigley writes clearly for clergy and laity. Readers get a thorough guide to Catholicism's daily prayer.
1006-divine-comedy-cary-s-translation-pu:
Halfway up Dante's great journey stands the mountain of Purgatory, where souls climb toward light by owning and shedding their faults. This volume gives that middle canticle alone, in the English verse of Henry Francis Cary, whose version first brought Dante to many English readers.

Virgil leads Dante past terraces where the proud bend low, the envious shut their eyes, and the wrathful walk in smoke, each soul learning the cure for its own sin. Friends and kings from Dante's age speak as they climb. The canticle is gentler than Hell and more hopeful than earth, and Cary's lines keep its grave, musical pace.
10067-the-mystery-of-the-boule-cabinet-a:
Burton E. Stevenson's 1911 detective story, dedicated to a fellow Sherlockian, opens with a connoisseur's vagary and a first tragedy. A wounded hand and a thunderbolt follow, as Grady takes a hand and a woman enters the case.

Later chapters bring Rogers's shock, guesses at the riddle, burning eyes, and a frightened Godfrey. A distinguished caller and a veiled lady appear, all around a boule cabinet, a piece of inlaid furniture with secrets. Stevenson writes in the classic detective manner. Mystery readers get a puzzle built around one beautiful, dangerous object.
10068-the-power-and-the-glory:
Grace Macgowan Cooke's 1910 novel opens with the birth of a woman-child and the birth of an ambition, then a peak in Darien, the use of feet, and the moccasin flower. Weavers and weft, a view above the valley, and the use of wings follow.

Later chapters bring a bit of metal, the sandals of joy, a new boarder, the contents of a bandanna, and a patient for the hospital. Cooke, author of Mistress Joy, writes of a woman's growth with sympathy. Readers get a novel of ambition and love, where small things, like sandals and flowers, carry large meaning.
10082-the-hampstead-mystery:
John R. Watson and Arthur J. Rees's 1916 mystery opens with a telephone call: Detective-Inspector Chippenfield of Scotland Yard rings Hampstead Police Station and asks, urgently, for Inspector Seldon. The Yard man waits with the receiver to his ear, studying a sheet of paper on his desk.

From that call, the Hampstead mystery unfolds in the classic British manner, with police procedure, suspects, and a trail through London's northern suburb. Watson and Rees keep the puzzle tight. Mystery readers get a brisk, workmanlike detective tale from the age of the first Yard procedurals.
10161-english-poets-of-the-eighteenth-ce:
Ernest Bernbaum, professor of English at the University of Illinois, selected and edited this 1918 anthology of English poets of the eighteenth century, with an introduction. Its contents open with John Pomfret's Choice of 1700 and Daniel Defoe's True-Born Englishman of 1701, with his Hymn to the Pillory.

Joseph Addison's Campaign of 1704 and Divine Ode of 1712 follow, with Matthew Prior's poems to a child of quality and a lady, and his dying Hadrian to his soul. The anthology traces Augustan verse in short, chosen pieces. Students get the century's poetry in a compact, scholarly selection.
10339-an-antarctic-mystery:
Jules Verne published this Antarctic adventure in French in 1897 as Le Sphinx des Glaces, translated here by Mrs. Cashel Hoey in 1899. It serves as a sequel of sorts to Edgar Allan Poe's tale of Arthur Gordon Pym, following a ship called the Halbrane south toward ice and mystery. Verne builds on Poe's hints with his own science and suspense.

The Halbrane meets ice floes, a rescue by the Tasman, Dirk Peters in the crow's nest, and a ship fast in an iceberg. Hunt, William Guy, and other sailors face cold, wreck, and fear. Readers get a thrilling polar voyage, rich in ice, ships, and the lure of the far south.
10448-the-anti-slavery-harp-a-collection:
William W. Brown, a fugitive slave, compiled this songbook in Boston in 1848 for anti-slavery meetings. Brown gathered recent songs, many never before in print, with debts to the Liberty Minstrel and Anti-Slavery Melodies. The book was meant to be cheap, singable, and rousing.

Songs ask, Am I not a man and brother, and call on Christ and mercy to end bondage. They were sung at meetings to stir hearts and bind crowds in common cause. Readers get a moving, historic songbook of the abolition movement, full of faith, protest, and hope.
10552-roy-blakeley-his-story:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh published this Boy Scout story in 1920, with Roy Blakeley telling his own tale from the troop book of the First Bridgeboro Troop. Roy, helped by Pee-wee Harris, narrates adventures on land and sea, and particularly in the mud. The book was approved by the Boy Scouts of America.

Troubles of his own, a big conclave, swatting a spy, a plot growing thinner or thicker, and a tight place fill early chapters. Weetonka, a terrible chief, adds Native lore and camp fun. Readers get a cheerful, first-person scout adventure, full of humor and troop spirit.
10655-autobiography-of-sir-george-biddel:
Sir George Biddell Airy served as Astronomer Royal of Britain from 1836 to 1881, and this autobiography, edited by his son Wilfrid and published in 1896, tells his working life. Airy describes himself not as a romantic genius but as a hard-working man of business, whose daily task was the Royal Observatory at Greenwich. His letters, reports, and records supply the detail.

The book follows his schooling, his rise through Cambridge, and forty-six years of running an observatory, dealing with instruments, staff, visitors, and the state. It shows science as steady labor rather than sudden discovery. Readers interested in Victorian science get a frank, detailed life of one of its great organizers.
10699-character-writings-of-the-seventee:
Henry Morley, professor at University College, London, edited Character Writings of the Seventeenth Century in 1891, gathering short portraits of human types. The book reaches back to Theophrastus and Thomas Harman's rogues, then gives Ben Jonson, Sir Thomas Overbury, and their fellows full room. Overbury's sketches include a good woman, a dissembler, a courtier, a flatterer, and a pedant.

These "characters" sketch a type in a page or two, with wit and moral judgment. Morley's collection shows how the age saw itself, from country gentlemen to serving-men. Readers get a lively anthology of early English social satire, useful for students and delightful for browsers.
10705-the-history-of-rome-book-v-the-est:
Theodor Mommsen closes his History of Rome with Book V, on the establishment of the military monarchy. In Dickson's translation, the volume follows the end of the republic's civil wars and the rise of rule by generals, ending in the settlement that made one man master of Rome. The book explains how republican forms gave way to imperial power.

Mommsen treats Caesar's heirs, the armies, and the provinces with the same legal and narrative skill as the earlier books. His account of the new monarchy shaped debate for generations. Readers finishing the history here see Rome remade, from republic to empire, by the great historian of the subject.
10816-the-giant-hands-or-the-reward-of-i:
Alfred Crowquill's fairy tale The Giant Hands, or The Reward of Industry, published in London and New York in 1856, teaches children that hard work wins its reward. Poor little Willie comes home from the forest laden with wood, hungry and weary, his father dead since early spring and his mother toiling for a scant living. He lights a cheerful blaze and warms his swollen feet by the hearth.

The text is printed in divided syllables, so young readers can sound out each word as the story unfolds. Willie’s industry, set against poverty, points the moral of the title. Families get a short, old-fashioned fairy tale, made for the nursery and the schoolroom.
10860-the-gracchi-marius-and-sulla-epoch:
A. H. Beesley's The Gracchi, Marius and Sulla, in the Epochs of Ancient History series with maps, published in 1921, covers Rome's revolutionary century. It opens with Scipio Aemilianus and the tribunate of Tiberius Gracchus, whose agrarian proposals met fierce opposition from landholders and the tribune Octavius. Tiberius stands again, and is murdered.

Later chapters follow Caius Gracchus, his corn law, courts, colonies, and franchise plans, then Marius and Sulla and the republic's slide into civil war. Beesley writes a clear school history, defending Gracchus's wisdom while telling the violence plainly. Students get a compact guide to the men who broke the Roman republic.
10908-manual-for-noncommissioned-officer:
The War Department published this Manual for Noncommissioned Officers and Privates of Infantry in 1917, as document number 574 of the Adjutant General's office. Approved at Washington on April 14, 1917, days after America entered the First World War, it was issued for the information and government of all concerned. Engineer companies dismounted and coast artillery companies used it for infantry training.

The manual covers drill, duties, and conduct for sergeants, corporals, and privates, in the plain language of orders. Its date marks the army's rapid expansion for war. Readers get a primary source on how American soldiers were trained in 1917.
1091-on-heroes-hero-worship-and-the-hero:
Thomas Carlyle argues in six lectures that history is made not by masses or machines but by great men: heroes as gods, prophets, poets, priests, men of letters, and kings. Odin, Mahomet, Dante, Shakespeare, Luther, Knox, Cromwell, and Napoleon each get a lecture, praised as the soul of their age made flesh.

Carlyle's prose thunders with praise and scorn, and his doctrine of hero-worship shaped Victorian thought for good and ill. Critics now fault his contempt for common folk and his love of strong rule. The book still matters as a landmark of nineteenth-century ideas, and it reads with a force few lectures ever match.
10912-the-infant-s-delight-poetry:
Short poems for very young children fill this illustrated book, with words split into syllables to help beginners read aloud. Games, seasons, and animals supply the subjects: blind man's buff by the fire, snowballing on New Year's Day, boats on the water, and poppies gathered in the corn. Pictures face many of the verses, so a child can follow the scene while reading.

Several poems carry a gentle moral or a note of faith, including a robin fed each morning by a girl named Minnie and verses on snow obeying God's command. The tone stays warm and simple throughout, with short lines and clear rhymes. Parents reading aloud will find it an easy first poetry book, pitched at children just learning their letters.
10987-the-extraordinary-adventures-of-po:
An 1850 story founded on fact follows three-year-old Henry, who loses his mother on a village lawn and is tricked by a naughty boy, Bill Boldface, into running into the woods. Henry calls for his mamma, trips, rests, and meets his dog Fidelle, who runs ahead as night falls and the wind turns cold. Lost and bewildered, the child wanders to a mountain and, at last, to an old abbey.

Shut up in the abbey for three weeks, Henry is cared for by birds, whose sweet evening songs reconcile him to his strange kingdom, while his parents search in confusion. The tale, by the author of Nothing At All, mixes fright with comfort for very young readers. Its old-fashioned moral is clear: a cruel joke can endanger a child, and kindness can sustain one.
11022-sowing-and-reaping-a-temperance-st:
Frances E. W. Harper, the African American poet and novelist, wrote this temperance story, rediscovered and edited by Frances Smith Foster. John Andrews gives up his saloon business, to neighbours' surprise, because his wife opposes the trade and values home peace over profit. Other men argue that a wife should not interfere in how a living is earned.

Later chapters turn darker, with a murder committed by a drunken man who spent freely on Lizzie Wilson and threatened a rival, Loraine. The victim's wife and children mourn, and the novel links drink to ruined homes. Harper writes with moral force and sympathy for wives and families, making the book both a temperance tract and an early African American novel of domestic life.
11052-the-custom-of-the-country:
Edith Wharton wrote this 1913 novel about Undine Spragg, a beautiful, ambitious young woman from the Midwest who climbs New York and Paris society through marriages. Undine snatches a note from her mother's hand at the Hotel Stentorian, where gilt chairs, salmon-pink damask, and portraits of Marie Antoinette frame her family's pretensions. Mrs. Heeny, a professional visitor, admires Undine's form.

Undine marries Ralph Marvell, then leaves him for wealth and status, chasing a life of balls, houses, and admiration. Cables from home, including one saying Ralph wants her, interrupt her pleasures abroad. Wharton writes with sharp irony about American wealth, divorce, and social climbing. The novel remains one of her finest studies of ambition and its costs.
11496-poetry:
Arthur Quiller-Couch's Poetry, in his Cambridge lectures manner, opens with Plato's tale of Er the Pamphylian, slain in battle and returned on the twelfth day to report the other world. Er saw the great Spindle of Necessity reaching to heaven, planets revolving in whorls, each with a Siren hymning a single note, eight notes forming one harmony. Quiller-Couch draws a moral: the universe's stability rests on ordered motion, a balance of tremendous forces harmoniously composed.

Theology asks by whom, philosophy how, and natural science maps what it can, but all agree on harmony, the lecture argues. The book treats poetry as attention to that order. Readers of criticism will find Quiller-Couch's blend of classical story and plain argument characteristic of his teaching.
11532-a-kentucky-cardinal-a-story:
James Lane Allen's story opens on New Year's Day 1850. Sun shone cloudless yet wrought no thaw. Frost flowers stayed on the panes, and a lean hare limped twice across a Kentucky lawn.

The narrator sits by a hickory fire with his dog. He stretches a horse-hair across the window to sweeten the north wind's noise. A cardinal among snow-buried cedars gives the book its emblem. The narrator watched it from a childhood window. The tale that follows is a quiet Kentucky romance, told through seasons, birds, and household talk.
1155-the-secret-adversary:
Agatha Christie introduces Tommy Beresford and Tuppence Cowley, two bright young people broke after the Great War. They take on a case for the government: missing treaty papers and a vanished girl, both tied to a mastermind called Mr. Brown. The hunt runs through London hotels, strikes, and spy plots.

Tommy and Tuppence bicker, flirt, and bluff their way into danger, and the pace never slackens. The novel launched Christie's second great pair of sleuths. It remains a brisk, charming thriller and the start of a long partnership in crime solving.
11587-the-school-book-of-forestry:
Charles Lathrop Pack, president of the American Forestry Association, wrote this 1922 school book to teach children why forests matter. A people without children faces a hopeless future, he says, and a country without trees is almost as helpless.

Chapters cover forest fire guards in tree tops, nurseries, grazing ranges, and the Secretary of Agriculture's rules for sheep, cattle, horses, hogs, and goats. Cattle graze valleys and lower slopes, while sheep and goats take high meadows above timberline. The book mixes science with citizenship, urging care for woods that renew themselves.
11628-gossip-in-a-library:
Edmund Gosse's 1913 book gossips through a library, chapter by chapter, from Camden's Britannia and A Mirror for Magistrates to a poet in prison, Death's Duel, and Gerard's Herbal. A volume of old plays, a censor of poets, and the romance of a dictionary follow.

Later chapters take up Lady Winchilsea's poems, Amasia, love and business, what Ann Lang read, cats, Smart's poems, and Pompey the Little. One passage quotes a lover of Eliza Haywood's Love in Excess, where a gentleman prowls by moonlight while a lady watches in agitated disorder. The book is a critic's pleasure in old books.
11719-kincaid-s-battery:
George W. Cable's 1908 novel, Kincaid's Battery, opens in Carrollton Gardens, with carriage company, a general's choice, and manoeuvres. Hilary, Anna, Flora, and Constance carry a New Orleans story through the Civil War.

Chapters follow a fight for the standard, a parked battery raising dust, and swift going down stream with hard going up. The Callenders and Valcours believe New Orleans can jeer at Farragut and Butler, and that Mobile shares the two cities' fortune. The novel mixes romance with artillery, as a Louisiana battery faces invasion and a city under threat.
11878-three-plays-the-fiddler-s-house-th:
Padraic Colum's 1916 volume gathers three short Irish plays written for the early Irish National Theatre, a small stage with few furnishings and an audience keenly alert to national character. Colum wrote for players who were his colleagues and teachers, and the plays keep that intimate scale.

The Land celebrates the passing of Irish acres from alien landlords after the 1903 Land Act. It also faces emigration, as young people leave for America not only from need but from a lack of life and freedom at home. The Fiddler's House and Thomas Muskerry complete a trio about home, work, and the pull of the wider world.
11924-the-loves-of-krishna-in-indian-pai:
W. G. Archer's study traces Krishna through Indian painting and poetry, from the hero of the Mahabharata to the cowherd of the Bhagavata Purana. Chapters follow his birth and early adventures, his loves among the cowgirls, and the death of the tyrant Kansa. A Kangra painting of Radha and Krishna in the grove, about 1785, serves as frontispiece.

Archer pairs pictures with verses, showing how painters and poets returned to the same scenes. Those scenes include Krishna meeting Kansa's washermen, the herd-girls forgetting husbands and household tasks to look at him, and Radha pleading, shy and agitated, for his favor. The book reads Indian art as a devotional language, not merely as illustration.
11937-the-symbolism-of-freemasonry:
Albert G. Mackey's 1882 work explains the science and philosophy of Freemasonry through its legends, myths, and symbols. Mackey, a physician and Masonic scholar, takes as his epigraph a Latin maxim from Cardanus: writings should offer present usefulness, a certain end, and an unshakable foundation.

The book treats Masonic symbols not as secret decorations but as a system of moral and philosophical teaching, with legends read for the ideas they carry. Footnotes, renumbered and moved to the end in this edition, support a study that has long served both Masons seeking the meaning of their ritual and outsiders curious about its symbolism.
11983-poetic-sketches-a-collection-of-mi:
Thomas Gent's Poetic Sketches, a collection of miscellaneous poetry, appeared in a second edition in 1808. It opens with a self-deprecating epigraph: in mercy spare me when I do my best to make as much waste paper as the rest. Gent dedicates the volume to George Canning, secretary of state for foreign affairs and privy councillor, praised as scholar and statesman.

The sketches mix occasional verse, satire, and sentiment in the manner of early nineteenth-century miscellanies, written for friends, patrons, and local occasions. Gent's modesty is conventional. His collection preserves a minor poet's view of Regency literary life, where dedication to a minister could matter as much as a poem's merit.
11986-the-book-of-american-negro-poetry:
James Weldon Johnson's Book of American Negro Poetry gathers Black American verse with an essay on the Negro's creative genius. It was published by Harcourt, Brace and Company in 1922 and printed by Quinn and Boden at Rahway, New Jersey. Johnson, author of Fifty Years and Other Poems, argues for a distinct tradition, not a footnote to American poetry.

Contents open with Paul Laurence Dunbar, including A Negro Love Song, Little Brown Baby, Ships That Pass in the Night, Lover's Lane, The Debt, and The Haunted Oak. The anthology gave early twentieth-century readers a canon in formation, placing Dunbar and his successors at the center of American literary history.
1201-an-essay-on-the-trial-by-jury:
Lysander Spooner argues that trial by jury, rightly understood, gives jurors the right to judge law as well as fact, and to refuse unjust laws. The essay, a classic of American individualist thought, defends jury nullification. Spooner, a lawyer and abolitionist, wrote the essay in 1852, as jury rights were debated.

Spooner traces jury history from Magna Carta onward, insisting that a jury must be free, not a tool of judges. Lawyers and libertarians still cite the essay, and its argument continues to stir debate in courtrooms. His argument, that jurors may judge law, still appears in courtroom debates today.
12052-half-a-century:
Jane Grey Swisshelm's Half a Century, published in 1880, opens with Browning's lines on mankind's ignorance and on friends who deprecate rough handling of a lie. Its preface addresses a general belief that the antislavery struggle, which culminated in the Emancipation Proclamation, is fully understood, and sets out to correct that assumption.

Swisshelm, a journalist and abolitionist, writes a memoir of fifty years of American life, from frontier journalism to the Civil War and its aftermath. Her book is both personal history and political argument, insisting that the struggle against slavery involved women, newspapers, and ordinary readers, not only generals and presidents. Her pages stay close to daily life in print shops, homes, and meeting halls.
12175-the-nest-of-the-sparrowhawk-a-roma:
Baroness Orczy, creator of The Scarlet Pimpernel, set this romance in seventeenth-century England and published it in 1909. The action opens in a Kent squire household under Puritan rule and moves to London and the coast.

Adam Lambert, a young gentleman fallen on hard times, shelters an exiled French prince and becomes entangled in secret service, betrayal, and a tinder-box plot. His wife Editha, married young, must choose between loyalty and safety as soldiers, spies, and creditors close in. Orczy keeps the pace brisk and the villains clear. The novel trades on disguise, honor, and narrow escapes, hallmarks of her popular historical fiction.
12200-delsarte-system-of-oratory:
Edgar S. Werner published the fourth edition of this manual in 1893, gathering the teaching of Francois Delsarte, the French singer and theorist of expression. Delsarte system shaped American acting, preaching, and public speaking in the late nineteenth century.

The book combines Delaumosne on the voice, Arnaud writings, Delsarte own remains, and lessons by his daughter Marie Geraldy, with essays by Giraudet, Durivage, and Berlioz. It treats voice in relation to vowels, intensity, and measure, then lays out laws of gesture for head, torso, arms, and hands. For modern readers it explains a lost art: how speakers once trained body and voice as one instrument.
12224-we-girls-a-home-story:
Mrs. A. D. T. Whitney published We Girls in Boston in 1870, with a later edition in 1890. Whitney wrote popular domestic fiction for girls, and this home story follows a household of sisters in a country town near a great city.

Chapters move through holidays, winter nights, emergencies, and small crises: Ruth takes responsibility, Barbara buzzes with schemes, and the family copes with servants, sick rooms, and social calls. The tone is warm and moral, praising cooperation and good humor over wealth. Modern readers may find the lessons plain, but the book preserves a detailed picture of middle-class girlhood, housekeeping, and sisterly affection in post-Civil War New England.
12320-civilization-and-beyond-learning-f:
Scott Nearing published Civilization and Beyond in 1975 through the Social Science Institute at Harborside, Maine. Nearing, a veteran radical economist, presents the book as a study of history meant to be read whole, not in fragments.

The contents move from an introduction on history and civilization through a pageant of experiments with civilization, weighing empires, revolutions, and social systems. Nearing argues that most contestants who set out to conquer the world found disappointment and disaster, while even the few who reached the summit found frustration. The book is a late-life synthesis: plain, polemical, and convinced that civilization must be judged by what it does to ordinary people.
12443-the-jute-industry:
T. Woodhouse and P. Kilgour, both teachers at Dundee Technical College, set out in 1921 to trace jute from field to finished cloth. Their manual belongs to Pitman's series on common commodities, and it treats a fibre trade centred on Dundee and Bengal, with mill practice as its main concern.

Chapters move in order through growing, retting, sorting and baling, then mill work: batching, carding, drawing, roving, spinning, winding, weaving and finishing. Photographs and diagrams show fields, presses, ships and machines at each stage. The result reads as a working handbook for students and mill hands, plain in aim and packed with trade detail, rather than a general history of textiles.
12587-the-man-who-laughs-a-romance-of-en:
Victor Hugo's Man Who Laughs, a romance of English history, opens with preliminary chapters on Ursus and the Comprachicos, child-buyers who reshape faces. Part one, book one, Night Not So Black as Man, follows Portland Bill, a child left alone, alone, and questions. The tree of human invention, struggle between death and night, and the north point of Portland follow.

Book two, The Hooker at Sea, adds superhuman laws, troubled men on troubled seas, and a cloud different from others. Hardquanonne, help thought at hand, superhuman horrors, night and the charge confided to a raging sea follow. Hugo writes in grand, grotesque romance, about a laughing man, a blind girl and English cruelty. The novel remains a vast, strange masterpiece of exile.
12617-recollections-of-calcutta-for-over:
Montague Massey's 1918 recollections of Calcutta, sold for the Red Cross Fund and dedicated to Lady Carmichael, founder of the Bengal Women's War Fund, span over half a century. Massey warns at the outset that his reminiscences hold no sensational elements, lest readers expect disclosures that must for ever lie buried.

Startling incidents fresh in memory are left out, he says, as out of place in a work of this nature. Instead the book gives a descriptive account of Calcutta's wonderful transformation, its streets, people and institutions over decades. Massey writes as a long resident looking back, fond and orderly. The volume offers a calm, first-hand portrait of a colonial capital changing.
12624-our-lady-saint-mary:
J. G. H. Barry's 1922 Our Lady Saint Mary, dedicated to members of the League of the Blessed Virgin, treats devotion to Mary in two parts. Part one covers loyalty and the meaning of worship. Part two follows Mary of Nazareth through annunciation, visitation, Joseph, nativity, magi, presentation, Egypt and Nazareth. Temple, Cana, who is my mother, holy week, crucifixion, burial, resurrection, forty days, ascension, descent of the Spirit, home of St John, assumption and coronation follow.

Barry, quoting Origen on being called a fool for believing such things, writes as an Anglo-Catholic devotional author. The book offers a systematic, reverent meditation on Mary's life, for readers who practise Marian devotion.
12821-the-brook-kerith-a-syrian-story:
George Moore's 1916 novel retells the life of Jesus from an unusual angle, through the eyes of Joseph of Arimathea and his circle. It opens with a grandmother telling the boy Joseph how Saul sought his father's lost asses, then moves to the Syrian hills, the Jordan, and the ministry years. A storm on the lake, with Jesus teaching as water enters the boat, is one vivid scene.

Moore imagines a Jesus who survives the cross and lives on in quiet, raising hard questions about faith, legend, and truth. The book stirred debate for its bold retelling of the Gospel story. It remains a striking, meditative novel for readers open to a fresh view of familiar ground.
12845-the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-:
Edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton, this twelfth volume of The World's Greatest Books surveys modern history through short summaries. America, England, France, Germany, Greece, Holland, India, Russia, Spain, Sweden, and the Papacy all appear, with Eliot, Prescott, Clarendon, Macaulay, Voltaire, Tocqueville, Carlyle, Motley, and Ranke among the authors sampled.

A passage on Louis XIV shows a king who, entering the Spanish Succession war, had lost his old grasp of affairs, while Marlborough, cool-headed general and politician, did France great harm. Each summary gives argument in brief. The volume works as a fast gateway to long histories.
1301-the-french-revolution-a-history:
Thomas Carlyle tells the French Revolution as a storm of crowds, orators, and guillotines, from the fall of the Bastille to the rise of Napoleon. His history follows Mirabeau, Danton, Robespierre, and the sans-culottes through terror, war, and hunger, in prose that thunders like a prophet's.

Carlyle writes history as drama, not as dry record, and his verdicts are fierce: he scorns cant and praises heroic force. The book made his fame and shaped how English readers saw the Revolution. It remains a great, if one-sided, work of historical writing.
13158-the-weapons-of-mystery:
Joseph Hocking's Weapons of Mystery, published by Ward, Lock in 1890, is a novel of strange science, hypnotism, and hidden power. Its chapters run from Christmas Eve and Christmas morning to Voltaire's story of the East and a journey toward London. The narrator, Justin, is hedged in by secrets he cannot explain, even to friends who press him.

A comic Cornishman named Simon agrees to stand experiment, tough as a crocodile's tongue, but balks at vaccination against cholera and smallpox. Later, a sword of Damocles hangs over Justin, yet joy fills him when a feared turn proves harmless. Hocking mixes mystery, faith, and pseudo-science in a tale that keeps its secret close until the end.
13208-characters-and-events-of-roman-his:
Guglielmo Ferrero's Characters and Events of Roman History, the Lowell Lectures of 1908, translated by Frances Lance Ferrero, runs from Caesar to Nero. Lectures cover corruption in Rome, Antony and Cleopatra, Gaul, Nero, Julia and Tiberius, wine, and social growth. Ferrero writes for a general audience, with modern parallels in mind.

He takes Columbus, who sought India and found America without knowing it, as a type of history's surprises. Rome's conquest of Gaul, he argues, began European civilization, since Græco-Latin culture spread through it. Later he traces Tiberius's friends and foes, and the clash between old Roman tradition and young nobility. The lectures are lively, opinionated, and broad in sweep.
13251-the-chums-of-scranton-high-on-the-:
Donald Ferguson's 1919 Chums of Scranton High on the Cinder Path follows schoolboys through sport, mystery, and loyalty. Chapters run from nut foraging and the old quarry road to training for a great tournament, treachery in the air, and a prowler caught in the act. Later chapters bring a gala day, a marathon race, and the final mile of the course.

Hugh Morgan, tricked by a covered pit of twigs and leaves, falls into a deep hole and must break his bonds to climb out. A missing runner, K. K., may have tripped on a vine and broken a leg, or sprained an ankle too badly to limp on. The chums search quarry and road to find him. Ferguson's tale is a cheerful school story of teamwork and fair play.
13278-women-of-the-country:
Gertrude Bone's Women of the Country, in the Roadmender series, sketches rural women in town and field. Bone opens with market scenes, where farmers stand in groups with a planted air, and cattle business ends early, leaving the day for bargains, hats, tailors, and canes. Her chapters follow women at work, in service, and in care.

One portrait shows a blind woman in a ward, proud of her knitting, who re-foots thick stockings so well that a visitor cannot tell her patching from patchwork. She calls her feeling looking, and her mind is alert and cheerful. Bone writes with quiet respect for country women's skill, patience, and humor, in a book of gentle social observation.
13335-the-jesus-of-history:
Written for Advent Sunday 1916 and signed from Lambeth by Randall Cantuar, this study tries to see Jesus as a figure of history through the Gospels. It opens with the Gospels as sources, then follows childhood and youth, the man and his mind, and the teacher among his disciples.

Parables help rebuild home, market, and country life, while close attention to words, looks, and habits sketches quickness, sympathy, and feeling for fact. The book stresses a faith that needs no ritual aid: trust in God shown in action, and moral choice with real consequence. It aims to make the Gospel figure vivid without losing him in antiquarian detail.
13453-the-testing-of-diana-mallory:
Mrs. Humphry Ward's 1908 novel tests Diana Mallory, a young woman whose past, family, and choices are weighed by society and by herself. Diana hangs photographs from Italian pictures in her drawing room, each breathing memory of a villa on the Portofino road and short visits to Lucca and Florence with her father.

Marsham, a politician, finds Diana astonishingly well versed in the details of his measures, and wonders if she has been getting them up, and why. Teasing and deference, her old hold upon him, return in conversation. Ward writes a novel of conscience, politics, and love, in which a woman's character is tried by what she knows, hides, and at last declares.
13461-mistress-and-maid-a-household-stor:
Miss Muloch, author of John Halifax, Gentleman, tells a household story of mistresses and maid in 1864. The Misses Leaf take into their kitchen a tall, awkward, strongly built girl of about fifteen, daughter of Mrs. Hand, a widow washerwoman. The ladies doubt at first whether they were rash to take her.

Hilary, the maid, later searches London landladies for a missing Mr. Leaf, who left no address, and sits with her mistress on kitchen stairs at four in the morning through a silent watch by candlelight. Missing and lost advertisements fill the newspapers as the household faces calamity. Muloch writes of class, service, and affection across the kitchen divide with Victorian moral care.
13827-fields-of-victory:
Mrs. Humphry Ward visited France under the armistice and wrote this 1919 account of victory. Chapters cover the defensive battle of spring 1918, tanks and the Hindenburg Line, and Gouraud at Strasbourg. Alsace-Lorraine, Verdun, and America in France follow, with a study of staff work, tanks, and aeroplanes. Maps and a statistical chart support the text.

Ward walks ruined streets, including Amiens, and notes traffic signs guiding travellers through rubble. She praises French endurance and American energy in equal measure. The epilogue weighs what victory cost and what peace must build. The book mixes travel writing with military history. It gives a civilian's view of France just after war.
13890-canterbury:
Gordon Home wrote Canterbury in 1911 for the Beautiful Britain series, with illustrations. He opens with Chaucer's April showers and pilgrims wending to Canterbury from every shire's end. Home traces the city from Romano-British Durovernum, destroyed and forgotten, to the Saxon town that grew above it. Streets, cathedral, and old houses follow.

Home writes as a guide and antiquary, praising views and buildings. His text suits walkers who want history with their stroll. Illustrations picture the town in its early twentieth-century state. The book belongs to a series celebrating British beauty. It offers a gentle, readable introduction to Canterbury.
13908-pipes-o-pan-at-zekesbury:
James Whitcomb Riley published Pipes o' Pan at Zekesbury in 1895, a book of Hoosier poems and sketches. Dedicated to his brother John, it opens at Zekesbury, then moves down around the river. Poems include Kneeling with Herrick, Romancin', Has She Forgotten, and The Lost Path. Rhymes of rainy days, a tree-toad, and a worn-out pencil follow.

Riley writes in Indiana dialect, with humour and nostalgia for home. One sketch mocks a native talent abused for grotesque, ridiculous effects. His poems praise mothers, childhood, and old songs. The collection shows Riley at his most regional and musical. Readers of American dialect verse will find it characteristic and warm.
13928-plays-acting-and-music-a-book-of-t:
Arthur Symons published Plays, Acting, and Music in 1909 as a book of theory, dedicated to Maurice Maeterlinck. Essays cover Nietzsche on tragedy, Sarah Bernhardt, Coquelin and Molière, Réjane, and Yvette Guilbert. Sir Henry Irving, Duse, and annotations follow. Later pieces treat Tolstoi, problem plays, censorship, and the test of the actor.

Symons argues that an optimist dialectic, armed with syllogisms, drives music out of tragedy and destroys its essence. He defends symbol, mood, and the speaking of verse. The book blends criticism with memoir of performances seen. It suits readers of theatre history. Symons remains a key voice on Symbolist drama.
1398-the-dore-lectures-being-sunday-addr:
Thomas Troward gave the Dore Lectures as Sunday addresses at the Dore Gallery in London, on mental science and the power of thought. The lectures set out his philosophy of mind, spirit, and creative law. Troward, a judge in India turned philosopher, lectured in London in 1909.

Troward argues that thought shapes life, and that the individual mind shares in a larger creative mind. The lectures became a founding text of New Thought, and they still draw readers seeking a reasoned spiritual philosophy. The Dore Gallery talks drew seekers who wanted reason with their spiritual teaching.
13983-the-book-of-the-epic-the-world-s-g:
H. A. Guerber retold the world's great epics in story form in 1913, with an introduction by J. Berg Esenwein. Greek, Latin, French, Spanish, Portuguese, and Italian epics appear, plus British tales. The Iliad, Odyssey, Aeneid, Song of Roland, and Cid lead. The Divine Comedy, Beowulf, Arthur, Robin Hood, and Paradise Lost follow.

Guerber tells each epic plainly, naming Helen, wife of Menelaus, whose suitors swore to aid her recovery. Sixteen illustrations from master paintings support the text. The book suits readers meeting epics for the first time. It also serves teachers seeking summaries. Guerber's clear retellings keep heroic stories accessible.
14049-the-pointing-man-a-burmese-mystery:
Marjorie Douie wrote The Pointing Man, a Burmese mystery published in New York in 1920. Destiny moves pieces on a board in the opening chapter, and a loss affects the Rev. Francis Heath. Mrs. Wilder grows secretive, while Craven Joicey the banker finds memory untrustworthy. Hartley, head of police, smells apple orchards in a fool's paradise.

Atkins explains facts by people, not people by facts, in Douie's method. A boy named Absalom closes a shop and places a chair at steps' top on orders. Burma's heat, temples, and colonial society frame the puzzle. The novel blends detective work with exotic romance. It suits readers of early twentieth-century mystery fiction.
14051-the-end-of-the-world-a-love-story:
Edward Eggleston's 1872 novel sets a love story against a backwoods panic over the end of the world. In an Indiana settlement, a singing-master named Humphreys preaches the coming close of days with single-eyed zeal. Neighbors listen, doubt, and quarrel, while young August falls sick at the castle and friends weigh faith against common sense. Jonas, a talkative farmer, supplies comic commentary in tall, tangled speech.

Romance steadies the satire. Cynthy Ann, Julia, Betsey Malcolm, and Mrs. Abigail form a circle of affections, rivalries, and small kindnesses. Eggleston, author of the Hoosier Schoolmaster, knew this country speech and its church life from inside. The novel pokes fun at prophecy without mocking believers, and it ends as a story of patience: love and work continue even when the sky refuses to shut like an umbrella.
14106-the-belfry:
May Sinclair's 1916 novel opens with a narrator who cannot yet publish his story, since its people still live. A man who took every risk in living tells him to take a job: if you can risk living at all, you can risk that. The couple at the center managed life by daring, and the narrator watches their gamble unfold.

Compromise drives the crisis. A man takes Viola to Ghent meaning to compromise her, yet insists he did not mean to marry her at all. He feared marriage as a risk she should not take, and believed happiness could follow without it. Rooms in the same hotels at Antwerp and Ghent, with no English witnesses who mattered, seal the scandal. Later, a perfect motor car stands like an idol in a garage, never used. Sinclair writes psychological fiction at its sharpest: desire, risk, and reputation weighed in fine detail.
14187-the-dangerous-age-letters-and-frag:
Karin Michaëlis's Dangerous Age, translated from Danish and published by John Lane in 1911, gathers letters and fragments from a woman's diary. Marcel Prévost introduces the French edition, praising a northern novel with Latin clarity and violent sincerity, comparable to famous masculine confessions. Michaëlis, little known in France, reaches readers through German publishers and reviews, as Scandinavian letters often did.

Middle age forms the subject. The diarist longs for weeks and months to glide past unnoticed, marked only by forest tints and alternations of heat and cold. She confesses self-deception, living as if on a Tyrol holiday while pretending she could begin life over again, and shivers at sleepless nights. Spring brings torment of another kind: steamboats driven, it seems, by song, with patriotic choruses from morning till night. Honest, restless, and modern, the diary made Michaëlis known beyond Denmark.
14194-france-in-the-nineteenth-century:
Elizabeth Wormeley Latimer's history covers France from 1830 to 1890, drawn from private papers and contemporary magazine writing. She admits at the start that she first wrote for herself, without full notes, and hopes any borrowed gold thread will be read as appreciation rather than theft. The frank note sets a readable, personal tone for a long public story.

Revolution and reaction alternate. After Louis Napoleon's coup, members of the Left spend December 2, 3, and 4 trying to reassemble while police hunt them and barricades rise. Baudin dies on one, reckless and to no purpose, yet republicans still decorate his grave. Years later, the Commune issues decrees against Thiers and his ministers, arrests priests as hostages, closes churches after Easter, and hangs red flags where crosses stood. Latimer keeps people in view amid the barricades, and the century reads as tragedy and farce together.
14342-ireland-in-the-new-century:
Sir Horace Plunkett wrote Ireland in the New Century in 1904, a study of Irish life and policy. Plunkett, a statesman of the cooperative movement, divides the book into theory and practice. Early chapters treat the English misunderstanding of Ireland and the Home Rule movement under Gladstone. Later chapters turn to land, labor, and self-help. The book dedicates its best to the memory of W. E. H. Lecky.

Plunkett praises Ulster Protestants for thrift, industry, and enterprise, which built a world wide commerce. Their farms drew large yields from poor soil, and their city firms traded round the globe. Yet religious bigotry, he writes, tarnishes heroic deeds meant to be honored. His remedy is organized self-help among wealth producers, backed by sound teaching. The book argues that Ireland's future lies in practical work, not in old quarrels.
14501-the-forest-of-vazon-a-guernsey-leg:
This 1889 Guernsey legend, published by Harrison and Sons of Pall Mall, imagines the island's forested past in the eighth century, before its annexation to Normandy. The preface admits that little authentic history survives from that age.

Chapters move from tradition and superstition through devotion, revelation, affliction, and consolation to annihilation, as Jean paddles by moonlight past a hostile fleet near Lihou. Cromlechs, menhirs, and monkish chronicles supply the background. The tale blends local lore with romance, and it preserves a Victorian islander's sense of Guernsey's deep past. Its forest setting gives the island a mythic origin story.
14526-the-little-city-of-hope-a-christma:
F. Marion Crawford's 1907 Christmas story follows John Henry Overholt, a poor man who sits, in the book's phrase, on Pandora's box. A small boy helps him build a miniature city of hope. Macmillan published the tale in London.

Chapter by chapter, man and boy make bricks without straw and endure a famine in the city. They suffer a siege when the box lid comes off, and a little woman saves the town. The toy city becomes a parable of patience and kindness. Crawford's story is gentle, fanciful, and warm, a Christmas book for readers of all ages.
14577-the-teaching-of-history:
Ernest C. Hartwell, superintendent of schools at Petoskey, Michigan, wrote this 1913 Riverside monograph on teaching history, edited by Henry Suzzallo of Columbia. The booklet assumes a prepared, healthy teacher and starts from there.

Hartwell covers beginning the course, assigning lessons, running recitations, reviewing, using written reports, and testing progress. He urges advance questions, such as why the first United States Bank was not rechartered while state banks suspended specie payments. The monograph is a practical Progressive-era guide, still clear on method. Hartwell's monograph joined a series for working teachers.
14578-from-death-into-life-or-twenty-yea:
The Reverend William Haslam, late incumbent of Curzon Chapel, Mayfair, told the story of twenty years of ministry in this memoir, reprinted at Brockville, Ontario, after selling 130,000 copies. The chapters run from a broken nest in 1841 to open-air preaching.

Haslam describes ordination, antiquarian research, a new parish, and his awakening and conversion in 1851, followed by cottage meetings, drawing-room gatherings, and opposition. Billy Bray and other Cornish figures enliven the tale. The memoir is an evangelical classic, plain in style and full of revival incident. Its Cornish revivals drew crowds to chapels and fields.
1458-dream-life-and-real-life-a-little-a:
Olive Schreiner's little African story, written for her brother's school magazine, follows a child of the veld whose dreams and waking life run side by side. In dream she wanders a bright, kind world; awake she faces the hard facts of farm life, loss, and the grown-ups who do not see her inner life.

Short and tender, the tale speaks for children whose fancy is their refuge and their truth. Schreiner's prose is plain and lyrical by turns. The book is a small classic of South African writing, loved for its sympathy with a child's mind and its quiet protest against dull cruelty.
14587-the-crest-wave-of-evolution-a-cour:
Kenneth Morris delivered this course of lectures on history to the graduates' class at Raja-Yoga College, Point Loma, in the college year 1918 to 1919. The lectures interpret history through theosophical cycles of rise and fall.

Morris moves from Homer, Aeschylus, Socrates, and Plato through the Mauryas of India, Confucius, Rome, Augustus, and Julian to Bodhidharma, tracing crest-waves of civilization. A lecture on Confucius praises his scrupulous public service as a young official. The book is earnest, wide-ranging, and mystical, a theosophical history rather than a scholarly one. Point Loma's community shaped its hopeful view of cycles.
14632-the-mystery-of-mary:
Grace Livingston Hill Lutz's 1910 novel, reissued in 1912, opens with a young man arriving late by train, glancing at his watch as the train vanishes into a tunnel. Electric light outlines the station steps against the city's dark.

He walks cold streets, recalls an evening of music at Mrs. Bowman's, and hopes to find again a young woman whose dark days he glimpsed. A sharp knock next morning wakes him from a brief sleep. Lutz writes a gentle mystery of romance and faith, in her popular style, with the heroine's secret slowly unfolding.
14647-the-cave-in-the-mountain-a-sequel-:
Lieutenant R. H. Jayne's 1894 boys' adventure, a sequel to In the Pecos Country, sends its young heroes into a mountain cave of gloom, strange guides, and daring exploits. The Mershon Company published it in New York.

Chapters run from alone in the gloom through mining and countermining, fishing for a friend and a prize, groping in darkness, and standing between two fires. A lad learns to ride a plunging horse while Mickey coaches his style. The book is brisk dime-novel adventure for boys, full of Apaches, caves, and narrow escapes.
1465-the-wreck-of-the-golden-mary:
Told by a sea captain who went to sea at twelve, this Christmas story follows the wreck of the Golden Mary and the long struggle of her people afterward. Storm, hunger, and the discipline of a ship's company test captain and crew, and the tale is told with a sailor's plain detail and steady nerve.

Short chapters carry the survivors from the wreck itself through rescue and return, with side tales of loyalty and loss along the way. The mood is grave rather than sensational. It is a seafaring Christmas book about endurance, duty, and the bonds formed when a ship goes down.
14669-jaffery:
William J. Locke's 1915 novel centres on Jaffery, a big, warm-hearted man whose strength and sudden tenderness shape every room he enters. Friends gather round him, women are drawn to him, and his restless energy keeps pulling him toward new schemes, quarrels and reconciliations.

Told with affection and humour, the story moves between domestic life, friendship and romance. Jaffery's loyalty counts for more than his judgment, and his mistakes cost him dearly before they are forgiven. Locke makes him less a hero than a force of nature: generous, impulsive and hard to forget, even when those closest to him wish he would sit still.
14708-the-laurel-bush-an-old-fashioned-l:
Dinah Maria Mulock Craik's The Laurel Bush, an old-fashioned love story, takes its title from a lopsided, crooked bush in a garden near the gate. Craik was already famous for John Halifax, Gentleman.

The owners set a rough letter-box in a fork of the bush, where letters could wait for the house a good way off. Around it gather Miss Williams, the boys Archy and Davie, and Mr. Roy, who made the box. The story follows quiet affections, letters, and memories, with the humble bush standing for years of feeling that outlast its makers.
14710-uncle-titus-and-his-visit-to-the-c:
Johanna Spyri's Uncle Titus and His Visit to the Country, translated by Louise Brooks and published in Boston in 1886, is a story for children and for those who love children. Spyri is best known for Heidi.

An ailing man, Uncle Titus, and his little companion join the daily walkers under the lindens at Karlsruhe. Then they visit the country around Tannenburg. Chapters follow long days, a flood, a frightful deed, charades, and long-wished-for happiness, with a family celebration and a quickly put-out fire. Spyri writes warmly of kindness, patience, and country pleasures.
14772-acton-s-feud-a-public-school-story:
Frederick Swainson's 1901 school story follows Acton through a feud that starts with a foul on the field and a penalty that rankles. Biffen's house, its progress and its concert, Cotton and his jackal, and a younger brother all play parts in a term of shifting loyalties.

Later chapters bring Todd to pay his bill, a raffle-like scrape at Rotherhithe, a downward road and a stable confrontation, before Grim's suspicions and Todd finding himself close the arc. Swainson writes school life with energy: games, houses, prefects and codes of honour. The feud matters because, for boys, a slight can feel like a matter of standing, and standing is everything.
14777-hochelagans-and-mohawks-a-link-in-:
W. D. Lighthall's 1899 paper, read to the Royal Society of Canada, tackles the origin and early history of the Iroquois peoples. He links the Hochelagans, the people Jacques Cartier met at Hochelaga, with the Mohawks, arguing for a shared history that helps explain later Iroquois power.

Part of the story runs south, toward the Tuscaroras and Cherokees, while another part shapes early Canada and frustrates French hopes in America. Lighthall weighs traditions, place names and early accounts with care, admitting where the record is thin. Short and scholarly, the paper remains a useful early attempt to join archaeology, language and history into one Iroquois story.
14835-the-burglar-and-the-blizzard-a-chr:
Alice Duer Miller's 1914 Christmas story strands a burglar and a household in a blizzard, with illustrations by Charlotte Harding. Geoffrey Holland surveys a restaurant for his party, while a young lady disposes of silver and a man named McVay is let out of a closet.

A woman dressed in her sister's sables prepares to leave, a voice asks Holland to move back toward the fire, and a slight token is offered in honour of the day. Crime, comedy and Christmas feeling meet in seven short chapters. Miller keeps the burglar human and the blizzard real, so the holiday ending feels earned rather than pasted on.
14887-pipe-and-pouch-the-smoker-s-own-bo:
Joseph Knight's 1895 anthology, dedicated to his friend and fellow smoker Walter Montgomery Jackson, gathers poems for smokers. Its preface defends anthologies in an age of floods of books: busy readers and students alike need good selections, even if they discourage wide reading.

Knight argues that no one can sprint through every book, as Andrew Lang says Gladstone does, so a well-chosen volume has its place. Poems on pipes, tobacco, leisure and talk follow, drawn from many hands. The book is a period piece now, charming for its subject and its defence of browsing, and it captures a late Victorian habit of reading in company with a pipe.
14895-all-he-knew-a-story:
John Habberton, author of Helen's Babies, opens All He Knew on a Capital Express train dashing into Bruceton one bright afternoon. A brakeman is touched on the shoulder by a man holding a small fig box. It was left in a seat three stations back and still holds several figs. The man asks whether its owner will send back for it.

The brakeman answers with a scornful curl that twists his black moustache. Of course not, he says, for the owner left it so train boys might impose it on the travelling public. From that small object grows a story of a man who knows little of the world and much of his own honesty. Habberton writes American small-town life with humour and a gentle moral.
1495-the-golf-course-mystery:
Chester K. Steele's mystery opens on a golf course, where a body is found and a quiet club world turns to suspicion. Clues gather hole by hole: a nineteenth hole, a water hazard, poisonous plants, and a private safe, while Viola, Harry, and Captain Poland each hold a piece of the puzzle.

The plot moves from the inquest to confessions and a poor fishing expedition that nets more than fish. Steele writes in the brisk manner of the early detective tale. It is a light, period mystery for readers who like their crimes served with fresh air and a clubhouse chat.
15007-the-belles-of-canterbury:
Anna Bird Stewart's 1912 play The Belles of Canterbury is a Chaucer tale out of school, in one act for eleven girls. It was published by Samuel French for twenty-five cents and dedicated to Miss Dorothy Conrey. Persons in the play include four pupils at a girls' school: freshman, sophomore, junior and senior.

Characters from Canterbury Tales join them: Wife of Bath and Prioress from the prologue, first and second nuns, Emily from the Knight's Tale, Hippolyta and Griselda from the Clerk's tale. Costumes are simple for amateurs, school dresses modern with elaborate hair, Hippolyta in Amazon dress or armour if possible. Stewart's play lets schoolgirls meet Chaucer by playing his pilgrims.
15165-welsh-lyrics-of-the-nineteenth-cen:
Edmund Jones selected and translated these Welsh lyrics of the nineteenth century, in a first series printed at London and Bangor in 1896. Poets include Alun, Ieuan Glan Geirionnydd, Glasynys, Ioan Emlyn, Trebor Mai, Caledfryn, and Ceiriog, whose songs run from Myfanwy to Liberty and Homewards. Islwyn and Mynyddog appear too.

Songs of shepherds, fishermen, cottages, and graves sit beside nightingales, cuckoos, and mountain rills. Jones keeps the Welsh feeling in plain English verse. Readers who love Celtic poetry will find the book a rare, welcoming door into Welsh song of a century ago.
15223-doctor-claudius-a-true-story:
F. Marion Crawford's 1883 novel, subtitled a true story, opens with Dr. Claudius insisting he is old, though his broad shoulders, thick flaxen hair, and steady hand say otherwise. He sits by a small window, pen in hand, feeling a gap between his life and that of his companions. The puzzle of his age drives the tale.

Crawford follows Claudius through love, learning, and strange fortune, in the romantic style that made Mr. Isaacs famous. The dedication honors a countess and a doctor of philosophy. Readers who enjoy Victorian romantic novels will find the book earnest, mysterious, and full of old-world color.
15253-the-advance-of-science-in-the-last:
T. H. Huxley's 1889 lecture on the advance of science in the last half-century opens with industry: machines, new processes, and better transport multiplied goods and comforts. Pestilence and famine receded, and time and space shrank for human intercourse. Local ignorance, he adds, began to fade as well.

Huxley, Darwin's bulldog, surveys fifty years of science with confidence in progress and in method. The lecture is short, clear, and Victorian in its optimism. Readers of science history will find it a crisp statement of how the nineteenth century saw its own achievements.
15289-the-truce-of-god-a-tale-of-the-ele:
George Henry Miles's Truce of God, with an introduction by John Reville, sets a tale in the eleventh century, when Gothic temples were new. A Scott motto on ancient deeds, feuds, and towers now holding hares fronts the book. The reader is invited to leave a utilitarian age for a time of faith.

Feuds, forests, chiefs under gray stone, and the Church's truce against private war drive the plot. Miles writes in a romantic, Catholic style, praising an age of faith over an age of experiment. History lovers will find the novel earnest, atmospheric, and full of medieval color.
15337-a-source-book-of-australian-histor:
Gwendolen Swinburne compiled this 1919 source book of Australian history, printed in London, to give students documents rather than mere narrative. Part one covers discovery and exploration: Tasmania, Western Australia, Bass Strait, the Investigator, and crossings of the continent south to north and west to east.

Part two treats general history: first settlement, the Bligh mutiny, wool, transportation, gold, and the founding of colonies. Each extract lets readers hear explorers and officials in their own words. The book serves students and general readers who want Australia's past in primary sources. Teachers will find the documents well chosen for classroom use.
15447-a-history-of-english-romanticism-i:
Henry A. Beers wrote this history of English romanticism in the eighteenth century, opening with a Schiller epigraph on what must die in life to live in song. Beers warns at the start that a rigid definition of romanticism would steal the book's substance. His aim is to let readers examine documents and think, before forming a full notion of the thing.

Eleven chapters trace the movement: the Augustans, the Spenserians, landscape poets, the Miltonic group, the school of Warton, the Gothic revival, Percy and the ballads, Ossian, Chatterton, and the German tributary. The book treats romanticism as a growth in taste, not a sudden revolt. For students of English literature, it remains a clear, old-fashioned guide to how the eighteenth century learned to love the wild, the old, and the strange.
15495-in-a-green-shade-a-country-comment:
Maurice Hewlett published this country commentary in London in 1920, with G. Bell and Sons. Most essays had appeared in periodicals, from the Westminster Gazette and Daily News to the New Statesman, Cornhill, and Fortnightly Review, and all were revised for the book. Hewlett wrote from Broadchalke in January 1920.

Contents range from change and the peasantry, a hermitage in sight, and church and the man, to Bessy Moore, the maids, poetry and the mode, and Polyolbion. Later essays treat harvest moons, Sheridan as maniac, a footnote to Coleridge, and a commentary upon Butler. Hewlett writes as a countryman and a man of letters at once, loving fields, books, and old customs. The volume suits readers who like essays that wander, observe, and remember.
15698-a-review-of-uncle-tom-s-cabin-or-a:
A. Woodward, M.D., published this review of Uncle Tom's Cabin, or an essay on slavery, in Cincinnati in 1853, with Applegate and Company. The preface tells how a still small voice whispered write for two years, in private and public, at home and abroad, while Woodward pleaded incapacity, poverty, and want of time. Disease in autumn 1852 forced him from medical practice, and he began the work at last.

Woodward had planned an essay on African slavery to close a larger volume, after about a hundred pages of preparation. The introduction answers a Northern letter detailing shocking things seen and heard in the South, with severe strictures on domestic slavery. A young lawyer anecdote follows: asked how he could state falsehoods before a court, he answers he was well paid. Woodward writes a pro-slavery Southern reply to Stowe, defending slavery against her novel's charges.
15775-the-rejuvenation-of-aunt-mary:
A comic novel by Anne Warner, first copyrighted in 1904 and issued in a new edition by Little, Brown and Company in 1910. Aunt Mary, a stern old lady, finds her settled life upset by Jack and a tangle of love affairs. Warner, known for Susan Clegg tales, writes light comedy with a sharp ear for talk. Pictures from the stage play join this edition.

Jack falls in love, marries, and faces another man, while Aunt Mary watches, judges, and slowly softens. Chapters trace the day after falling in love, the downfall of hope, and fresh developments at every turn. Warner keeps the tone bright and the dialogue quick. The book delights as a comedy of age and youth: an old lady learns to live again, and young lovers learn to wait.
15808-the-history-of-richard-raynal-soli:
A historical novel by Robert Hugh Benson, written as the supposed diary of a solitary in Henry VIII's England. Richard Raynal, a hermit, speaks plainly to the King in Westminster Hall and is taken for it. Benson, a Catholic writer, builds the tale on old speech and old faith. The book reads as a saint's life told in his own voice.

Richard faces a privy parlour, a second audience, and detention, then temptations that test his vow. A parson disputes the whole matter, and a lieutenant whips the prisoner for his meat. Through it all Richard holds to prayer and truth. The novel endures as a moving portrait of conscience against power, told with rare simplicity and fire.
15931-a-history-of-english-romanticism-i:
A history of English romanticism in the nineteenth century by Henry A. Beers, author of A Suburban Pastoral and The Ways of Yale. Henry Holt and Company issued it in New York in 1918. Beers opens with a romance epigraph: a love dwelling in a northern land, a grey tower in a forest green, leagues of yellow sand, and lily-white deer fleeing the light. The image sets his theme.

Beers traces romance from its roots through Scott, Byron, Shelley, and Keats to later Victorian writers. Medievalism, nature, and the supernatural each get careful chapters. His prose stays clear and scholarly, aimed at students. The book still serves as a sound guide: romanticism, mapped from tower to heath, in one firm volume.
15936-the-sad-shepherd-a-christmas-story:
A Christmas story by Henry Van Dyke, issued by Charles Scribner's Sons in New York in 1911. Van Dyke, a beloved preacher and writer, sets his tale near the Pools of Solomon. The first section is called Darkness. Snow lies smooth as feathers on a dove's breast in the Valley of Gardens.

A sad shepherd walks far above the friendly valley, under crisp stars and a small round moon. Springs overflow on the hillside, and grass stays green even in dead winter. His sorrow and his search for light carry the story to Christmas. The tale charms as a gentle nativity meditation: darkness, a shepherd, and hope born at night.
16016-going-to-maynooth-traits-and-stori:
An Irish tale by William Carleton, Going to Maynooth, part five of Traits and Stories of the Irish Peasantry. Young Denis O'Shaughnessy, son of old Denis, prepares for the priesthood at Maynooth. Old Denis, a great historian and perplexing controversialist, reads Gallagher and Pastorini, and knows Harry the Eighth and Luther's partnership with the devil. His light drab frieze earns him the nickname Walking Pigeon-house.

Denis's tall figure and odd dress open a tale of faith, family, and Irish learning. Carleton writes with humour for the old controversialist and warmth for his son. The road to Maynooth tests both. The tale stands as a fond Irish portrait: a father full of history, a son full of hope, and a church that shaped them both.
1627-the-evil-genius-a-domestic-story:
Wilkie Collins's domestic story opens before the story proper with Miss Westerfield's education and a jury trial, where a foreman of clear head and ready tongue helps decide a case. From there the novel follows a governess, a marriage, and a child caught between parents, with Collins's usual tangle of wills and secrets.

Dedicated to Holman Hunt, the book treats domestic life as a field of moral danger, where an evil genius, in human form, works quietly against a home. The plotting is intricate. It is a late Collins novel, less famous than his masterpieces, but full of his domestic suspense.
1678-an-historical-mystery-the-gondrevil:
Balzac's Historical Mystery, also called the Gondreville Mystery, opens in the autumn of 1803, one of the finest in the early part of the century, with a chapter called Judas. A kidnapping, a trial, and a political conspiracy under Napoleon entangle a family of royalists, a police spy, and a senator's household.

Dedicated to Monsieur de Margone, in memory of Balzac's stay at the Chateau de Sache, the novel blends history with detective work. Its plot turns on documents, disguises, and a long-buried secret. The book is a gripping Balzac mystery, and a vivid picture of France under the Consulate.
1723-cow-country:
Bud is a ranch boy with more ambition than sense, and this western follows him from a trail herd to the day he must prove himself a man. Chapters track his roping, his warnings to older hands, his coin-flip with fate, and the woman he meets when the work turns serious.

Bower writes the cow country from the saddle: horses, ropes, dust, and the small codes by which a crew judges a newcomer. The novel's charm is Bud himself, young and headstrong, learning that courage counts for little without judgment. It reads as a coming-of-age story dressed in chaps and spurs.
1730-michael-brother-of-jerry:
Michael is an Irish terrier whose brother Jerry starred in London's earlier dog story, and his own life runs through training rings, performances, and beatings. The foreword states London's aim plainly: he came to dislike trained-animal shows because curiosity led him behind the glitter to the beatings that made the tricks possible.

Michael's story is told from the dog's side of the bargain — loyalty, hunger, and the defence of his meat against all comers. And it builds into an attack on the whole business of breaking animals for applause. Readers who know The Call of the Wild will recognize London's method, and his anger here is aimed at men, not at beasts.
1845-zuleika-dobson-or-an-oxford-love-st:
Zuleika arrives at Oxford, a music-hall performer, and every undergraduate in the university falls into despair over her. The note to the 1922 edition recalls Beerbohm in Italy when the book first appeared. He was surprised to hear friends speak of Zu-like-a, a name he hardly recognized as his own.

The comedy turns on love as epidemic: young men, told they cannot have Zuleika, choose drowning instead. One hero, troubled that he can swim, walks to the river anyway. Beerbohm writes the satire with perfect manners and a straight face, and the novel remains the classic Oxford fantasy, witty, cruel, and impossible to forget.
1864-hero-tales-from-american-history:
Henry Cabot Lodge and Theodore Roosevelt join forces in this book of hero tales. The tales are chosen to show Americans — in the editors' phrase, nurtured in freedom and well born — doing glorious deeds in public and private life. Mad Anthony Wayne, hard-fighting general of the Revolution, leads the parade, and Gouverneur Morris writes from Paris in August 1792 with Horace on his lips.

The tales run from the Revolution through the Civil War, with each hero given a short, stirring chapter. Written before Roosevelt's presidency, the book is a deliberate work of civic teaching. It reads as a window into how two future statesmen wanted young Americans to remember their past.
1872-the-red-house-mystery:
A country house, a guest found dead, and a host who has vanished. That is the setup Milne offers, with an apology for adding one more detective story to the shelf. Milne then supplies one, set in a country house where a guest is found dead and the host has vanished.

Antony Gillingham, an amateur detective on holiday, teams with Bill Beverley to work the case, and Milne plays fair with clues, timetables, and secret passages. The novel is a model of the golden-age puzzle, witty and civilized, and it shows the Winnie-the-Pooh author in a different, sharper mood.
1888-the-bittermeads-mystery:
E. R. Punshon's Bittermeads Mystery opens with a lone passenger, a fight in the woods, and a coincidence that pulls an ordinary man into a conspiracy. A woman weeps, a woman and a man meet. A discovery in an attic raises the stakes, until Dunn, following Deede Dawson into a dark attic, is appalled by the man's rashness.

Punshon writes the thriller of his day with energy, and the novel moves from woods to house to captivity and capture without pausing for breath. The mystery's pull is its villain, a man whose boldness frightens even his own accomplice, and a hero who must outthink rather than outfight him.
1969-catherine-a-story:
William Makepeace Thackeray's Catherine, a story, retells the life of Catherine Hayes, a notorious murderess of the eighteenth century, as a warning against the sentimental criminal romance. Thackeray writes the tale in a deliberately plain style, refusing to make his heroine glamorous or her crimes romantic.

The novel follows Catherine from servant girl to thief to murderer, with Thackeray pausing to argue that crime fiction should show crime as it is, not as readers wish it to be. The book is an early work, sharp and moralizing, and it shows Thackeray already arguing with the popular fiction of his day.
19771-henrietta-temple-a-love-story:
Benjamin Disraeli wrote Henrietta Temple as a love story, published in 1837. Its background reaches back to Tudor risings under Henry the Eighth. A Lord Tewkesbury in the tale was beheaded after a failed rebellion. His estates were forfeited and his blood attainted. A younger branch of the family turned Protestant and married into Walsingham's line. Old disgrace shadows the lovers' world.

Disraeli, later prime minister, began as a fashionable novelist. Henrietta Temple is his most direct love story. It draws on his own early passion, lightly disguised. Politics stays at the edges; feeling takes the center. Readers meet the romantic before the statesman formed. The novel helps explain Disraeli's lifelong taste for drama.
19925-at-the-sign-of-the-barber-s-pole-s:
William Andrews wrote At the Sign of the Barber's Pole as studies in hirsute history. Old shop signs have mostly been swept away, he notes. The pawnbroker's three brass balls survive, and so does the barber's pole. Round those relics Andrews builds his chapters. Beards, shaving, and barbers' customs across centuries fill them. The tone is antiquarian and amused throughout.

Andrews collected curious history by profession and delight. Hair makes a surprisingly rich thread through social life. Kings, priests, and soldiers all legislated the chin. The barber was once surgeon as well as shaver. Andrews records that double trade in detail. His book is a small classic of trade folklore.
1996-the-divine-comedy-volume-2-purgator:
Dante Alighieri carries his great poem onward in this middle volume, translated by Charles Eliot Norton, as Dante climbs the mountain of Purgatory with Virgil at his side. Souls who delayed repentance wait here, cleansed step by step. Norton, an American scholar of Dante, aimed for a faithful prose version that students could follow canto by canto.

Canto by canto, Dante meets Manfred, Belacqua, Sordello, and the princes in the valley, hearing their stories and learning the order of the afterlife. Norton keeps the sense clear and steady, making this a sound English door into Dante's second realm. Purgatory, the middle realm, suits readers who find Hell too grim and Paradise too remote, since hope grows here.
20105-the-land-we-live-in-the-story-of-o:
Henry Mann published The Land We Live In in 1896, the story of the United States told for general readers. For the Battle of New Orleans, Mann draws on a rare source. Vincent Nolte wrote Fifty Years in Both Hemispheres, printed in Hamburg in 1853. Nolte owned the cotton that Jackson seized before that battle.

Nolte also served as a volunteer in the fight itself. Mann treats him as a strong voice on what truly happened there. The book moves through the nation's growth in a clear, brisk line. Readers get American history with an eye for firsthand tales and odd details.
2018-the-library:
Andrew Lang published this 1881 guide for people who love books and want to build a sound private library. With a chapter by Austin Dobson on modern English illustrated books, it covers old manuscripts, early printing, and the pleasures of collecting. Lang, a Scottish critic and folklorist, wrote for the growing class of readers who bought books for home shelves.

Lang writes about bookstalls, book thieves, bindings, and the care of volumes, mixing practical advice with stories from his own shelves. The result still reads as a friendly handbook for readers who value books as objects as well as texts. His advice still helps collectors, since he treats a library as a living room companion, not a museum piece.
20258-hunter-s-marjory:
Hunter's Marjory is a story for girls, set in woods and country homes. Marjory's dog begins to whine softly as her own mood shifts. Suddenly the whines turn to growls deep in his throat. He shakes free of her arms and stares into the wood beyond.

A dog's alarm in such tales often warns of danger close at hand. Marjory must face whatever waits among the trees with nerve. Girls' stories of the era prize courage, kindness, and quick thought. Readers get a wholesome tale where a girl and her dog stand together.
20297-ten-american-girls-from-history:
Kate Dickinson Sweetser published Ten American Girls from History in 1917. One tale opens with warriors marching in single file through forest settlements. They lead a captive white man to Powhatan for judgment and sentence. Crowds of onlookers hurry in along the wood trails to see him.

That captive is Captain John Smith, in the famed Pocahontas story. Sweetser retells such moments through the eyes of ten real girls. Each girl stands at a turning point in early American history. Young readers get biography, adventure, and patriotism in short, vivid lives.
20357-jerry:
Jean Webster published Jerry in 1907, a light novel of Americans in Italy. Jerry jokes that a letter is indeed a love-letter, since Gustavo asks. In fact, his sister writes that they arrive tonight by train. They will pull out for Riva by the first boat tomorrow.

Lake Garda's Riva gives the tale its sunny Italian stage. Webster, famed for Daddy-Long-Legs, writes with wit and warm economy. Jerry's banter hides a growing love he teases others about freely. Readers get a bright, brief romance in Webster's clear, charming style.
20384-david-lannarck-midget-an-adventure:
David Lannarck, Midget is an adventure story about a circus performer of very small stature. David leaves the show world behind him. He becomes friends with big, rangy Sam Welborn, and the circus midget decides to make his home in the wide open spaces of the West.

The friendship between the tiny performer and the big ranchman drives the tale. David must prove himself in a land built for larger men. The story mixes humour, loyalty, and outdoor adventure, and it gives young readers a hero who wins by grit and good sense rather than size.
20436-sunshine-factory:
Pansy, the pen name of Isabella Alden, wrote Sunshine Factory as a story for children about making cheer at home. Its young characters learn to bring light into dull days. A kind grown-up, Uncle Jack, shows them how play can be made from almost nothing.

Uncle Jack teaches a girl to cut holes in paper for a mask. He shows her how to cut a whole family of paper dolls, and pretty things for Willie. Then he takes a tea tray and rolls a marble round it. The book's lessons ride on such small, warm scenes.
20516-christmas-a-story:
