Zona Gale's Christmas: A Story is set in Old Trail Town, the small town she made famous in her fiction. The town watches a quiet wonder in one woman's garden. There she has a great patch of purple violets blooming out of season.

All Old Trail Town takes account of its neighbors' flowers, of the migratory birds, and of eclipses. So the whole town comes to see the wonder of violets at Christmas. Gale builds her tale of giving around that bloom, in the plain, tender style that won her a wide and loyal readership.
20548-the-secret-of-the-storm-country:
Grace Miller White's The Secret of the Storm Country, published in 1916, continues the story she began in Tess of the Storm Country. The scene is the squatter country along Cayuga Lake in New York. It opens in the lazy warmth of a May afternoon.

That spring follows Orn Skinner's release from Auburn Prison. Three men lounge on the shore in front of Satisfied Longman's shack, with the lake waters at their feet. Old wrongs and a hidden secret hang over the settlement. White's tale mixes romance and hardship among the fisher folk of the lake.
2056-the-life-of-william-carey-shoemaker:
George Smith tells the life of William Carey, the Northamptonshire shoemaker who became a Baptist missionary in India and a pioneer of modern missions. Carey sailed in 1793 and spent forty years in Bengal. Smith, a biographer of missionaries, wrote Carey's life from letters and from Indian records.

Smith draws on the promise of Carey's colleague Joshua Marshman to write the life, and on Carey's own letters. The book follows translation, printing, schools, and reform, and it presents Carey as a working man turned scholar and servant. Carey's work in translation gave India the Bible in Bengali and other tongues, a labour of decades.
20584-you-should-worry-says-john-henry:
George V. Hobart's You Should Worry, Says John Henry, published in 1914, collects the slang monologues of his comic hero John Henry. John Henry is a cheerful New York sport with an opinion on everything. Dance crazes, schemes, and city types all pass through his talk.

We are not a couple of patsies with the pumps, he protests. We can learn enough in two lessons to make good in this boob community. He vows to start a tango craze that will put life and ginger in the whole outfit. Hobart's John Henry books caught the street slang of their decade exactly.
20620-rosemary:
Rosemary is a novel for girls about three sisters in a quiet house, watched closely in the opening scene. Sunlight picks out their hair one by one. One head glows a deep red, and another turns to a fairy web of spun yellow silk. The light searches out a faint copper tint in the dark locks of the third.

The girls sit motionless, their faces turned toward the stairs, as silent as everything else in that silent house. From that held breath, the story opens into the sisters' home life, work, and hopes. Rosemary herself carries the book's warmth, in the domestic series fiction of its day.
20756-rabbi-and-priest-a-story:
Milton Goldsmith published Rabbi and Priest in 1891, a tale of Russian Jewish life. The preface owns that names and dates are not strictly exact. Still, it follows Mendel Winenki from boyhood to old age with care.

Through Mendel, readers see the faith, pain, and pride of a scorned people. A rabbi and a priest stand for two worlds that clash and meet. Goldsmith aimed to win fair thought for Russian Jews in hard times. The book mixes story with plea, a common shape for fiction that hoped to soften real hate in its readers.
20782-triplanetary:
Two patrol ships vanish without a word in Triplanetary, and a captain draws the grim lesson. At three losses, he says, it would get to be a habit. Detector screens and new arms guard his own ship, yet clear ether feels like a trap.

E. E. Smith opens his Lensman saga with space war on a vast scale. Alien foes, bold fleets, and secret plans span ages of hidden strife. Smith's tales set the mold for grand space opera in the pulp age. Readers who like vast stakes and swift action will find this first book a brisk start.
20805-lloyd-george-the-man-and-his-story:
A Welsh countryside boy found no path up, so he moved to Manchester to teach. There his son David was born on January 17, 1863. That boy, Lloyd George, would rise to lead Britain in war and peace.

The Man and His Story, from 1917, traces that climb while it still unfolded. Village roots, law, Parliament, and reform mark the stages of the tale. Lloyd George pushed pensions, insurance, and bold budgets before the war. When this life came out, he had just taken the top post. Readers get a wartime portrait of a leader at his peak.
20848-an-elementary-study-of-chemistry:
A full list of the elements waits in the appendix of An Elementary Study of Chemistry. Stars mark the common ones a pupil must know well. A third of the whole list, the book says, suffices for sound basic grasp.

William McPherson and William Henderson built this text for first courses in the science. Atoms, gases, metals, and acids proceed in clear, tested order. Lab work and plain talk share the pages. The book shows how American colleges taught chemistry then. It stays firm on facts and keen on experiment throughout.
20912-the-daffodil-mystery:
Thornton Lyne lounges at his desk, too sure of his own genius to heed a warning look. Edgar Wallace opens The Daffodil Mystery on that sober grey-eyed gaze. Lyne's wealth and pride set him square in a killer's path.

Wallace, king of the fast thriller, spins murder, blackmail, and London low life here. Daffodils left with the dead give the case its odd name. Short chapters and sharp twists keep the pages turning at speed. The book shows why Wallace ruled crime fiction in his day: no fuss, no pause, just plot wound tight as wire.
20967-a-guide-to-peterborough-cathedral-:
Peada, son of Penda of Mercia, founded the monastery of Medeshamstede in 655, this guide recounts. The Saxon chronicler counts 5,850 winters from the world's birth to that reign. A Guide to Peterborough Cathedral opens its brief history at that deep root.

From Saxon minster to Norman giant, the cathedral's growth fills the guide's pages. Tombs, chapels, carved bosses, and buried queens mark the guided walk. Katharine of Aragon and Mary, Queen of Scots both once lay here. Small guides like this taught Victorian visitors to read a great church stone by stone, saint by saint.
20992-tom-dick-and-harry:
Cold sweat, shaking limbs, and hair on end wake the teller of Tom, Dick and Harry. He sits bolt upright at midnight, chin on knees, in a grip of fright. Talbot Baines Reed opens his school tale on that raw, comic scare.

Three boys whose names became a phrase for any lads at all star here. Reed's school world of dorms, games, and scrapes fills the tale with life. He wrote scores of such tales for The Boy's Own Paper and kin. This one shows his warm, brisk touch, with fear and fun in near equal parts from the first dark page.
20996-an-epoch-in-history:
Four hundred ninety-nine trained teachers sailed from San Francisco to school a new land. P. H. Eley calls that sailing An Epoch in History in his 1904 book. Their task: plant free public schools through the whole Philippine Islands.

The Thomasites, as those teachers were named, reached Manila in 1901 aboard the Thomas. Eley, himself of that band, tells of schools raised from bare rooms. Language, custom, and war's wreckage made the work vast and slow. His book keeps a proud, dated view of America's school crusade in its new Pacific colony.
21070-a-middy-of-the-slave-squadron-a-we:
One of the last books Harry Collingwood wrote, this West African story puts a young midshipman aboard His Majesty's corvette Psyche. First Lieutenant Perry mops his brow in the heat as the ship works against the slave trade. The squadron patrolled the coast to intercept slave ships.

Collingwood was a naval architect in real life, and his handling of sea terms is exact throughout. Orders, skylights, and night watches are rendered by a man who knew ships from the drawing board. The tale gives young readers patrol duty, danger, and discipline on the West African station, told in his late, practised style.
21095-she-and-i-volume-1-a-love-story-a-:
John Conroy Hutcheson is known for sea stories. But this early novel stays in a dull London suburb just after the middle of the nineteenth century. Its hero spots a pretty young woman in church and falls in love at once. His first problem is simply getting an introduction.

He manages that, but the girl's mother looks hard at money: the hero is not well off, while richer suitors are less likeable. Church parties and outings move the courtship along until the wooing seems to succeed. Hutcheson fills chapters with poems and foreign quotes, in a style quite unlike his later nautical books.
21096-she-and-i-volume-2-a-love-story-a-:
Volume Two of John Conroy Hutcheson's love story keeps the same cast as the first. The vicar and Miss Pimpernell, Lady Dasher and her daughters, curate Mawley, and Min Clyde all return. The hero, Lorton, loves Min, the girl with the striking grey eyes. Their affair now deepens toward its outcome.

Hutcheson opens with a dream of Min and quotes Shakespeare on dreams before plunging back into visits, doubts, and jealousy. French, German, Italian, Latin, and even Greek quotes dot the pages, as in Volume One. The two volumes together form a full Victorian courtship, told as a life history.
21102-tom-and-some-other-girls-a-public-:
Rhoda Chester has been taught at home by governesses while her brothers went out into the world. When her German governess leaves to marry, her father decides Rhoda should try boarding school at last. Her mother dislikes the idea, but Rhoda herself is keen to go.

Mrs George de Horne Vaizey sends Rhoda among Tom and the other girls of the title, where she enjoys school and does well. Then an important exam looms, and Rhoda overworks until her brain fails her in the exam hall. The story treats ambition, health, and friendship among schoolgirls of the period with unusual sympathy.
21107-on-board-the-esmeralda-martin-leig:
Martin Leigh loses his naval officer father in Africa and then his mother. He is left to an uncle's household, where Aunt Matilda makes his life miserable. John Conroy Hutcheson sends the orphan to a cheap boarding school whose fine prospectus hides grim reality. Martin bears it for years, helped by his friend Tom.

After a Guy Fawkes prank brings expulsion, the boys run away and stow aboard a small coaster. Its captain beats them worse than their headmaster had. Martin's log then follows him to kindness, to sea aboard the Esmeralda, through fire and wreck off South America, and home again.
21118-etheldreda-the-ready-a-school-stor:
The Saxon family's Christmas holidays start with parties and pleasure in Mrs George de Horne Vaizey's school story, then a shadow falls without warning. Mr Saxon hides in his study looking old and worn. Mrs Saxon smiles a twisted smile and sends for the governess, Miss Bruce, in haste.

The parents slip away to their country house on some worrying errand, leaving the household in suspense. Etheldreda, the ready and capable girl of the title, stands at the centre of the family as trouble unfolds. Vaizey mixes schoolgirl life with a household mystery, keeping the tone warm even when the parents' secret hangs over everything.
21123-english-literature-and-society-in-:
Leslie Stephen delivered these Ford Lectures at Oxford in 1903, though illness kept him from reading them himself. His nephew Herbert Fisher read them aloud in his place, and Stephen published them in London in 1904. The lectures ask how social conditions shaped English writing in the eighteenth century.

Stephen argues that literature grows from the life of its age: its readers, publishers, coffee houses, and class habits. The book is divided into five chapters from the six lecture sections. Written in Stephen's clear, dry style, it became a lasting short study of the age of Pope, Johnson, and the rising reading public.
21210-thomas-davis-selections-from-his-p:
Thomas Davis, the young poet of Ireland's Nation newspaper, died at thirty in 1845, and this selection gathers his prose and poetry in one volume. T. W. Rolleston introduces the book for the Library of Irish Literature series. It opens with Davis's study defending the Irish Parliament of James II.

Articles from The Nation and other papers follow, on history, literature, and politics, then a selection of the poems and ballads. Rolleston aimed to give everything of lasting value Davis wrote in prose, plus his best verse. Davis helped invent a cultural nationalism for Ireland, and this volume shows both the arguments and the songs that carried it.
21233-all-s-well-or-alice-s-victory:
Emily Sarah Holt set this novel in the Weald of Kent in 1556, in the first heat of the Reformation. A local family has turned Protestant in private while still seeming Catholic in public. Their priest hears confessions, learns their secret, and carries it to the Bishop.

One young woman of the family, Alice, is strongest in the new faith. She is taken before the Bishop, jailed on straw with only bread and water, and badly treated. Her prison is improved only because she is to be burned alive. Holt wrote many such tales of Protestant sufferers, and Alice's victory is one of faith under sentence of death.
21254-in-africa-hunting-adventures-in-th:
John T. McCutcheon, cartoonist of the Chicago Tribune, traded his drawing board for a rifle. He took an African hunting trip and published this account in 1910. He calls it merely the record of a delightful trip along the Equator. There the roar of the lion and the crack of the rifle still ruled. His own photographs and cartoons illustrate it.

McCutcheon had wanted since boyhood to hunt lions and elephants, unsure whether he would rather be an Indian fighter. In Africa he lives in what he calls a story-book atmosphere of thrilling adventures. The book is dedicated to adventurous souls who resent the beaten path.
21264-the-four-pools-mystery:
Jean Webster, who later wrote Daddy-Long-Legs, published this mystery with the Century Company in 1908. The narrator arrives at Four-Pools Plantation in Virginia, where a ha'nt is said to walk and a robbery stays unsolved. Terry Patten, a New York newspaper man, is on the story's track from the first chapter.

Cat-Eye Mose creates sensations, a detective is sent for and sent back, and an inquest follows a tragedy in a cave near Luray. False clues pile up before Terry searches the abandoned cabins and finds the bonds. Polly's confession and proposal close a mystery mixed with romance and Virginia local colour.
21411-holborn-and-bloomsbury:
Holborn and Bloomsbury, by Sir Walter Besant and G. E. Mitton, forms one part of the Fascination of London set. The booklet came out in 1903, after Besant's death, from his great survey of the city. Its aim was to save the history held in London's streets.

The authors walk two districts rich in old inns, courts, and homes of writers. Staple Inn, at Holborn Bars, stands at the front as a famed survivor. Street by street, the book ties places to the folk who lived and worked there. Local readers and students of London both find much to keep here.
21431-mary-powell-deborah-s-diary:
Anne Manning joins two linked tales in Mary Powell and Deborah's Diary, reissued by Dent in 1908. Mary Powell was the wife of John Milton, and her home at Forest Hill still drew visits long after. The last scraps of the house were pulled down in 1854.

Manning tells of Milton's spring, the walnut trees, and the church on the hill near Mary's home. The tales wear the dress and speech of the seventeenth century with care. A warm portrait of Mary, drawn from an old praise of a fair milkmaid, opens the book. It suits readers who love quiet, well-kept historical tales.
21465-hurricane-hurry:
Hurricane Hurry is a long historical novel by W. H. G. Kingston, set around the year 1780. The printed book ran to some four hundred and seventy pages of small type. Its hero bears the odd name Hurry, though the text twice slips and calls him Poynder.

Kingston writes ship and storm with his usual fine touch. By the ninth chapter Hurry has fallen for a young American lady. Her father is a colonel serving on the Rebel side in the war. Love and war thus pull the hero in two ways at once. Sea fights, divided loyalties, and family secrets fill the tale.
21623-usury:
Calvin Elliott attacks interest on money in Usury, a scriptural, ethical, and economic view, copyrighted in 1902. The Anti-Usury League of Millersburg, Ohio, published the book. Elliott begs readers to follow his argument in its set order, as it grew in his own mind.

Chapters move from a definition of usury to the law of Moses. David and Solomon, Jeremiah and Ezekiel, and Nehemiah's reform come in turn. The teachings of the Master and the parables of the talents and pounds get close reading. Elliott builds a full biblical case against lending at interest, step by step.
21649-a-cluster-of-grapes-a-book-of-twen:
Galloway Kyle gathers new verse in A Cluster of Grapes, a book of twentieth-century poetry issued in 1914. His title comes from Sidney's praise of poetry, a cluster given at a vineyard's gate. Kyle refuses to sort his poets into schools or isms.

No group, he insists, is set above another in the gathering. The aim is a taste that makes the reader long to pass further. Poems stand as examples of the present century's art, each under its own author's rights. The slim book serves as a period tasting of British verse on the edge of the Great War.
21663-aunt-mary:
Mrs Perring, who wrote The Story of a Mouse, tells a children's tale in Aunt Mary, issued in 1881. A pretty suburban villa opens the tale, with new neighbours to judge. Mr Maitland and his two sweet children promise pleasant society for the street.

Routledge of London and New York published the book, with a picture of Aunt Mary at the front. Perring's tales of cats, castles, and cottages had already won young readers. Kindness, home manners, and small trials shape the story's world. The book is a fair sample of the gentle, moral tale Victorian children were given to read at home.
21685-the-cockatoo-s-story:
Mrs George Cupples lets a white cockatoo tell his own tale in The Cockatoo's Story, issued in 1881. The bird owns he is ashamed of himself and brought his troubles on his own head. Twelve pictures, from a greedy dog onward, fill the book.

Mrs Polly, a small gray parrot across the room, walks her perch fast and ruffles her feathers. She calls the cockatoo sulky and ungrateful, and offers to peck him well. The boy who owns them, she insists, means only kindness. Chat between caged birds carries a gentle lesson for young readers, in Cupples's known style.
21687-the-youngest-girl-in-the-fifth-a-s:
Angela Brazil promotes Gwen in The Youngest Girl in the Fifth, a school story drawn by Stanley Davis. Gwen protests she has done nothing, under looks fit for a criminal and a martyr. Miss Roscoe's word has moved her up a form, youngest in the Fifth.

Chapters promise a false step, trouble in the Fifth, and a casting vote. Gwen keeps Christmas, turns henwife, meets a storm, and learns first aid. A gymkhana, a tennis tournament, and the Senior Oxford exams crown the year. Gwen to the rescue is the last chapter's promise, in Brazil's bright, loyal school world.
21748-black-ivory:
Black ivory was the traders' grim name for enslaved people, and this Ballantyne novel confronts the East African slave trade head-on. A wreck casts two heroes ashore on the east coast of Africa. There, Arab and Portuguese traders still run their trade despite British patrol ships. The castaways meet a slaver almost where they land.

Rescued by a warship that takes a slaver's dhow, they reach Zanzibar and push inland with fresh funds. What they find in the interior fills most of the book. Ballantyne meant the tale to open young eyes to a trade still alive in his day. It is one of his most earnest books, adventure carrying a real charge of outrage.
21751-the-middy-and-the-moors-an-algerin:
Piracy and slavery on the North African coast drive this Algerine tale by R. M. Ballantyne. A middy, a young naval officer in training, falls into the hands of Moorish captors in the world of Algiers. Ballantyne researched Algiers and deep-sea diving for the book, as the notes to this edition record. The Barbary coast was famed in his day for corsairs and Christian captives.

The tale follows the young sailor through capture, hardship, and the strange life of the city that holds him. Escape and rescue hang over every chapter. Ballantyne writes it as a boy's adventure with a serious core. It asks what slavery meant in a foreign land, and what courage freedom took.
21891-the-brand-of-silence-a-detective-s:
Fog in New York harbor opens The Brand of Silence, a 1919 detective story by Harrington Strong, issued by Street and Smith's Chelsea House. The tramp steamer Manatee wallows in from a three-day fight with the ocean, rusty and lurching like a drunk. Aboard her come a girl, some discourtesies, and the first threads of the mystery. A man called Murk stands near the center of it.

Chapters promise battered keys, liars, a moment of violence, and a startling story before the truth comes out. Strong writes in the pulp manner: short chapters, sharp turns, and a campaign planned like a battle. Kate Gilbert's part and a trip up the river deepen the plot. It is a brisk period mystery, built to be read at one sitting.
21913-the-talking-leaves-an-indian-story:
Two girls on a mountain watch a crowd of men stoop and hunt in the grass in William O. Stoddard's The Talking Leaves, an Indian story of 1882. Rita leans over her pony's neck, her long hair falling, while Ni-ha-be sits still in her silver-mounted saddle. The air is so clear among the snow-capped ranges that far things seem close. The men below have found something in the grass, and hunt for more.

Talking leaves is the girls' world name for written pages, and paper drives the mystery. Stoddard wrote many tales of the frontier for young readers. His West mixes scouts, native peoples, and lost parties in bright mountain light. The two heroines, alike in size and unlike in all else, carry the tale's wonder.
21944-the-pleasant-street-partnership-a-:
A shop run as a neighborhood partnership anchors Mary F. Leonard's The Pleasant Street Partnership, a story published in 1903. The Terrace where the tale sits is rather far downtown, with the busy city closing in on commonplace houses, schools, and noisy car lines. A wave of improvement starts the chapters. Chapters follow the naming of the shop, an alien arrival, and Miss Wilbur's place in the scheme.

Leonard writes of loyalty, spools of twist, and the adventures of a birthday cake with a neighbor's eye. Charlotte, to whom the book is offered, presides over its affections. Frank T. Merrill drew the small boy surveying the partners with great composure. It is a cozy American neighborhood story, where trade and friendship share one counter.
21953-aurelian-or-rome-in-the-third-cent:
Rome under the Emperor Aurelian is rebuilt in letters in William Ware's Aurelian, a historical novel first issued in 1838. The tale is told as letters of Lucius M. Piso from Rome to Fausta, daughter of Gracchus, at Palmyra. It follows Ware's Zenobia, and was first named Probus before foreign editions settled on the better title. This fifth edition of 1874 gathers both volumes in one.

Zenobia's Palmyra and Aurelian's campaigns stand behind the letters. Ware, a Unitarian minister, loved the early Church's world and stocked his fiction with its debates. Pagan Rome and rising Christianity meet in his pages. The novel was among the earliest American works of Roman historical fiction, and readers abroad reprinted it for decades.
21964-the-short-story:
Nine master tales teach the short story form in this 1916 school anthology edited by W. Patterson Atkinson of Lincoln High School, Jersey City. Atkinson opens with a history: mankind has always loved tales, from the storyteller at the cave mouth onward. His contents run from Irving's Rip Van Winkle through Poe's Gold Bug and Purloined Letter to Hawthorne's Birthmark. Bret Harte's Outcasts of Poker Flat and Stevenson's Markheim follow.

Kipling's Wee Willie Winkie closes the set, with notes and a bibliography behind it. Portraits of the authors face their tales. Atkinson defines the form, traces its growth, and sorts its kinds before letting the masters speak. Generations of American schoolchildren met the short story here first, in a book built to be taught from and loved.
21969-the-outcry:
Old pictures in a great house stir modern greed in Henry James's last completed novel, The Outcry, published in 1911. Banks the servant reports that no stranger has yet arrived at Dedborough Place. Lady Sandgate crosses the hall, a folded telegram pink in her hand, to meet Lord John. Around them the house breathes two hushed centuries of stored treasure: portraits, cabinets, and tapestries of high distinction.

The outcry of the title is the public noise raised when national treasures are sold to foreign buyers. James turns an art sale into a comedy of manners and morals. Love and money tug at the same canvas. Written first as a play, the novel moves in scenes of brilliant talk. It is late James at his most theatrical.
22002-a-simple-story:
Elizabeth Inchbald wrote A Simple Story, first printed in 1791 and reprinted many times after. Inchbald had spent thirteen years on the stage despite a speech impediment. In her preface she admits the book was written through weariness, not inspiration. The story centres on Miss Milner, a lively young ward, and her grave guardian Dorriforth.

Miss Milner falls in love with the man meant to guide and correct her. Pride, temper, and rash acts wreck what might have been a happy match. Years later the tale turns to her daughter, who must face a cold house and a bitter father. Readers still value the book for its sharp scenes and its honest picture of feeling ruled by pride.
22057-kid-wolf-of-texas-a-western-story:
Ward M. Stevens published Kid Wolf of Texas, a western story, in 1930. His hero rides into view whistling a Texas tune. Kid Wolf is a lean young rider in fringed buckskin touched with bright Southwest colours. His California stock saddle is decorated with silver conchas, and he sits his horse like part of the animal.

Stevens wrote for the cheap western trade, where a hero's look told readers what to expect. Fast riding, gunplay, and a code of honour drive such tales. Kid Wolf's adventures belong to the pulp years, when westerns filled newsstands every week. The book is a plain sample of that hard-riding popular fiction.
22064-tess-of-the-storm-country:
Grace Miller White published Tess of the Storm Country in 1909, and it became her best-known novel. Tessibel Skinner is a squatter's daughter living by Cayuga Lake near Ithaca. The squatter law let her people keep land once they raised a hut on it. But the authorities kept tightening the game laws until the fishermen dared only draw their nets by night, though the fish were their food.

Tess fights for her father, her baby charge, and her people's right to live. A rich man's son and a young minister cross her rough world. White's melodrama was filmed again and again, once with Mary Pickford. It still defines the storm-country squatters for most readers.
22173-the-grell-mystery:
Frank Froest, a former Scotland Yard superintendent, wrote The Grell Mystery in 1913. Froest knew police work from the inside, and his fiction shows it. Robert Grell, the victim at the story's centre, was a daring explorer famous on two continents. His friend Fairfield, a writer on travel and peoples, matches him in fame.

Grell's murder sets detectives hunting through London clubs and beyond. Froest builds his case from clues, timetables, and patient inquiry rather than genius flashes. The book appeared just before the Great War, in detective fiction's golden dawn. It remains a solid specimen of the police novel written by a real policeman.
22179-old-rail-fence-corners-the-a-b-c-s:
Old Rail Fence Corners calls itself the A.B.C.'s of Minnesota history. Lucy Leavenworth Wilder Morris started the project, gathering tales from the state's old settlers. A book committee of pioneer women edited and issued it, copyrighted in 1914. The incidents are advertised as authentic, gleaned from the old settlers themselves.

Old-timers argue in its pages over roads, claims, Indians, and winters. One growls that anyone who travelled the old mud roads would be glad they are gone. Such talk is the book's treasure: first-hand memory of territorial Minnesota. Committees like this one saved pioneer recollection across America before the witnesses died.
22219-the-flight-of-pony-baker-a-boy-s-t:
William Dean Howells, the dean of American letters, wrote The Flight of Pony Baker as a boy's town story. It follows his memoir A Boy's Town, drawn from his Ohio childhood. Pony Baker is a small boy in a river town who dreams of running away. All the fellows gather round to ask what he is going to do now.

Howells turns the runaway plot into gentle comedy about boyhood fears and glories. The town, its gangs, its circuses, and its terrors are drawn from real memory. Nothing very terrible happens, and that is the point. Few American writers wrote about boys with Howells's honesty, and this small book shows why his town stories were loved.
22225-mary-louise-in-the-country:
Edith Van Dyne, the pen name behind the Aunt Jane's Nieces books, wrote Mary Louise in the Country in 1916. Van Dyne was in fact L. Frank Baum, the creator of Oz, writing girls' books under another name. Mary Louise arrives at a country station that disappoints her. After a sumptuous train, she finds only a shed-like structure, open on all sides, serving as the station house.

The Kenton place, the folks across the river, and village quarrels fill her summer. Mary Louise becomes a peacemaker, as one chapter title admits. A red-headed mystery and calls for help enliven the quiet. The book shows Baum's gift for girls' series fiction in a realistic, small-town key.
22243-dwell-deep-or-hilda-thorn-s-life-s:
Dwell Deep; or, Hilda Thorn's Life Story is a religious novel told in the first person. Hilda grows up in an English boarding school until she is nineteen. Then she goes to an old cousin in London. For three years she lives a quiet, uneventful life in a dull square, seeing little society beyond elderly ladies and a few clergymen.

From that narrow world the novel draws its drama of faith and feeling. Hesba Stretton, who wrote under initials and moved millions with Jessica's First Prayer, shaped such tales of tested piety. Hilda's inner life, not incident, carries the book. It is a fair specimen of the evangelical novel at its most inward and domestic.
2231-all-roads-lead-to-calvary:
Jerome K. Jerome's 1919 novel opens with a young woman journalist stepping into an old London church to gather copy on its history. Joan, ambitious and modern, finds herself drawn from newspaper work into deeper questions of faith, duty, and the lives of women around her. London's churches, streets, and drawing rooms frame her search.

The book follows Joan as work, friendship, and belief pull her in new directions, and as the war's shadow touches everyone she knows. Jerome writes with warmth and plain good sense about a woman making her own way. Readers get a thoughtful, humane story of a modern heroine finding what she truly stands for.
22310-in-the-border-country:
In the Border Country was published in 1908, with no author named in the record. The passage preserved in the catalog is a tense, pleading talk between two people. One voice begs the other not to risk something grave.

The speaker gives his word that her present state of mind makes the risk wrong. Yet he insists she could change both her mind and her conditions. If she would only say she could, he would risk anything himself. That push and pull gives the work its emotional charge. Readers meet a story built on persuasion, doubt, and a choice that will not wait.
22408-chatterbox-stories-of-natural-hist:
Chatterbox Stories of Natural History packs short animal tales into one children's volume. Its contents promise a singular habit of the woodcock first. The skylark, the story of a seal, and the king of the mountains follow.

Cunning wood-pigeons get a story of their own here. Rats carrying eggs up stairs earn another curious entry. A heron attacked by a hawk makes a third dramatic scene. A battle between a fox and a swan closes the list shown. Each tale takes one striking animal act as its hook. Young readers learned natural history as a string of wonders, not as dry classroom facts.
22463-chivalry:
James Branch Cabell wrote Chivalry, a book of tales published in 1909. Cabell set his stories in a bleak, florid age of knights. His preface asks readers to interpret his makeshift widely.

In that age, he says, chivalry named a world-wide code. It was rarely a matter of personal trait alone. All estimable people lived and died by that code's terms. Cabell's tales play within those rules with sly, elegant irony. He later built a famous cycle around such medieval romance. These early stories already show his polished, teasing style. Readers get knights, ladies, and honor handled by a writer who loved and mocked them together.
22571-frank-merriwell-s-bravery:
Frank Merriwell's Bravery, issued by Street and Smith in 1903, continues Frank's western tour. Readers of former books know Frank does not travel alone. Professor Scotch, his guardian, tours with him on this trip.

Barney Mulloy, Frank's old schoolmate from Fardale, also travels along. The professor and Barney did not want to stop at Oklahoma. They went on ahead, leaving Frank to catch up later. Left behind, Frank faces the adventure that tests his bravery alone. Merriwell stories made a formula of pluck, sportsmanship, and rescue. This volume gives that formula a western stage and separations. Boys read Frank as the model of what they should be.
22790-the-accomplisht-cook-or-the-art-my:
Robert May wrote The Accomplisht Cook, or The Art and Mystery of Cookery, the great English cookbook of the seventeenth century, first published in 1660. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. May, trained in France and servant to noble households, set down the cookery of the age in some five hundred recipes.

One section promises all manner of carbonadoes of flesh or fowl. It adds all manner of fried meats, collops, and eggs. It ends with the finest way of making pancakes, fritters, and tansies. Banquets, pies, and preserved fruits fill the rest. May writes for professionals, assuming a kitchen brigade and a lord's table. Food historians treat the book as the fullest record of English cooking before the Civil War's world vanished.
22794-the-shellback-s-progress-in-the-ni:
Thomas Runciman wrote The Shellback's Progress in the Nineteenth Century, a sailor's account of life in the merchant sailing fleet as steam closed in. The catalog record gives no year. A shellback is an old sailor, one who has crossed the line, and Runciman writes as one, watching his world of canvas give way.

The sample shows the old order at anchor. A large fleet waits at anchor: sailing brigs, barques, and schooners, all hoping for a favorable wind and spring tides. Only then can they put to sea without risking their keels on the Bar. The vessels had waited loaded for several weeks. Many were bound to the Baltic. Such waits governed a shellback's life. The book records the seaman's nineteenth century from the deck up, in the years when sail still earned its keep.
22836-town-versus-country:
William's steadiness anchors Town Versus Country, a village tale by Mary Russell Mitford. Talk in the excerpt praises the young man warmly. Young men all take their foolish turns, one speaker allows. William, though, shows unusual steadiness for his years. His master thinks so well of him that he now serves as foreman in the business.

Mitford sets that country-bred character against the pull and glitter of town life. Work, courtship, and family pride all test where a young man belongs. Her method is patient and close, built from talk at cottage doors and in workshops. The story asks an old question in a local accent. Which life makes the better man, the town's or the village's? Mitford lets her people answer.
22906-a-war-time-wooing-a-story:
Captain Charles King's A War-Time Wooing, published in 1888, opens on news of victory. Authentic word has come at last. Word arrives that Lee has abandoned the field and withdrawn beyond the Potomac. Union supporters everywhere exhale at last. Newsboys yell through crowded streets while evening trains are besieged by buyers hungry for lists of the killed and wounded.

Against that backdrop of war's end, King builds a courtship. He wrote from inside the army world he depicts, and his officers and their families carry conviction. Wooing under wartime rules, with honor and absence pressing on both sides, gives the romance its shape. Readers get a period love story framed by the Civil War's closing campaigns.
22994-the-frontier-in-american-history:
Frederick Jackson Turner builds The Frontier in American History, published in 1920, around a census bulletin. The Census of 1890 declared that the unsettled area had been so broken into by isolated settlement that a frontier line could hardly be said to exist. From those dry words Turner drew his famous thesis on American development.

The essays gathered here argue that the frontier shaped American democracy, energy, and individualism. Land at the edge, he held, remade Europeans into Americans. Later historians have argued with Turner for a century, and the argument itself proves the book's force. Anyone studying how Americans explain themselves must pass through these pages. The prose is measured, the claim enormous, the influence unmatched.
23186-the-handbook-to-english-heraldry:
The Handbook to English Heraldry is a guide to coats of arms and the rules behind them. In the editor's notes, the editor admits to changing unclear wording so the true, intended meaning stands out. Points that rest on deduction, and so on opinion, are treated with more care.

On those points, the book keeps Mr. Boutell's own views, even where the editor does not fully share them. That candour tells readers what kind of handbook this is: a working reference that sorts firm rules of heraldry from one expert's judgement, and says plainly which is which.
23187-mistress-margery:
Mistress Margery is a work of historical fiction set at Lovell Tower in the spring of 1395. Sunlight falls on the tower's battlements and window frames. Inside, though it is barely seven in the morning, the house is already full of bustle and noise.

Dame Lovell oversees her serving women as they get dinner ready. The early hour and the scale of the work show a great household run on strict routine. Readers are placed inside medieval domestic life, where a lady's standing rests on order, food, and the smooth running of her hall.
2398-the-renaissance-studies-in-art-and-:
Walter Pater's Renaissance: Studies in Art and Poetry changed how English readers saw the Italian Renaissance, treating Botticelli, Leonardo, and Michelangelo as figures of sensuous, fleeting beauty. Pater's essays argue for art experienced intensely, in the moment, and his famous conclusion urges readers to burn with a hard, gemlike flame. The prose itself is the argument.

The book influenced Wilde, the aesthetes, and generations of critics, for better and worse. Its subjectivity shocked Victorian moralists. Students of art and literature still read Pater for his style and his daring. Pater's conclusion was condemned by Oxford moralists and cut from later editions.
2516-redgauntlet-a-tale-of-the-eighteent:
Walter Scott sets this tale in Scotland in the years after the Jacobite rising of 1745, when loyalty to the exiled Stuarts still burned among Highland families. Two young friends, Darsie Latimer and Alan Fairford, are pulled apart when Darsie is seized by his uncle, Hugh Redgauntlet, a fierce Jacobite plotting a fresh rising.

The novel follows their efforts to escape, reunite, and untangle a family past tied to the old cause. Scott mixes courtroom wit, border chases, and scenes of Highland pride with a sober view of a lost cause. Readers get both a fast adventure and a portrait of Scotland caught between loyalty to a fallen prince and life under a new order.
260-an-introduction-to-the-study-of-robe:
Hiram Corson, professor of English at Cornell, wrote this guide for readers daunted by Browning. An Introduction to the Study of Robert Browning's Poetry, third edition from 1886 in a 1910 printing, opens with a map of Greek terms for the poems' classical allusions. Corson calls Browning the subtlest assertor of the soul in song.

Chapters explain Browning's dramatic monologues, his obscurity, and his faith in human growth. Corson pairs close reading with biography and philosophy. The guide suits students meeting Pippa Passes or Rabbi Ben Ezra. It remains a patient companion to a hard poet.
2615-discourses-on-satire-and-on-epic-po:
John Dryden wrote these two discourses late in life, and the 1888 Cassell edition presents them as his maturer thought, beyond even his famous Essay of Dramatic Poesy. Dryden weighs what satire can do, how it bites without mere abuse, and what an epic poem demands of its hero and its age.

He draws on Horace, Juvenal, Virgil, and Homer, judging ancients and moderns with a critic's confidence. The prose is clear, learned, and full of good sense about craft. The discourses still serve as an introduction to Dryden the critic, and to the rules that shaped Augustan verse.
2695-jeff-briggs-s-love-story:
Bret Harte sets this love story at Eldridge's Crossing, where rain and wind batter stately pines and hysterical willows alike. Jeff Briggs, a rough camp man, falls for a woman far above his station, and his courtship must survive gossip, rivals, and his own pride.

Harte writes the tumult of weather as a mirror of feeling, and the comedy of camp manners with warmth. Jeff's honesty wins out over polish, in the author's favorite moral. The story charms as a frontier romance, short, funny, and tender at its core. Rain, wind, and camp gossip frame the courtship.
2728-hunter-quatermain-s-story:
H. Rider Haggard frames this hunting story as a tale heard at Sir Henry Curtis's hospitable Yorkshire house. Sir Henry, as everybody knows, is one of the most hospitable men on earth, and over his hospitality the narrator hears the story he now transcribes.

Hunter Quatermain's tale runs through African bush, dangerous game, and narrow escapes, told in the hunter's plain voice. Haggard writes with the authority of a man who loved the veld. The story charms as a fireside yarn, short, vivid, and full of the Africa of his imagination.
2736-the-champdoce-mystery:
Emile Gaboriau wrote this mystery as a sequel to Caught in the Net, opening with a ducal monomaniac. A traveler from Poitiers to London takes the stage coach to Saumur, and the polite clerk warns him to take his seat punctually, a small detail that soon matters.

The Champdoce family, its madness, its marriages, and its crimes tangle across France, with detectives picking up the thread. Gaboriau, a father of the detective novel, writes with method and suspense. The book rewards readers who like a long, knotty plot unwound with patience.
2764-the-mahatma-and-the-hare-a-dream-st:
H. Rider Haggard wrote this dream story of a mahatma and a hare, opening with a good hare found in the field. Hounds press her, the hunt arrives at a cliff edge, and the hare's fate becomes a parable of life, death, and mercy.

The great white road, the shooting, the coursing, and the coming of the red faced man carry the dream through hunting fields to a judgment beyond them. Haggard writes with mystical earnestness, pleading for kindness to hunted things. The story stands as his most unusual plea, short, strange, and moving.
2799-eben-holden-a-tale-of-the-north-cou:
Irving Bacheller wrote this tale of the north country, opening with hardy wood choppers coming west out of Vermont early in the last century. They founded homes in the Adirondack wilderness, clearing rough acres with axe and charcoal pit.

Eben Holden, a kind, shrewd hired man, guides a boy through years of toil in a rigorous climate, toward learning and manhood. Bacheller writes with warmth about frontier endurance and neighborly grace. The novel became a beloved American bestseller, and a portrait of a vanishing pioneer age. Bacheller's Vermont woods smell of pine and charcoal smoke.
286-laddie-a-true-blue-story:
Little Sister tells the story of her brother Laddie, who loved and asked no questions. Gene Stratton-Porter's Laddie, a true blue story, follows the Stanton family through school days, weddings, and a mystery at the Pryor house. The Princess from the house of mystery draws Laddie on.

Chapters cover an angel boy, a wedding gown, Shropshire sheep, and keeping Christmas the family way. Mr. and Mrs. Stanton face life shoulder to shoulder, and the Pryor mystery resolves in faith. Stratton-Porter dedicates the book to her brother. It remains a warm family classic.
2930-criticisms-on-the-origin-of-species:
Thomas Henry Huxley published these criticisms of the Origin of Species in the Natural History Review in 1864, reviewing foreign commentaries on Darwin's work. He notes that Sir Charles Lyell had drawn a parallel between the development of species and that of languages. The German philologist Schleicher had independently published a pamphlet supporting similar views. The notice in the Reader for February 27 praised Schleicher's argument.

Huxley weighs genetic classification against other kinds, asking whether a genetic relation might underlie even the classification of minerals. The inorganic world, he notes, has had its metamorphoses and a long development out of a nebular blast. The essay shows Victorian science debating Darwin across national and disciplinary lines.
3147-a-summer-in-a-canyon-a-california-s:
Kate Douglas Wiggin sends a party into a California canyon for the summer in this 1914 story. Preparation and departure lead to the journey itself, then to life in the canyon, where the heir apparent loses himself. Rhyme and reason, a forest of Arden, and good news follow, with Queen Elsie paying a visit to the court.

The book is a holiday tale, full of children, talk, and outdoor play. Wiggin, beloved for Rebecca of Sunnybrook Farm, writes the canyon as a place where young people invent their own kingdom. Readers get sunshine, scrapes, and a gentle moral: a summer lived outdoors teaches more than a summer spent indoors.
3180-a-double-barrelled-detective-story:
Mark Twain sets this detective tale in Virginia in 1880. It opens with a wedding joining a good-looking young man short of money to a wealthy young woman. Instant love rushes them into a quick marriage that the girl's widowed father fiercely opposes. Jacob Fuller, the bridegroom, is twenty-six, from an old but unconsidered family that had come down in the world.

From that domestic quarrel Twain builds a story of revenge and detection, turning the methods of the famous fictional detectives inside out. Clues are followed with great solemnity to absurd ends. Twain's late, darker comedy is on full show: a solemn inquiry collapsing under its own machinery.
3230-the-counterpane-fairy:
Katharine Pyle wrote and illustrated this children's fantasy, published by Dutton in New York in 1898. The contents promise a princess of the golden castle, owls and a gamblesome elf, and two children named Starlein and Silverling. A magic circus, the edge of the polar sea, and a ruby ring follow, with rainbow children and Harriett's dream.

Down the rat-hole and the counterpane fairy herself close the journey. The book is a bedtime voyage: a sick child's quilt becomes a landscape, and each square opens a new wonder. Pyle's pictures match her prose, gentle and fanciful. Young readers get a classic of the nursery fantasy kind, where the smallest room can hold a whole world.
3243-glengarry-school-days-a-story-of-ea:
Ralph Connor returns to Glengarry County in this story of early school days. A spelling match opens the book, followed by the deepole, the examination, and the new master. A crisis, one that ruleth well his own house, and Foxy with his partner follow, leading to Hughie's emancipation and a bear hunt.

John Craven's method, a downfall, and rounds of fighting close the schoolroom drama. Connor, who knew Glengarry's Scottish settlers well, writes their children with affection and without sentimentality. Learning, loyalty, and fists decide the schoolhouse world, where the settlement's center was a classroom.
3310-a-forgotten-empire-vijayanagar-a-co:
Robert Sewell recovers a lost Hindu empire in this contribution to the history of India. Vijayanagar, the city of victory on the Tungabhadra, ruled much of southern India for over two centuries, then fell to ruin. Sewell gathers its chronicles, inscriptions, and travelers' tales into a single narrative, giving a forgotten power back its story.

The book follows kings, temples, and wars, with Portuguese visitors as witnesses to the capital's splendor. Its title states its claim: an empire forgotten by Europe, but central to India's past. Readers interested in Indian history beyond the Mughals will find here a whole world: a Hindu state at its height, told from its own records and from strangers' eyes.
3419-rebecca-mary:
Annie Hamilton Donnell writes a gentle story for children about a small girl named Rebecca Mary. The book is built from short episodes with names such as The Dream, The Cookbook Diary, and The Bereavement, each following Rebecca Mary through a day or a small crisis. In one scene she counts her stitches aloud, waiting with grave care for the hundred and first.

The charm lies in the child's point of view. A doll, a cookbook, a lost article, or a family sorrow all matter greatly at her scale, and Donnell treats them with respect rather than mockery. Young readers will recognize the mix of pride, worry, and wonder in growing up, while older readers will enjoy a quiet, old fashioned tale of home life.
3635-mother-a-story:
Kathleen Norris writes a novel about family life centered on a schoolteacher named Margaret. The book opens at the end of a school week. Little girls downstairs in the playroom plan holidays over cold lunches, while Margaret looks out at gray rain and feels sick of it all. She has spent her days among small girls who sulk, cry over lost lunch baskets, and catch colds with no handkerchiefs.

Norris follows Margaret from the schoolroom into home life, where mothers, daughters, and daily work shape the story. The novel praises the patience and love that hold a family together through small trials. Readers who enjoy early twentieth century domestic fiction will find a gentle, warm tale of a woman learning what motherhood means.
3659-the-rosary:
Florence Barclay writes a romance centered on a rosary and the people it passes among. The chapters open with the entrance of a duchess, introduce the Honourable Jane, and follow a surprise packet, Jane's volunteering, confidences, and the lifting of a veil. Garth finds his rosary, then added pearls, then a cross, while a house party, a doctor's prescription, and a revelation move the plot.

Barclay, famous for sentimental romance, writes about love, faith, and sacrifice in an English country house world. The rosary beads become a symbol of prayer and of a promise kept. The novel suits readers who enjoy early twentieth century romance with a religious thread and a tender, old fashioned heroine.
3784-the-sheridan-road-mystery:
Paul and Mabel Thorne set this Chicago mystery on a still October night. Policeman Murphy, on his two o'clock round, finds Sheridan Road deserted save for a belated taxi's red tail light. A shot soon draws Detective Sergeant Morgan into a case that runs through an apartment across the hall, a cable from London, a stolen suitcase, and a last letter. The contents list promises a trail that grows clearer, then darker, with a kidnapping and a closed country house.

Morgan and his men pick over peculiar facts in the Atwood apartment while Mr Marsh's part in the affair shifts under their eyes. The Thornes keep the plot moving at a brisk clip, with a night call and a fallen pine among the later turns. Readers who like fair play detective tales will find a tidy puzzle with Chicago streets as its stage.
4060-the-renaissance-studies-in-art-and-:
Walter Pater's Renaissance studies follow the soul's steps from love of a physical object to love of unseen beauty. His thoughts, however little their positive value, connect to springs of deep and passionate feeling beneath them, and his analogies lift the reader upward.

Essays on Botticelli, Leonardo, Michelangelo, and others made Pater famous for the claim that art should be judged by the quality of its moments. The prose glows with a vehemence that recalls poetry itself. Readers who like art history written as literature will find a landmark book of Victorian criticism.
4207-aesthetic-poetry:
An essay on aesthetic poetry weighs songs of morning and dawn, where terrors known in all their forms give way to strange tenderness. The crown of one English poet's book is an appreciation of dawn, praying for one prayer between closed lips and one thought among the stars.

Summer night wanes, morning light slips faint and gray between aspen leaves and cloud bars waiting patiently. The essay favors beauty, mood, and the music of verse over moral argument. Readers who enjoy criticism of poetry will find a short, lyrical study of dawn as a muse.
4231-the-malady-of-the-century:
A novel of Berlin in 1871, The Malady of the Century, opens on a hot summer day, June 16. Sun streams down on Unter den Linden, and life gathers in a restless throng. The bustle differs from eleven months before, with joyful excitement in the air, in children's laughter and girls' talk.

Beneath the celebration, the novel probes a generation's spiritual sickness, the malady that gives the book its name. Set just after the Franco-Prussian War, it follows young Berliners seeking meaning after victory. Readers who enjoy European novels of ideas will find a serious, atmospheric work.
4249-in-the-sweet-dry-and-dry:
Christopher Morley and Bart Haley wrote this comic novel in Philadelphia in 1919, on the eve of Prohibition, and dedicated it to G. K. Chesterton. Its chapters promise a mystery of the unexpected julep, a house on Caraway Street, gooseberry bombs, the treachery of Miss Chuff, and a band of pilgrims calling themselves the Decanterbury Pilgrims.

The foreword warns readers not to draw conclusions about the authors' own habits from the story, which follows drinkers, schemers, and reformers through an election and a mock war over alcohol. It is a light satire of the dry age, written while the law was still about to arrive, and it keeps its jokes close to the politics of the moment.
4326-the-expansion-of-europe-the-culmina:
Ramsay Muir, professor of modern history at the University of Manchester, wrote this survey of Europe's expansion. He treats that expansion as the culmination of modern history. In his preface he states a twofold purpose. He wants to explain how world politics and imperial rivalries now touch every life.

He also wants to give general readers a brief, clear summary of how that came about. Muir traces the greater states of western civilization as they spread trade, settlement, and empire across the globe. The second edition keeps the argument compact and readable. It serves as an introduction to imperial history, written before the First World War reshaped those rivalries.
4383-maria-chapdelaine-a-tale-of-the-lak:
Louis Hemon wrote this tale of the Lake Saint John country in Quebec, translated by W. H. Blake and published in New York in 1921. Its contents run from Peribonka and home in the clearing through Francois passing by, wild land, and the vows, to the stuff of dreams and a meager reaping. Maria Chapdelaine stands at the center.

The novel follows a farm family clearing land at the edge of the forest, through seasons, courtships, and losses. Hemon's prose is plain and unsentimental, and Maria's choice between suitors becomes a choice about the land itself. The book became a classic of French Canada, and a portrait of a people holding to soil and faith.
4395-in-wicklow-and-west-kerry:
John M. Synge gathered these Irish sketches in 1912, reworking articles from the Shanachie and the Manchester Guardian. The Wicklow pieces treat the vagrants of Wicklow, the oppression of the hills, life on the road, and the people of the glens. A Wicklow fair, a landlord's garden, and Glencree complete the first part.

The West Kerry pieces continue Synge's walking tour of the west, listening to speech and watching work. Synge writes as a listener rather than a judge, letting island and hillside voices carry the book. The volume pairs naturally with his Aran Islands, as a record of rural Ireland before its old ways faded.
4636-a-tramp-through-the-bret-harte-coun:
Thomas Dykes Beasley, author of The Coming of Portola, wrote A Tramp Through the Bret Harte Country, with a foreword by Charles A. Murdock. A verse from Dickens in Camp stands at its head, with pines, a slowly drifting moon, a singing river, and dim Sierras lifting minarets of snow. Chapters begin with reminiscences of Bret Harte, Plain Language from Truthful James, and the glamour of old mining towns, before the tramp itself begins.

The route runs from Stockton to Angel's Camp, Tuttletown and the Sage of Jackass Hill, and Tuolumne to Placerville. Charm of Sonora, San Andreas, and Mokelumne Hill follow, with Bradley and the Cary House, ruins of Coloma, and James W. Marshall and his pathetic end. Auburn to Nevada City, Grass Valley to Smartsville, and Smartsville to Marysville close the walk. Readers get a literary walking tour of gold country, full of Harte lore and pioneer memory.
4653-god-s-good-man-a-simple-love-story:
Marie Corelli calls God's Good Man a simple love story, dedicating it to the living original of the Reverend John Walden and his wife. Her epigraph quotes the New Testament: there was a man sent from God whose name was John. The book opens in May-time in England, after a long, hard winter whose last frost has melted from broad, low-lying fields, and whose young corn now sprouts thick and tender green.

Buds nipped by cruel cold, biting east winds, and stormy northern caprices have played havoc with woodland blossoms. Into that English spring comes a tale of a good clergyman, love, and duty, told in Corelli's warm, earnest manner. Readers get a popular Edwardian romance of faith and feeling, with country detail and a moral heart, for readers who like a story that wears its goodness openly.
4707-the-valley-of-silent-men-a-story-of:
James Oliver Curwood sets The Valley of Silent Men in the Three River country, opening at Athabasca Landing before the railroad bit its way through the wilderness. That landing, still called Iskwatam, the door, opens to the lower Athabasca, the Slave, and the Mackenzie. Its history, Curwood says, runs through more than a hundred and forty years of romance, tragedy, and adventure, about a hundred and fifty miles north of Edmonton by the old trail.

Beyond that door the wilderness still howls as it always has, and the story follows men and women caught in its silence, law, and violence. A frontispiece shows a girl's revolver spitting smoke and flame, a sign of the action to come. Readers get a northern adventure of pursuit and justice, with rivers, forests, and remote settlements, in Curwood's fast, vivid style.
4789-black-caesar-s-clan-a-florida-myste:
Albert Payson Terhune wrote Black Caesar's Clan as a Florida mystery story, dedicated to John E. Pickett. Its contents run from The Hidden Path and The Man in the Dark, through The Mocking Bird and The Stranger from Nowhere, to Traps and Trapper and In the Day of Battle. Secrets, The Siege, The Figure in White, and The Ghost Tree follow.

The foreword begins not with a villain but with a wiggling, brainless, slimy atom, the coral worm, and trillions of its kind. Living and dying on the sea bottom, successive generations piled higher on skeletons and lifework of those before. At last a coral reef rose in uncharted waters tall enough to smash a wooden ship's keel. Above the waves it nosed its way, greyish white, until a mangrove bud floated a hundred miles to touch it. Readers get a mystery rooted in a Florida island's strange birth.
4918-the-lilac-sunbonnet-a-love-story:
Ralph Peden rests under a thorn bush above the Grannoch water in Galloway, and this love story follows the young man through heather, lochs, and parish life. His father's friend Allan Welsh, minister of the Marrow kirk at Dullarg, questions him closely about his soul's health and his life among the pious folk of the great city.

The novel weaves romance with Scottish religious life, as Ralph finds love amid preaching, grasshoppers, and bees drunk on heather scent. The catalog record names no author, so the story stands on its own pastoral charm. Readers get a gentle tale of faith and feeling in a countryside rendered with affectionate detail.
5155-c-sar-s-column-a-story-of-the-twent:
Ignatius Donnelly's dystopian novel, published in 1890 under the pen name Edmund Boisgilbert, imagines America a century ahead. A wealthy oligarchy rules it, while workers starve in an underworld beneath a great city. Its narrator reaches the city, meets Estella Washington, and is drawn into a secret brotherhood plotting revolt.

Donnelly, better known for his comet theories, wrote one of the earliest American dystopias, complete with airships, poisoned knives, and a sermon on the ruined world. The book's warning about concentrated wealth and class war struck a nerve in the 1890s. It remains an early landmark of science fiction as social protest.
5182-the-old-english-baron-a-gothic-stor:
Clara Reeve's Gothic novel, written as a reply to Horace Walpole's Castle of Otranto. It tells of a young man raised in obscurity who proves to be the rightful heir of a barony. Ghosts, a haunted castle, and a long-hidden crime drive the story, as the hero's true birth is revealed and justice returns to the house.

Reeve aimed to join the romance of old tales with the realism of the modern novel, keeping the supernatural within bounds of belief. The book became a founding work of Gothic fiction, and it offers readers a gentler. It is a more moral ghost story than Walpole's, with a plot that turns on inheritance, honour, and proof.
5198-the-library:
George Crabbe's poem The Library argues that books console a troubled mind by replacing its own distress with a lighter kind. Its argument moves through the arrangement of a library, from ancient chained folios to pamphlets and numbers. Its classes run through divinity, controversy, medicine, law, history, drama, and romance.

Crabbe reflects on sceptical authors, the friends of religion who do more harm than its foes. He also reflects on the hopes of an author to be known in distant times. The poem ends with the genius of the place answering the poet's doubts. It offers readers a thoughtful, verse-length meditation on reading itself.
5270-the-film-mystery:
Arthur B. Reeve's Film Mystery brings Professor Craig Kennedy into the world of moving pictures. A camera crime, a tiny scratch, and a fatal script open the case. Chapters follow tangled motives, white-light shadows, chemical research, and an antivenin, as Kennedy and his friend Jameson investigate among actors and studios.

Enid Faye, Lawrence Millard, Emery Phelps, and Marilyn Loring are among the film people caught in the mystery. Jameson himself becomes a detective before the banquet scene closes the case. The novel offers a lively early look at Hollywood, where science meets show business and every clue may be a performance.
5308-the-paradise-mystery:
Fletcher's Paradise Mystery opens at the Close of Wrychester. American tourists halt in wonder before a thirteenth-century cathedral set on a great green sward, fringed by elms and beeches, its spire piercing skies where rooks circle and call. The novel's first chapter is called Only the Guardian, and the cathedral close holds its secret.

Fletcher, a master of the English detective story, builds a mystery around an ancient church, its guardian, and a hidden past. Readers will find a classic puzzle of place, with cathedral atmosphere, local characters. The solution turns on what the Close has long concealed.
537-tales-of-terror-and-mystery:
Arthur Conan Doyle gathers twelve tales of dread and detection in this volume, split into terror and mystery. The Horror of the Heights sends a pilot into a sky full of unseen beasts. The Leather Funnel and the New Catacomb chill with old crimes, while the Brazilian Cat stalks a lone man.

Doyle writes with brisk, eerie craft, mixing science with the uncanny. Mystery tales track a lost train, a beetle hunter, and a japanned box. Each tale closes with a twist that reframes all before it. The book shows Doyle beyond Sherlock Holmes, as a master of short, sharp shocks for readers who like a cold shiver.
5424-icelandic-primer-with-grammar-notes:
Henry Sweet wrote this Icelandic Primer as a short, easy introduction to the study of Icelandic, in a second edition dated 1895. The preface explains that students in England had long wanted such a book. The larger Icelandic Reader by Vigfusson and Powell was valuable, but it left room for an elementary primer, and its editors raised no objection to Sweet undertaking one.

The primer supplies grammar, notes, and a glossary, giving beginners the tools to read Old Icelandic texts. Sweet writes for students, not specialists, keeping the path into the language as clear as possible. Readers get a compact, practical textbook that still serves as a first step into medieval Icelandic literature.
5676-a-double-story:
George MacDonald opens a fairy tale in a country where nothing behaves as expected. Rain may turn to hail without warning. Milk may sour overnight, and a baby may wake sweet-tempered or cross for no clear reason. The tale is told in short numbered chapters, and its odd rules set the tone at once, as if the world itself were testing the people who live in it. Young readers are invited to watch how small choices play out under strange laws.

The story rewards patience, since its wonders unfold slowly and its lessons arrive through events rather than lectures. MacDonald mixes homely detail with outright magic, so a walk, a meal, or a meeting can turn surprising. Children and adults who enjoy old-fashioned wonder tales will find a gentle, curious book that treats goodness and folly as real forces in its invented land.
5695-jim-cummings-or-the-great-adams-exp:
Frank Pinkerton's dime novel dramatizes the great Adams Express robbery through the career of Jim Cummings and his gang. It opens in a back room in Chicago, where three men sit around a pine table behind drawn curtains, closed shutters, and a nailed blanket, plotting with a forged letter. From that secret council the story moves to detectives, hideouts, and a robber's retreat, as chapter titles promise.

Readers get fast, plain melodrama in the classic detective-story mold: conspirators plan, lawmen close in, and each chapter ends with a fresh danger. The book preserves the flavor of late nineteenth-century popular fiction, where crime and pursuit matter more than fine psychology. It suits readers curious about early American crime tales and the cheap, thrilling books that carried them.
5828-in-the-pecos-country:
In the Pecos Country opens in the valley of the Rio Pecos, where hardy New Englanders attempt a settlement years ago under a leader like a sort of Don Quixote. The leader travels hundreds of miles, passing richer land, balmier climate, and places protected by law, for the sake of locating where he chooses. Chapters warn, confer, and send Fred on guard, before facing Lone Wolf and the coming Apaches.

The book gives a classic frontier adventure of warning, attack, trees, capture, and escape, told in brisk chapters. Fred's trials among Apaches, old enemies, and hot quarters test a young hero's nerve. The book suits readers of vintage western adventure, while modern readers should note its period portrayal of Native peoples as part of its dated frontier viewpoint.
587-danny-s-own-story:
Don Marquis lets Danny, a foundling boy without a last name, tell his own tale in this comic novel. Danny begins life in a basket on Hank Walters's steps, where a drunken kick and a wife's sharp eye decide his fate. From hearsay and memory, Danny recounts farms, villages, and the grown-ups who raised, scolded, and loved him.

Marquis writes in Danny's warm, misspelled dialect, full of humor and heart. The boy's lack of a name becomes a running joke and a quiet ache. The book charms as a tall-tale memoir of rural America, where a nobody child talks his way into a place of his own.
5876-ten-englishmen-of-the-nineteenth-ce:
James Richard Joy presents Ten Englishmen of the Nineteenth Century in 1902, dedicating the work to his daughter Helen with a father's love. His preface states the object plainly: to set forth with as much clearness as possible the more important facts in the history of England in the nineteenth century. He chooses to do this through the medium of ten lives, letting biography carry history.

This introduces a century through its leading men, with each life illustrating politics, industry, reform, or letters. The method favors narrative over abstract survey, so a general reader can follow change through character. The book suits students of Victorian England, biography lovers, and anyone wanting a readable introduction to a century of transformation.
5970-lovey-mary:
Alice Hegan Rice presents Lovey Mary as a bundle of contradictions, from hands and feet meant for a big girl to high ideals that seem too large for her. The book belongs to the Cabbage Patch world of Mrs. Wiggs, and its chapters run from a cactus plant and a runaway couple to a hazy household and a denominational garden.

Neighborly advice, Labor Day, a timely visit, and a Christmas play fill the middle of the tale, with Mr. Stubbins and a pumpkin pie among the homely details. Rice writes with warmth about poor folk who keep their pluck. The cactus blooms at the end, a small emblem of care rewarded.
5972-a-fascinating-traitor-an-anglo-indi:
Richard Henry Savage follows Major Alan Hawke from a low hour at Geneva, where he feeds swans around Rousseau's Island and weighs ending his troubles. The tale then reaches back to Delhi, a veiled rosebud, a diplomatic tiffin, and a mysterious bungalow where safety has a price.

Three books carry Hawke through a devil-for-luck middle act and Prince Djiddin's visit to England, with cliffs at Jersey, a council at Granville, and a French fishing boat. Savage mixes Anglo-Indian service, court intrigue, and adventure. The traitor of the title moves between loyalties, and every alliance looks double-edged.
6059-confession-or-the-blind-heart-a-dom:
Gilmore Simms opens Confession, or The Blind Heart, with an epigraph from Goethe's Faust. It asks who dares bestow the infant his true name, and what we can know of the heart and mind of man. The few who felt and knew, and blindly gave their knowledge to the multitude, fell, crucified or burnt.

Simms answers that the pains and penalties of folly are not necessarily death today, though the present has penalties of its own. A domestic story follows, about secrets kept or spilled and hearts that cannot hold their fullness in. The novel treats confession as both relief and risk.
626-the-love-of-books-the-philobiblon-of:
Richard de Bury praises books and book lovers in this medieval treatise, here in E. C. Thomas's translation. De Bury, bishop of Durham and tutor to Edward III, collected books across England and Avignon, where he met Petrarch. His Philobiblon argues that books hold hidden treasure, to be taken up, kissed, and thanked for, as Thomas à Kempis urged.

A preface traces de Bury's rise from Bury St. Edmunds to chancellor of England. The treatise mixes lore, complaint against book neglect, and joy in reading. It endures as a classic hymn to libraries, where a bishop's love of books still speaks to any reader.
6311-a-knight-of-the-nineteenth-century:
Edward P. Roe, in the third volume of his works, dedicates this novel to his honoured father and opens with verse on knighthood within. He best deserves a knightly crest, the poem says, who slays the evils that infest his soul, for the world bows low to knightly deeds and stays cold to pleading. The chapters that follow test that claim in modern dress, through icebergs, passion's clamour, birds of prey, and a victim.

Haldane is arrested, meets a memorable company, and sits as a knight in jail, while Mr. Arnot's system works badly and wounded pride drives him at odds with the world. A paper poniard, a sorry knight, and God's angel mark later chapters, as public opinion is made and a man who hated himself learns to face consequences. Roe writes a moral romance of the nineteenth century, where chivalry means mastering one's own evils first.
6385-simple-italian-cookery:
Antonia Isola writes Simple Italian Cookery as a practical book, from soups and macaroni to rice, sauces, eggs, fish, vegetables, meats, salads, and desserts, with an index. Beef soup stock opens the soups. Round of beef, bones, carrots, potatoes, onion, tomato, and parsley are boiled slowly in two quarts of water, skimmed, salted, and finished with sherry after two hours. That stock forms the basis of all soups that follow.

Richer stock adds a turkey leg and chopped beef, meat jelly takes gelatine before straining, and a dark colour comes from a few drops of caramel, as the sample shows. A later recipe fries ham and onion golden in butter, adds uncooked rice, bouillon, nutmeg, and Parmesan for a risotto like dish. Isola writes plainly for home cooks, with quantities, times, and reasons, so that Italian food can be made without a restaurant kitchen.
6406-the-monastery:
Walter Scott, after Ivanhoe, chooses for his next scene the celebrated ruins of Melrose, near his own home, though he cannot recall the reason or caprice that dictated the change. The Monastery, in the Abbotsford edition of the Waverley Novels, complete in twelve volumes, opens with an 1830 introduction weighing that choice. Halbert Glendinning invoking the White Lady fronts the book.

A ruffian asks a sub prior what gold he would get for couching a lance, and what for levelling it at a heretic. The church answers with spiritual censures before Saint Peter's sword. A primate, the tale hints, recommends a little strangling and burning in aid of both. Scott writes border romance at Reformation's edge, where monastery, lady of the lake, and reforming sword contend for Scotland's soul.
6410-once-aboard-the-lugger-the-history-:
A. S. M. Hutchinson begins with excursions in a garden, where Mr. Christopher Marrapit dozes in a chair on the lawn, his darling cat Rose of Sharon asleep on his lap, and Mrs. Major, his companion, sits stiffly beside him, a masterly woman. The narrator warns that meeting strangers goes better with some knowledge of the first person met. At Paltley Hill, neighbourhood chatter fails to supply that knowledge.

Book One follows George, Book Two his Mary, through melancholy, hospitals, and life itself, with a heroine's arrivals. George, promising himself all night to say four words, at last says them: Mary, I love you. She laughs her clear, unique pipe of mirth, and he protests he is not foolish. Hutchinson writes a long, playful courtship, where a lugger voyage frames a love that laughs at itself.
6412-nature-s-serial-story:
E. P. Roe, in the first volume of his works, tells Nature's Serial Story as a tale of a house and its people, with Mr. and Mrs. Clifford from life. A hard brain worker, tired and losing zest, finds renewal in love of nature, Roe says in his preface. No one deeply interested in her manifestations can wholly lose life's savour. The house itself, built nearly half a century ago, has grown homelike with years, grey as its venerable owner, set back among elms and maples.

Late December shows the old homestead sharp in white landscape, sober hue matching dark tree boles. Under the mistletoe, buds blackened under the microscope tell a spring story. Webb cuts peach buds and finds eight of nine killed by nature's thinning, saving summer labour and promising larger fruit. Roe writes seasons as serial chapters, where a house, a garden, and a marriage mature together.
6431-the-law-of-the-land-of-miss-lady-wh:
Emerson Hough's 1904 novel opens with Miss Lady dancing alone before a great mirror in an old plantation house, sweet, strong, and full of grace, like a bird in all her motions. Feet scarce touching the floor, skirt held like wings between dainty fingers, she swims through air, darting, nodding, beckoning, and courtesying to something only she sees. The mirror gives her back line for line, flush for flush.

John Eddring, gentleman of the South, reads the deeper meaning of the law of the land that involves Miss Lady in mystery, while Colonel Blount, Mrs. Eddring, and a mother at a hotel shape the social world around her. Hough writes a southern romance of a girl, a dance, and a secret, where law means custom, honour, and the unseen ties that bind a household. The dance is the novel's emblem, light, free, and watched.
6463-a-handbook-of-ethical-theory:
George Stuart Fullerton writes A Handbook of Ethical Theory for students of ethics in universities and outside them, seeking clearer insight into moral maxims we hold with more or less confidence. Reflection and serious effort are needed, he argues in his preface, and in a field of so many differences of opinion, clearness and breadth of view are eminently desirable. The book asks first whether any accepted content of ethics exists.

Codes of communities follow, justice, veracity, and the common good, then codes of moralists, Epicurean and Stoic, Plato, Aristotle, and the Church. Ethical method, materials, and aim as science come next, with man's nature and environment, impulse, desire, will, and intention. A mid passage notes that a child, and many adults, live as parasites on society, their ends chosen by others. Fullerton writes ethics as a student's map, careful and plain.
648-wild-wales-its-people-language-and-s:
George Borrow walks Wales in this travel book, first published in 1862 and reprinted in a definitive 1907 edition. Borrow, who loved the Welsh tongue, praises Wales as a picturesque country deserving more notice, and quotes Taliesin's prophecy that the Welsh shall keep their language even if they lose their land. Plates show Llangollen, Snowdon, and the Devil's Bridge.

Borrow writes with keen, personal prose, meeting folk, hearing speech, and tracing his route on a map. The book mixes scenery, history, and talk in one long walk. It endures as a classic Welsh travelogue, where a wanderer finds a nation's soul in its hills and words.
6494-mr-world-and-miss-church-member-a-t:
Rev. W. S. Harris casts modern faith as a tale of two figures, Mr. World and Miss Church-Member, set against the rush of a new century.
