His preface notes the flood of new books each week, most soon lost, and hopes his own volume will find real use rather than an early grave. Friends and critics read the draft and urged small changes along the way.

Through twenty-five chapters, the allegory pits worldly pull against church life, testing what a believer does when fashion, gain, and ease call loud. Harris writes plainly, with scenes meant to be read as lessons rather than as mere fun. The aim is plain: to help a reader see daily choices in a sharper moral light.
6572-haste-and-waste-or-the-young-pilot-:
Oliver Optic, the pen name of William Taylor Adams, tells a boys' tale set on Lake Champlain, where a young pilot learns that haste brings waste. Adams, a Boston teacher for twenty years, knew boy life at close hand, and his books were loved for being both fun and clean. His life note, set at the front, traces his work from 1850 to his death in 1897.

The young pilot must steer with care, judge wind and water, and own his faults when speed tempts him past sense. Optic keeps the lessons inside the action, so the moral never halts the fun. Haste and Waste is a brisk, old-style adventure for young readers, with lake air and honest work on every page.
6605-unconscious-memory:
Samuel Butler, known for Erewhon and The Way of All Flesh, argues in this 1910 work that memory lives in the body, not just in the mind. A new introduction by Marcus Hartog frames the book, which Butler first set out as a paper with no claim to new tests or finds. Critics of his day, he notes, wished to block such bold ideas.

Butler holds that habit, instinct, and growth in living things show a kind of recall passed down through life itself. His prose is sharp, combative, and full of wit, taking on the science of his time head-on. Unconscious Memory is a daring, odd book, best read as a thinker's challenge to how we view life and learning.
6674-umbrellas-and-their-history:
William Sangster asks how a busy, practical people like the English, exposed to a fickle sky, could ever have lived without the umbrella. His motto, a shield against rain, sets the tone for a history that runs from ancient times to England, then to the parachute, umbrella stories, and the umbrella's rebirth. The opening chapter teases the reader with disbelief.

Sangster treats a humble object with wit and learning, showing how a rain shield became a mark of fashion and sense. His prose is light, yet full of fact. Umbrellas and Their History is a delightful, odd little book, perfect for readers who love the stories behind daily things.
6756-little-memoirs-of-the-nineteenth-ce:
George Paston sketches minor celebrities of the nineteenth century, chosen to show literary and artistic life in its first half. He picks subjects not lately overwhelmed by small biographers, and adds two foreigners, on the theory that a stranger's verdict matches that of later posterity. A German princeling and a gilded American democrat lead the outsiders.

Each memoir is short, vivid, and full of telling detail, from salons to studios. Paston's tone is urbane and amused. Little Memoirs of the Nineteenth Century is a delightful gallery of half-forgotten figures, for lovers of literary gossip and history.
6763-aristotle-on-the-art-of-poetry:
Aristotle's Art of Poetry, in Ingram Bywater's translation with a preface by Gilbert Murray, opens with Plato's attack on poetry in the Republic. Plato calls poetry a false siren, an imitator of shadows, and an ally of the low and weak in the soul. Yet he ends with a touch of compunction. He invites poet-lovers to defend her in plain prose.

Aristotle takes up that defense, showing poetry as both sweet and helpful to society and to human life. Bywater's Oxford text keeps the argument crisp. On the Art of Poetry is a short, essential work on tragedy, imitation, and why stories matter.
6805-the-mill-mystery:
Anna Katharine Green, author of The Leavenworth Case, opens The Mill Mystery with an alarm, a fearful question, and a girl named Ada. The Pollards, doubts and queries, a flower from their conservatory, and an unexpected discovery follow, with Rhoda Colwell and a secret under the mill floor. Dwight and Guy Pollard, correspondence, gossip, and a green envelope deepen the puzzle.

A last request, a fatal delay, an old mill, a vat, a cypher, and a final confrontation lead to the truth. Green, a pioneer of detective fiction, keeps the plot tight and the clues fair. The Mill Mystery is a classic, gripping whodunit from the queen of early American mystery.
6841-mosaics-of-grecian-history:
Marcius Willson and Robert Pierpont Willson aim, in Mosaics of Grecian History, to give a trustworthy and interesting history of Greece in moderate compass. Standard histories, they note, are seldom read by the people at large, while school manuals, mere outlines of larger works, fare no better. The outline system, they argue, inverts the natural order of learning and turns study into drudgery for the young.

Their mosaic method instead builds history from vivid pieces, anecdotes, and scenes, so beginners can grasp the whole. The book suits general readers and schools alike. Mosaics of Grecian History is a lively, old-style primer, made to make Greece live for new readers.
6907-from-wealth-to-poverty-or-the-trick:
Austin Potter, a minister, wrote this story of the drink curse from two motives he states plainly. He hated the rum traffic, which had brought hardship and suffering on himself and those dear to him. He also sought to expose the tricks by which the liquor party made the Dunkin Act fail, so as to bring that law into disrepute. He dedicates the book to the friends of prohibition the world over.

An Othello line on drink turning a sensible man first to a fool and then to a beast stands at the head of the tale. The story follows a fall from wealth to poverty, showing how drink and the trade behind it wreck a home. Potter writes as a preacher and a reformer, aiming to warn as much as to move.
7036-the-poorhouse-waif-and-his-divine-t:
Isabel Byrum tells the true story of a poorhouse waif and his divine teacher, opening with a deserted child scarcely a month old. A Crabbe verse at the head holds that the fondest and best are most tried, troubled, and distressed. A woman leaves the infant where hands are already more than full, and the contents trace life in the almshouse, from bad to worse, finding friends, and suffering for others faults.

A strange visitor, mysteries unfolding, and the discovery of God follow, with a witch's home, a contrast, and a search for light. Revelations on eternity, prayer, tobacco, and God's word lead through camp meetings to a call to service and a church found. The waif's journey from desertion to faith forms the book's arc.
714-the-bobbsey-twins-in-the-country:
Laura Lee Hope sent the Bobbsey twins, Bert, Nan, Freddie, and Flossie, from town to Meadow Brook for a country summer. An invitation starts the trip, and a train ride with their dog Snoop brings them to farm life. They pick peas, tend small gardens, and join a Fourth of July picnic.

Country fun turns to mild peril when a runaway, a circus, and a flood stir up the town. The twins help neighbours, find a well's secret, and end the stay with a camp for fresh-air children. The tale is gentle, wholesome, and full of small tasks done well, just the kind of summer story young readers loved.
7181-the-bushman-life-in-a-new-country:
Edward Wilson Landor's Bushman speaks for Britain's far colonies at a time when, he argues, they were too remote for sympathy and too weak for respect. The public and the government, he writes, obeyed the need to mind colonial welfare with reluctance, as if long neglect were a right. Yet the weakness of childhood was passing, and the colonies were growing into strength.

Landor sets that claim beside scenes of new-country life, kangaroo hunting among them, so that argument and experience stand side by side. His preface asks readers at home to take colonial wants seriously, not as distant news but as part of the empire's own business. The book mixes plea and picture in the voice of a man who knew the ground.
725-men-of-invention-and-industry:
Samuel Smiles profiled men who built modern industry with little schooling but great skill and grit. Phineas Pett laid the roots of English shipbuilding, and Francis Pettit Smith brought the screw propeller into practical use. Other chapters follow engineers, makers, and workers whose hands shaped ships, machines, and trade.

Smiles argues that such men, ignorant of letters yet rich in wisdom, freed nations by deeds rather than words. Each life is told as a lesson in patience, thrift, and steady work. The book is a Victorian hymn to self-help through craft, and it still offers vivid portraits of the age when Britain's workshops remade the world.
7284-the-chosen-people-a-compendium-of-s:
The author of The Heir of Redclyffe wrote this compendium of sacred and church history for schoolchildren. It opens with Hebrews on God speaking through prophets and, in these last days, through his Son. Verse follows on altars that blazed and died, on silence torn with song, and on a revolving sphere where no desert now hides from heaven's light and order.

The book traces the chosen people from old covenant to church, in short lessons suited to young readers. Its tone is devout and didactic, joining Bible story to church history in one clear line. Schoolchildren meet sacred history as a single unfolding tale, told with reverence and simplicity.
7517-sanctuary:
Edith Wharton's short novel opens with a young woman's undivided happiness, a feeling youth seldom allows itself. Kate Orme has yielded herself to happiness since her engagement to Denis Peyton two months before, letting it soak into every faculty like spring rain into a germinating meadow. She watches from the slopes above a lake as Denis approaches by the short cut from the Peyton place, her smile prolonged by the impossibility of her joy.

Wharton builds the novella around what that happiness must face: the past, the family, and the moral choices that test a marriage before it begins. Sanctuary, in Wharton's sense, is both a refuge and a question: what shelter can love offer against knowledge? The book is a concentrated Wharton, all her themes of society, conscience, and consequence in brief compass.
752-a-young-girl-s-diary:
An anonymous girl of the upper middle class kept this diary from age eleven to fourteen and a half. It reached print with a prefatory letter from Sigmund Freud, dated 27 April 1915. Freud called the diary a gem, praising its frank view of a young mind. Eden and Cedar Paul made the English translation.

The diary runs in four parts, one for each year, closing with a short conclusion. It records school, friends, family, first crushes, and the small dramas of growing up, in a voice that is candid and unguarded. The book matters as a rare, direct record of girlhood, and as a text that early psychoanalysis prized for what it shows of the mind at work.
7790-captain-january:
Laura E Richards's Captain January follows a lighthouse keeper who sells fine lobsters from his red dory. He washes her out with care before sailing home. On the wharf Captain Nazro hails him in a blue coat with brass buttons, asking after the little girl in his charge.

Contents list Star Bright, the story itself, Imogen and Bob, a visit, the captain's star, and a signal. Through seaside talk and tender care, the book tells how a rough old sailor raises a child found by the sea. Love, duty, and a light on the shore shape both their lives.
7836-jewish-history-an-essay-in-the-phil:
S. M. Dubnow's Jewish History, an Essay in the Philosophy of History, opens with praise for its author as a leading voice in Russian-Jewish letters. His work on Polish-Russian Jews and on Hasidism, the preface says, broke new ground, joining scientific care with ardent temper and vivid form.

Dubnow refuses the notion that fine form means thin thought, and his essay seeks the inner law of Jewish survival across exile, faith, and communal life. Through history and philosophy, it asks what holds a people together without a state, and why their story matters to all history.
7863-the-avalanche-a-mystery-story:
Gertrude Atherton's The Avalanche, a mystery story from 1919, opens with Price Ruyler wondering whether his wife's secret was buried by San Francisco's earthquake and fire. Born in a city of odd, whispered pasts, Helene shows subtle changes after a year and a half of uncommon happiness.

Her devotion never wavers, yet her spirits shift, and a silent mother-in-law hints at a past of her own. Ruyler, sure for six months that some gray cloud hangs over his marriage, begins to dig. Through society, money, and old San Francisco, the novel unearths a secret long held.
7897-the-gray-goose-s-story:
Amy Prentice's The Gray Goose's Story, in Aunt Amy's Animal Stories with thirty-two pictures and a color frontispiece by J. Watson Davis, opens by a pond beyond an apple orchard. Aunt Amy loves to wander there and meet bird and animal friends ready to tell tales.

Mr. Frisky Squirrel, old Mr. Plodding Turtle, and Mr. Bunny Rabbit greet her, but only yesterday, through Master Teddy's mischief, did she meet the gray goose. An angry hiss startles her, mistaken for a snake, and a new friendship begins. It is a gentle farm tale for small children.
7898-mouser-cat-s-story:
Amy Prentice's Mouser Cat's Story, with thirty-five pictures and a color frontispiece by J. Watson Davis, opens on a hard stormy day when Aunt Amy feels lonely, her human friends busy and no animal likely out. Watching rain streams run down the window glass, she expects no story telling.

Then Mrs. Mouser Cat speaks from the doorway, joking about pickles, an animal Aunt Amy knew well but never heard talk before. Surprised and pleased, Aunt Amy listens as the cat begins her tale. It is a cozy companion to the Gray Goose's story, for small readers who love farm animals.
7929-parisians-in-the-country:
Honore de Balzac's Parisians in the Country joins The Illustrious Gaudissart with The Muse of the Department, early and late work in one volume. Gaudissart, from 1832 at the height of Balzac's fancy, sketches a traveling salesman in the physiologie manner, with a beginning the introduction calls excellent.

The Muse, ten years later, draws on stores already dipped into, yet still rich. Villagers rolling the great Gaudissart amuse Balzac's Tourangeau pride, though the tale's ending lags its start. Together the pair show a master at flood and at ebb, both vivid with provincial France.
7930-the-advance-of-english-poetry-in-th:
William Lyon Phelps, Lampson Professor of English Literature at Yale, wrote this survey of the new poetry of his own time. He quotes generously, with permission, from publishers of Thomas Hardy, William Butler Yeats, Robert Frost, Vachel Lindsay, Amy Lowell, Edgar Lee Masters, Sara Teasdale, and many others. The book moves poet by poet, judging each voice on its own terms.

Phelps writes as an enthusiastic teacher rather than a theorist, and his aim is to help readers hear what is fresh in verse written after the Victorians. He pairs short critical essays with well-chosen passages, so the poems do much of the persuading. As a snapshot of how English poetry looked while it was still being made, it remains lively and readable.
7960-early-european-history:
Hutton Webster, Ph. D. , wrote this school textbook as a concise, connected account of human progress in ancient, medieval, and early modern times. It was designed for high schools and preparatory schools where a separate ancient history course was giving way to a broader survey leading into recent times. The preface quotes Samuel Johnson on history as the story of the human mind: its learning, arts, and revolutions.

Webster keeps the narrative clear and continuous, so students can follow Europe from its ancient roots through the Middle Ages to the modern threshold. Maps, structure, and plain exposition suit classroom use. The book still works as a brisk one-volume outline for readers who want the shape of European history before tackling specialist works.
8148-youth-and-egolatry:
Pío Baroja wrote Youth and Egolatry, translated from the Spanish by Jacob S. Fassett Jr. and Frances L. Phillips, with an introduction by H. L. Mencken. Its contents open with a prologue on intellectual love, then essays on egotism: fundamental ideas, the bad man of Itzea. Dogmatophagy, materialism, religion, Dionysus and Apollo, evil, Rousseau, music as a sedative, Wagner, and folk song. A second part turns to Baroja himself, the writer, and his youthful writings.

Baroja, a leading Spanish novelist of the Generation of 1898, writes here as philosopher and provocateur, aphoristic and contrarian. The essays suit readers who enjoy strong opinions and literary argument. They offer a sharp, personal introduction to a mind that distrusted systems and prized individual vision.
8161-fragments-of-ancient-poetry:
James Macpherson's Fragments of Ancient Poetry, presented as translations of old Gaelic verse, launched the Ossian controversy that divided eighteenth-century letters. This Augustan Reprint Society edition, with an introduction by John J. Dunn, presents the fragments that first made Macpherson famous. Readers at the time debated whether the poems were genuine ancient remains or Macpherson's own inventions dressed in antique style.

The fragments matter whatever their origin: they inspired Romantic poetry, fed interest in Celtic antiquity, and raised lasting questions about authenticity and translation. Their misty, heroic tone influenced writers across Europe. For students of literary history, this short volume is the starting point of Ossian, and of the modern cult of the ancient bard.
8221-a-study-of-poetry:
Bliss Perry, professor of English literature at Harvard University, wrote A Study of Poetry following the method he had sketched in his chapter on poetry in Counsel Upon the Reading of Books. His confidence in the genetic method, approaching poetry through impression, transforming imagination, and expression, was shared by many lovers of poetry. Though he hopes his insistence on that threefold process has not hardened into a set formula, since formulas have a dangerous usefulness.

Perry's study guides readers through how poems are made and felt, rather than through rules alone. His Harvard lectures give the book clarity and warmth. For students of poetry, it remains a classic introduction, and a wise warning against letting method replace the poem itself.
8407-the-christian-a-story:
Hall Caine's novel The Christian follows its story across about eighteen months, six months to each of its first three books, with an interval after. Caine, author of The Manxman, sets the tale in the last quarter of the nineteenth century, without fixing particular years. He follows characters tested by faith, love, and the claims of the church.

Caine was among the best-selling novelists of his day, and The Christian was a huge popular success, later staged and filmed. Readers get a Victorian religious novel at full stretch: earnest, emotional, and concerned with what a Christian life should cost. The book's scale and sincerity explain its fame, even where modern tastes differ.
8554-why-worry:
George Lincoln Walton, a neurologist at Massachusetts General Hospital, asks Why Worry? and answers with an old Chinese image: the legs of the stork are long, the legs of the duck are short, and you cannot make one like the other. Why worry, asks Chwang Tsze, quoted at the head, and Walton builds a small book of advice on accepting what cannot be changed.

Walton dedicates the book to his long-suffering family and circle of friends, who heard his advice often. Readers get an early self-help book by a doctor, plain and humane, on worry as a habit to be broken. The book's charm lies in its brevity and its humor, and it anticipates later books on anxiety by decades.
8665-a-strange-discovery:
Charles Romyn Dake published this 1889 novel as a supposed sequel to Edgar Allan Poe's tale of Arthur Gordon Pym, centred on the sailor Dirk Peters. The narrator claims he helped make a discovery of real literary importance, shared by only three men. Kept quiet for nearly twenty-five years because none of them had written for print before. One companion is quiet and retiring, the other erratic and forgetful, which helps explain the long silence.

From that frame, the book follows the search for Peters and the strange facts said to lie behind Poe's unfinished story. Dake plays a double game: part adventure, part literary detective work for Poe's readers. Fans of Pym will enjoy seeing its loose ends picked up. New readers get a brisk Victorian adventure that treats a famous mystery as if it had a real-world answer.
8691-the-american-judiciary:
Simeon E. Baldwin, a Connecticut jurist, examines the American judiciary in this scholarly volume, from its English origins to its practical working. Part one covers the nature and scope of judicial power in the United States, the organization of American courts. The separation of judicial power from legislative and executive power in American constitutions. Relations with the political departments, the force of precedents, and the courts' power to develop unwritten and written law follow.

Baldwin writes for lawyers, students, and citizens who want to understand how judges actually work, not merely what constitutions say. His account balances history, doctrine, and courtroom practice. The book remains a classic introduction to the American court system at the start of the twentieth century. A useful background to modern debates about judicial power, precedent, and the courts' place in a democracy.
8699-woman-and-her-saviour-in-persia-by-:
A returned missionary tells the story of woman's life in Persia and of Miss Fiske's fifteen years of labour there. Fine illustrations and a map of Nestorian country. The preface explains that many who knew Fiske's work wanted her to publish the facts. That the writer took up the task only when she could not, so that these records of grace might not be lost. Materials come from letters and firsthand reports, gathered up, in the Saviour's phrase, that nothing be lost.

The book describes Persian women's secluded lives, their sorrows and faith, and the schools and mission work that sought to reach them. It is a missionary document through and through, warm toward its subjects and confident in its message, and it must be read as such.
8823-dutch-life-in-town-and-country:
P. M. Hough describes Dutch life in town and country in this illustrated survey, with thirty-two pictures including the Delft Gate at Rotterdam. Chapters move from national characteristics, court and society. The professional classes, through the position of women and the workman of the towns. To canals and their population, a Dutch village, the peasant at home, and rural customs. Kermis and St Nicholas, amusements, music, theatre, schools, universities, and art and letters follow.

Later chapters cover the Dutch as readers, political life, justice, religion, army and navy, and Holland overseas. Hough writes for English readers curious about a neighbour often reduced to windmills and tulips, and he gives institutions their due. The book offers a thorough, sympathetic portrait of the Netherlands around 1900, useful for travellers then and for historians now. Still readable as a guided tour of a whole society.
8861-the-works-of-lord-byron-vol-1-poetr:
Ernest Hartley Coleridge edits this 1898 first volume of Lord Byron's poetry, in a new, revised, and enlarged edition with illustrations. The preface explains that the text rests on John Murray's 1831 Works in six volumes. Which followed the successive issues of plays and poems published in Byron's lifetime, revised by Byron himself or by Gifford and other accredited readers. Collation with manuscripts at Moore's disposal yielded variorum readings that appear in the notes.

The volume gathers Byron's early and middle poetry, from Hours of Idleness through the satires and tales that made him famous, with the apparatus of a scholarly edition. Readers can trace Byron's growth from a lordling poet to the voice of Childe Harold and Don Juan. In texts closer to his own revisions than many popular reprints. It serves students first, but any Byron reader gains from its careful, documented text.
8883-a-love-story:
A Bushman, writing in 1841, dedicates this love story to Lady Gipps, respectfully inscribed by a grateful friend. His preface explains at length why the work exists: as a solitary, companionless bushman, he found pleasure in lone evenings in creating. In creating living a being more intense. He expatiates on love for his adopted country, Australia, which greatly influenced the book's composition. His opening verse sends thoughts like swallows skimming the main, bearing his spirit back over earth and air, a wild bird and a wanderer.

Volume one follows that wandering spirit into a romance shaped by exile, landscape, and longing, written by a man who lived far from literary society. The author's very pseudonym, A Bushman, marks the book's claim: Australian experience told from inside the bush.
8906-mary-slessor-of-calabar-pioneer-mis:
W. P. Livingstone tells the life of Mary Slessor of Calabar, pioneer missionary, opening with a reflection on people who depart from normal procedure, follow ideals rather than rules. Use irregular, often unwise-seeming methods, yet accomplish important ends. Such a one was Mary Slessor, he says, poor or frail and of no account in her own estimation. Toward the end of her days she was urged to write her story, and this biography draws on her letters and on those who knew her.

Slessor, a Dundee mill girl turned missionary in Nigeria, lived among the Efik and Ibibio peoples, fought twin-killing, built schools, and became a trusted mediator and magistrate. Livingstone presents her as a saint of practical Christianity, and modern readers should weigh his admiration against colonial context. The life remains a classic missionary biography, and a portrait of a formidable woman who made Calabar her home.
9079-the-man-shakespeare-and-his-tragic-:
Frank Harris wrote this bold life of Shakespeare, arguing that the plays paint the poet himself. Harris dedicates it to Ernest Beckett, praised for practical genius and love of high endeavor. Book One reads Hamlet, Romeo, and Falstaff as self-portraits in turn. Book Two traces Shakespeare's love story through the Sonnets.

Harris claims that Shakespeare's tragic heroes voice his own griefs, loves, and pride. Scholars now dispute much of his case, yet his verve still grips. The book remains a lively, if daring, attempt to find the man behind the greatest plays in English.
9094-wild-flowers-or-pastoral-and-local-:
Robert Bloomfield published these pastoral and local poems in London in 1806. They follow his Farmer's Boy and Rural Tales, and keep close to village life. Contents include Abner and the Widow Jones, a familiar ballad, The Horkey, and The Broken Crutch. Shooter's Hill and Barnham Water add local color.

Bloomfield sings of old oak tables, harvest customs, and love of country in a plain, musical voice. His verse never strains for grandeur. The book still gives a warm, true picture of English country folk at the start of the nineteenth century.
9192-the-channings-a-story:
Mrs. Henry Wood, author of East Lynne, wrote this long story of the Channing family, in its two hundred and tenth thousand printing by 1901. Chapters open with an inked surplice, bad news, and Constance Channing, then no holiday today and Roland Yorke. Lady Augusta Yorke at home, Mr. Ketch, and an assistant organist follow.

Hamish's candles, a false alarm, and the cloister keys deepen a tale of church, family, and reputation. Wood keeps Victorian domestic suspense at full stretch. The novel remains a beloved example of her popular art, earnest, intricate, and warm.
9311-hetty-s-strange-history:
Published without a name, but by the author of Mercy Philbrick's Choice, this novel of 1877 tells Hetty's strange history. It opens with a sonnet on love: words are cheap, gifts cheaper still, and one thing remains unnamed on earth. That thing is giving one's own life up for love, not in a martyr's death, but in daily life's wearing groove.

Hetty's story tests that hard doctrine through years of quiet sacrifice. The novel asks what great love returns to such a giver. It remains a moving Victorian tale of devotion, praised for its moral seriousness and its tender, unsparing eye.
9399-a-roman-lawyer-in-jerusalem-first-c:
W. W. Story wrote this verse tale as a letter from Marcus, a Roman lawyer in Jerusalem, to Caius, his best friend in Rome. Marcus greets his friend, and his bearer Lucius, wearied with the East, longs for Rome again. Lucius calls the East hateful, blazing, barren, and bleak, and pants for the circus, its games, and its roaring crowds.

Story sets Roman grandeur against Jerusalem's strangeness, in blank verse rich with marble porticoes and sunlit awnings. The poem is a dramatic monologue of exile and homesickness. It remains a fine Victorian classical piece, vivid and melancholy.
972-the-devil-s-dictionary:
Ambrose Bierce wrote this dictionary of satirical definitions, begun in a weekly paper in 1881 and continued at long intervals until 1906. In that year much of it appeared as The Cynic's Word Book, a name the author had not the power to reject or the happiness to approve. The Devil's Dictionary is its final form.

Bierce defines love, law, politics, and religion with a sting, turning each word into a small essay on human folly. His wit is dark, precise, and unsparing, and his entries reward dipping in at random. The book remains a classic of American satire, quoted wherever cynics gather.
9746-the-ashiel-mystery:
Mrs. Charles Bryce wrote The Ashiel Mystery, a detective story of illness, houses, and hidden deeds. Sir Arthur Byrne, ill after three summers at a Black Sea consulate, takes sick leave and hurries home to Harley Street doctors. He blames drains and Eastern towns, yet fears his health may fail for good. The tale then turns to Ashiel, where a mystery waits.

Bryce, praised by Stevenson for police romance craft, builds suspense from character and place, not mere clues. Doctors, consuls, and country houses cross the plot. A reader gets a classic Edwardian mystery, urbane and tense, with a sick man's dread as its dark opening note.
9795-the-four-faces-a-mystery:
William Le Queux wrote The Four Faces, a mystery of angel faces, snares, and a glittering underworld. Chapters open with curiosity aroused in Linden Gardens, then a Hampstead mystery and a house in Grafton Street. Hugheson Gastrell, Osborne, and Mrs. Stapleton cross the plot, with a baron, a thin-faced stranger, and a channel mystery. Secrets of dusky fowl and modern vice darken the trail.

Later chapters unmask the four faces, as confessions and papers close the snare. Le Queux writes with brisk, Edwardian suspense. A reader gets a lively mystery of faces and disguises, from a master of the spy and crime tale.
9808-the-loudwater-mystery:
Edgar Jepson wrote The Loudwater Mystery in 1920, a tale of a lord, a lady, and a cat named Melchisidec. Lord Loudwater, buried in a Times leader, tugs his red-brown beard and snorts disgust through his nose. Lady Loudwater eats in thoughtful silence, brow faintly frowned. Melchisidec, excited by grilled sole, pricks his lordship's thigh and earns a futile kick at empty air.

From this comic breakfast, a country-house mystery grows, with marriage, money, and murder in its shadow. Jepson writes with dry, observant wit. A reader gets a wry Edwardian mystery, where a cat's prick opens a tale of dark deeds.
9897-introductory-american-history:
Henry Eldridge Bourne and Elbert Jay Benton, professors at Western Reserve University, wrote this school history in 1912. Instead of starting at Plymouth Rock, they begin far earlier, with the peoples of Europe and the ancient world who shaped the ideas America inherited.

Chapters follow Greeks and Romans, early Christians, medieval towns, traders, and explorers, before reaching English self-government and the Atlantic world. The aim is to show young readers why American institutions look as they do. It is a clear, old-style textbook, useful for its long view of the past.
a-double-barrelled-detective-story:
Mark Twain opens in Virginia in 1880, as he states, with a wedding between Jacob Fuller, a handsome young man of slender means, and a rich, proud girl of Cavalier blood. Her widowed father opposed the match bitterly. The marriage turns cruel, and the wronged husband swears a revenge that will take years to ripen.

Part two brings the case west. A boy with a miraculous sense of smell tracks men as a bloodhound tracks game. Sherlock Holmes himself appears there, to reason grandly and wrongly. Twain loads both barrels: one for the revenge melodrama, one for the detective story and its master. The result is part tragedy, part burlesque, and wholly his.
a-double-story:
A Double Story, by George MacDonald, is a fairy tale that opens in a country where nothing can be counted on. MacDonald warns that no one there can say whether it will rain or hail. The milk may sour or not. A week old baby may wake sweet tempered or cross, and nobody can tell beforehand. Fourteen chapters carry the disorder into two households at once, one rich and one poor.

The tale pairs a spoiled princess, Rosamond, with a shepherd's daughter, Agnes, whose lives the Wise Woman draws together. Pride in the palace and contentment in the cottage are weighed against each other, and the princess must learn what her nurses and parents never taught her. MacDonald, a minister turned storyteller, writes doctrine as wonder: selfishness shown from inside, and kindness practiced until it becomes strength.
a-fascinating-traitor-an-anglo-indian-st: Colonel Richard Henry Savage's Anglo-Indian novel opens with Major Alan Hawke brooding at Geneva over a past that reaches back to Delhi. Alliances, a veiled rosebud of Delhi and a diplomatic tiffin give way to a mysterious bungalow, a captivated viceroy and Prince Djiddin's visit to England. Daggers, councils at Granville and a French fishing boat carry an intrigue across India, Jersey and the Channel.
a-forgotten-empire-vijayanagar-a-contrib:
Robert Sewell reconstructs the great South Indian empire of Vijayanagar, a contribution, as his subtitle says, to the history of India. The empire held the Deccan against northern invaders for over two centuries, then fell in a single catastrophe. Sewell builds his account from chronicles, inscriptions, and the reports of Portuguese travelers who saw the capital in its glory.

Forty-one chapters trace the city's founding, its kings, its armies, its temples and markets, and the great battle that destroyed it. He prints the foreign visitors' descriptions at length, so the reader sees the bazaars and festivals through their eyes. The book revived interest in a lost capital whose ruins still cover miles of ground.
a-handbook-of-ethical-theory:
George Stuart Fullerton wrote his handbook, by his preface, to help students of ethics reach a clearer view of what morals mean and what ethical study aims at. He makes no apology for a clear, untechnical style. Part one examines the accepted content of morals: the codes of communities, justice, truth-telling, and the common good, then the codes of the moralists from Epicureans and Stoics onward.

Part two treats ethics as a science, its methods and materials. Part three studies man and his environment, bodily, mental, and social. Later parts take up theories of the good, duty, and the virtues. Fullerton writes fairly about every school, and the book served as a college text for students meeting moral philosophy in earnest.
a-knight-of-the-nineteenth-century:
Edward Payson Roe states his theme in verse in his preface: he best deserves a knightly crest who slays the evils that infest his soul within. The contents begin with Bad Training for a Knight and Both Apologize, then Chained to an Iceberg and Passion's Clamor. His young knight, Haldane, is a college man of strong impulses and weak guides.

Chapter titles chart the fall and recovery: birds of prey, their victim, Haldane arrested, our knight in jail, the world's verdict — a criminal — and the world's best offer, a prison. Roe, a minister whose novels outsold nearly everyone's, builds a tale of temptation, crime, and reform meant to arm young men for modern life.
a-maker-of-history:
A Maker of History is a 1905 novel by E Phillips Oppenheim, the English writer who became one of the most successful thriller authors of his age. Oppenheim worked in his father's leather business for almost twenty years before writing made him famous. By the time of this book he was building the career that would make him a pioneer of modern spy and intrigue fiction.

The novel belongs to his early run of suspense stories, the genre on which his reputation rests. Its title promises a tale in which private action shapes public events, told in the brisk, plot-driven style that won him a mass readership. Readers meet Oppenheim near the start of his long reign as a self-styled prince of storytellers.
a-strange-story:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton, a star of the Victorian book world, wrote this occult romance in 1862. Its hero is a young doctor drawn to a wise, dark man of great wealth and strange powers. Bulwer-Lytton had a deep taste for the lore of the hidden world.

The tale turns on mesmerism, alchemy, and the search for a drink that grants long life. Love, pride, and dread grow as the young man trades his soul's rest for dark lore. The book was the great public hit of its kind in its age, and it still grips.
a-summer-in-a-canyon-a-california-story:
Kate Douglas Wiggin pitches camp in Las Flores Cañon in California, in this popular edition of 1914, and lists her campers like a playbill: Dr. Paul Winship as mine host, his wife as guardian angel, small Dicky the scamp, Bell the camp poetess, Polly Oliver, Margery Noble, and Hop Yet, the Chinese cook. Eleven chapters cover preparation, the journey, and life in the cañon.

A lost heir apparent, rhymes and reasons, Queen Elsie's visit, Polly's birthday in two halves, and camp-fire stories fill the summer. The young people climb, ride, and act plays among the live oaks. Wiggin wrote the tale for young readers, and its sunshine and good humor made it a favorite California story.
a-tramp-through-the-bret-harte-country:
Thomas Dykes Beasley wrote A Tramp Through the Bret Harte Country as a walking tour of Gold Rush California. Beasley, author of The Coming of Portolá, follows the mining country Bret Harte made famous. Charles A. Murdock supplies a foreword. The chapters move town by town through the Sierra foothills.

From Stockton the tramp reaches Angel's Camp, Tuttletown, Sonora, and Mokelumne Hill. Ruins of Coloma recall Marshall, who found the first gold and died poor. Placerville, Grass Valley, and Nevada City yield pioneers' recollections. Old-timers explain the origin of mining laws and remember Harte himself. Beasley mixes memoir, gossip, and scenery with obvious affection. His book preserves the glamour of the old mining towns as their generation passed, photographs and all.
a-young-girl-s-diary:
An anonymous girl of the upper middle class kept this diary from age eleven to fourteen and a half, and the contents divide it by her school years. The edition is translated by Eden and Cedar Paul, as the title page states, and prefaced by a letter from Sigmund Freud dated April 27, 1915. Freud calls the diary a gem: nothing before it, he writes, lets readers see so clearly into the soul of a growing girl.

The editor states that nothing was toned down, added, or suppressed, apart from changed names to protect the writer. The entries follow friendships made and broken, family relations deepening, first love, and the dawning of sexual knowledge and the burden of keeping it secret. Freud commends the book to educators and psychologists.
aesthetic-poetry:
Walter Pater's essay Aesthetic Poetry defines the school of English verse that took art itself for its country. The aesthetic poetry, he writes, is neither a copy of Greek or medieval work nor a simple idealizing of modern life. It builds, above the transfigured worlds of older poetry, a still fainter and more spectral world, literally an artificial earthly paradise. Its secret is a kind of inverted homesickness, a thirst for escape that no actual life satisfies. Rossetti's ballads and William Morris's earthly paradise stand behind his account.

The essay first served as part of his Renaissance studies, and it reads as that book's manifesto in small. Sensation, strangeness, and beauty added to beauty are its tests. Readers get Pater's criticism at its most concentrated here, a whole movement explained from inside by its finest prose stylist.
all-roads-lead-to-calvary:
Jerome K. Jerome opens in an old London church, in the 1919 Hutchinson edition used here, where a young woman journalist slips in during a service. She had meant only to gather copy about old churches and their famous dead. Instead something in the service catches her, and the visit starts a change in her life.

Eighteen chapters follow Joan among editors, reformers, soldiers, and seekers in the years around the Great War. Talk of faith, feminism, and the price of public work fills the novel, as Joan tests what she owes herself against what she owes others. Jerome, famous for comedy, writes here in earnest, and the title states his theme: every road of sacrifice leads one way.
all-sorts-and-conditions-of-men-an-impos:
All Sorts and Conditions of Men, subtitled An Impossible Story, is a novel by Walter Besant about rich and poor meeting in London's East End. Angela Messenger, an idealistic Cambridge graduate with inherited wealth, resolves to use her money for good. She changes her name and takes lodgings in a Stepney boarding-house, determined to understand the East End and its people from inside.

At the same time, the young aristocrat Harry Le Breton haunts the same streets, discovering his own origins and a new sense of kinship with the poor. The novel works at once as a condition-of-England story and as New Woman fiction. It became one of Besant's best-known books, famous for imagining what goodwill and money might do in the slums.
an-essay-on-the-trial-by-jury:
Lysander Spooner argues his case across twelve chapters and an appendix on taxation. Juries, he says, have the right and duty to judge the justice of the law itself. They are not limited to the facts of a case. His first chapter states the claim outright. He grounds it in Magna Carta, whose history and language fill the second chapter.

Further chapters pile up proofs from the old common law, jurors' oaths, and judges' oaths, then handle objections and civil suits. Spooner calls modern juries and judges illegal where they deny this right. The essay, by an abolitionist lawyer, became a classic statement of the jury's power to refuse unjust laws.
an-historical-mystery-the-gondreville-my:
Honoré de Balzac opens in the autumn of 1803, under the Consulate, in Katharine Prescott Wormeley's translation. A senator, Gondreville, is seized by masked men, and a young nobleman has vanished. Royalist plotters, secret police, and old families of the Aube all hold pieces of the truth.

Two parts follow Laurence de Cinq-Cygne, a brave young royalist, through hiding, arrest, and trial, while agents of Fouché hunt the conspirators. Balzac based his plot on a real unsolved kidnapping of the period. The novel mixes detective work, court scenes, and the politics of a France not yet settled under Napoleon. Its tension comes from secrets kept under threat of the scaffold.
an-introduction-to-the-study-of-robert-b:
Hiram Corson's study guide introduces readers to the poetry of Robert Browning. The title page names Corson, a professor of English literature at Cornell, as the author. This printing is the third edition, first published in 1886. It opens with a personal letter from Browning himself, dated December 1886, thanking Corson and approving the notes.

Corson writes for students who find Browning hard going. He explains Browning's aims and methods, then works through major poems with commentary meant to open their dramatic monologues and dense thought to a first reader. The book reflects how Browning's reputation was being built in American universities during his lifetime, with the poet's blessing on the enterprise.
aristotle-on-the-art-of-poetry:
Aristotle's treatise on poetry appears here in Ingram Bywater's translation, first published at Oxford in 1920, with a preface by Gilbert Murray. Murray opens in Plato's Republic, where Plato, having denounced poetry as a false siren, offers her champions a chance to defend her in prose. Aristotle, he suggests, took up that chance.

The treatise itself takes poetry apart: imitation, the kinds of poem, and above all tragedy, with its plot, character, thought, and diction. Aristotle ranks plot first, explains the unity of action, and names the purging of pity and fear. No short book has governed storytelling longer; dramatists and critics still argue in its terms.
black-caesar-s-clan-a-florida-mystery-st:
Albert Payson Terhune sets Black Caesar's Clan among the Florida Keys, and his foreword builds the islands from scratch. A coral worm piles the reef upward, a mangrove bud takes root in salt water, and soil gathers in the tangle. On such a key, generations later, stands the hidden world of the tale.

Chapters follow a hidden path, a man in the dark, and a stranger from nowhere. Traps and a trapper, a siege, and a figure in white raise the mystery. The clan descends from Black Caesar, the pirate whose name haunts these waters. Terhune, famous for dog stories, here writes a treasure-and-smuggling mystery of the mangrove coast. Mockingbirds, ghost trees, and battle in the day carry a Florida adventure steeped in local colour.
c-sar-s-column-a-story-of-the-twentieth-: Ignatius Donnelly's 1890 future novel, signed with the pen name Edmund Boisgilbert, imagines a twentieth century ruled by an oligarchy above a ruined underworld. A visitor to the great city meets Estella Washington, joins a secret brotherhood and watches plots, spies and a council of the rich drive the world toward ruin. Gabriel's utopia offers the book's counter-vision of a just order.
catherine-a-story:
William Makepeace Thackeray published Catherine as a story by Ikey Solomons Jr, his burlesque answer to the Newgate novels that glamorized criminals. His heroine is Catherine Hayes, a real murderess burned at Tyburn in 1726 for killing her husband with her lover and a lodger. The contents promise genteel society, a narcotic administered, and Mr Brock's autobiography.

Brock, the villain posing as Captain Wood, receives curtseys and humble service from the company he deceives, while Catherine's son Tom Billings grows accomplished in crime. Thackeray keeps interrupting to scold readers who want vice made charming. The experiment, his first novel, ran in Fraser's Magazine and still shows his satire learning its trade on unsuitable material, deliberately.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-fleu:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Fleury, more fully Fleury-Saint-Benoît, calls it among the oldest and most famed Benedictine houses of western Europe. Its modern name, Saint-Benoît-sur-Loire, covers both monastery and township, and its imposing monastic church still looms solitary in the Loire plain.

The abbey's list of abbots holds eighty-nine names, from Merovingian St. Mommolus and Carolingian St. Abbo to Odet de Coligny and Armand du Plessis, Cardinal Richelieu. The last twenty-two abbots held Fleury in commendam, and Georges-Louis Phélypeaux, Archbishop of Bourges, ends the list in 1789. The entry celebrates a house whose church outlived its monks' stately home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achonry:
Achonry, Gaelic Achadh-Chonnaire or Connary's Field, is an Irish diocese under Tuam's archdiocese. The village stands picturesquely in the south of County Sligo. There St. Finian, who died in 552, founded a church and monastery on land given by the prince of Clann Chonnaire. Over it he placed Nathi O Hara, his pupil from Clonard, always called Cruimthir-Nathi, the Priest Nathi.

The monastery and its head soon won a remarkable reputation. A diocese formed about 560, with Nathi reputed its first bishop, perhaps only abbot-superior under the Irish monastic system. He is the diocese's patron, feasted on 9 August, and his monastery church served as cathedral, with traces still visible. The diocese, once also called Leyney, now covers parts of Roscommon and Mayo and most of Sligo.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-adultery:
Adultery is considered here only with reference to morality, while its bearing on the marriage bond belongs under divorce. The discussion runs under three heads: nature, guilt, and duties laid on offenders. Adultery means carnal ties between a married person and an unmarried one, or another's spouse. It differs from fornication in that one or both agents are married.

That marriage need only be ratified, not yet consummated, what church writers call matrimonium ratum. Sex with one engaged to another does not, on the general view, count as adultery. Yet lewd acts between a married person and someone other than the lawful spouse, while less guilty, share adultery's malice, as Sanchez notes. St. Alphonsus adds that even lawful spouses commit adultery when intercourse takes the form of sodomy. Among savages generally, adultery meets stern condemnation and punishment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alan-of-tewke:
Alan of Tewkesbury was a Benedictine abbot and writer who died in 1202. Gervase of Canterbury, a chronicler of the time, states Alan was English by race, not Norman or immigrant. He supposedly spent some years at Benevento in Italy, then entered Canterbury's Benedictine novitiate, becoming prior in 1179.

He zealously espoused the clergy's cause against Henry II in the struggle leading to St. Thomas's martyrdom. He was removed from Canterbury to Tewkesbury Abbey, where opposing Henry's encroachments on church rights grew harder. His intimacy with St. Thomas and lifelong acquaintance with the age's church-state controversies fitted him for the Life of St. Thomas, printed as Life of Becket in the Materials for the History of Thomas Becket. Alan also gathered the saint's epistles into an arrangement. Critics doubt the genuineness of other works ascribed to him by tradition.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambrosian-lib:
The Ambrosian Library, among the world's famous libraries, was founded by Cardinal Federigo Borromeo at Milan between 1603 and 1609. Borromeo meant it to be more than books and art: a writers' college, a savants' seminary, and a fine-arts school. It stood near Milan's then-centre, by the Holy Sepulchre Church, its plans drawn by Fabio Mangone.

A plain Ionic portico inscribed BIBLIOTHECA AMBROSIANA opens to a single ground-floor hall. The library opened not only to college members but to Milan's citizens and all visiting strangers. Borromeo appealed to friends, popes, cardinals, princes, priests, and religious, who gave generously, Benedictines among them. It could not rival the Vatican, Florence's Laurentiana, or Venice's Marciana, yet enjoyed greater popularity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ambulatory:
An ambulatory is a cloister, gallery, or alley, a sheltered straight or circular place for walking, and the aisle circling a church's apse. The central eastern apse was often ringed by a semicircular aisle, in three species: with tangential chapels, without chapels, and variants. By far the commonest type radiates chapels to the northeast, east, and southeast, while a chapelless Romanesque ambulatory is so rare that supposed examples count doubtful. A rectangular ambulatory appears at Romsey's eastern chapel.

Ambulatories run inside or outside buildings, in thoroughfares wholly or partly covered or open to the sky, for walking only. The term also covers a covered walkway round a building, such as a peripteral temple's column-and-cella space or monastic cloisters like Pisa's Campo Santo. It can also mean an ancient basilica's atrium, and can equal cloister or atrium.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andre-hercule:
Andre-Hercule de Fleury was born at Lodeve in 1653 and died at Paris in 1742. A protege of Cardinal de Bonzi, he became chaplain to Maria Theresa and then, in 1683, to Louis XIV. He was made Bishop of Frejus in 1698, but resigned in 1715, taking the Abbey of Tournus and becoming tutor to the young Louis XV. Cold and imperturbable, he stayed in the background during the regency.

When Louis XV came of age in 1723, Fleury had the Duc de Bourbon made prime minister, quarrelled with him, and pretended to retire to Issy. Louis exiled the duke and gave Fleury the government, though Fleury never took the title. Made cardinal in 1726, he guided French politics until his death. D'Argenson joked that Richelieu bled France, Mazarin purged it, and Fleury put it on a diet, pointing to his economy, which slowed the military navy while merchant shipping grew.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antiphonary:
Antiphonary, Latin antiphonarium, Greek antíphonon, is a liturgical choir book, originally holding principally the antiphons of the Roman liturgy. It once covered Mass antiphons (antiphonarium Missarum, or graduale) and Hour antiphons (antiphonarium officii); now it means only the sung Office portions.

The Missal holds Mass texts, the Breviary Office texts; Mass chants the choir sings carry no notation there, only the accentus. The antiphonary holds the sung portions with notation. The Gregorian antiphonary reached England with Augustine, sent by Gregory, as Egbert of York attests. Under Pius X the commended Ratisbon edition gave way to the commanded Vatican edition, its texts and melodies revised to match recent chant studies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arthur-o-lear:
Arthur O'Leary, Franciscan, preacher, and polemical writer, was born at Faniobbus, Iveleary, County Cork, in 1729 and died in London on 8 January 1802. Educated with the Franciscans of Saint Malo, where he was ordained and served as prison chaplain until 1777, he returned to Cork for missionary work. Famous as preacher, writer, and controversialist, he published tracts marked by learning, religious feeling, toleration, and steadfast loyalty to the crown.

His zeal against religious bigotry drove him to rash admissions and to danger of heterodoxy, or unorthodox belief. His writings include A Defence of the Divinity of Christ and the Immortality of the Soul, and Loyalty Asserted, or the Test Oath Vindicated. They also include an Address to Roman Catholics on the feared French invasion, an Essay on Toleration, and a reply to John Wesley. A wit and honorary member of the Monks of the Screw, he was called the Catholic Swift of Ireland.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-assumption-of:
The Assumption of Mary, feast on 15 August, is also known in old liturgical books as Pausatio, Nativitas for heaven, Mors, Depositio, and Dormitio of St. Mary. It has a double object: Mary's happy departure from this life, and the taking up of her body into heaven. It ranks as the principal feast of the Virgin. About the day, year, and manner of her death, nothing certain is known.

The first known reference to the Assumption appears in the Greek work On the Death of the Holy Lady, while Catholic faith derives knowledge of the mystery from apostolic teaching. Epiphanius, who died in 403, admitted he knew nothing definite about it. Dates assigned range from three to fifteen years after Christ's ascension, and two cities claim her departure, Jerusalem and Ephesus, with common consent favouring Jerusalem, where her tomb is shown.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-athenry:
Athenry is an inland town in County Galway, in western Ireland. Its old name, Athnere, points to a ford linked with a king. Anglo-Norman settlers made it their first town in Connacht, and it grew into a place of real weight in the Middle Ages. Its Dominican house, finished in 1216, grew rich and served as burial ground for the Earls of Ulster.

Fire, sack, and war wore the town down over the centuries. Its church burned in 1423, the town was sacked in 1577, and northern forces burned it again in 1596. A Franciscan friary founded in 1464 added to its church life, and the Dominicans briefly revived their house as a university in 1644. Cromwellian ruin left only tower and east window standing, and the Board of Works repaired the remains in 1893.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auguste-franc:
Auguste Francois Maunoury was a French Hellenist and Bible commentator, a scholar of Greek and Scripture, born in 1811 who died at Seez in 1898. He studied classics at the preparatory seminary of Seez, returned there after his theology course, and spent his whole priestly career in that house. Until 1852 he taught classics with great success. He then held the rhetoric chair for twenty-two years and wrote Greek grammars that marked him as one of the best Greek scholars of his day.

Around 1866 he turned to commenting on Scripture, at first in his diocesan paper, and after 1875 he gave himself fully to Bible study. From 1878 he published commentaries on all the New Testament Epistles in five volumes, leaning on Chrysostom and Theodoret. In 1894 he added a two-volume Latin commentary on the Psalms, based on the Vulgate and the Septuagint. His one apologetic work defended religion for worldly readers in 1887.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-auguste-josep:
Auguste Joseph Alphonse Gratry was a French priest and writer born at Lille in 1805 who died at Montreux in 1872. After classical studies and the Paris polytechnic school, he spent months at the Bischenberg convent and chose the priesthood. He was ordained at Strasburg in 1832, directed the College Stanislas from 1841, and served as chaplain of the Ecole Normale Superieure from 1846. A polemic with Vacherot over the Alexandrine school cost both men their posts.

With Abbe Petetot he worked to restore the Oratory in France, and in 1863 he became professor of moral theology at Paris. In 1867 he entered the French Academy, taking the seat once held by Voltaire. At the Vatican Council of 1870 he wrote against papal infallibility, and his letters were condemned by the Bishop of Strasburg. The entry finds in his pages both ideal grandeur and a vague, dreamy cast, with high thoughts on the soul's rise to the infinite.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aumbry:
An aumbry, also written ambry or aumbrye, is a cupboard, a word reaching English through French from the classical Latin armarium. It never lost that broad sense, but even in classical Latin it had gained a special sense: a cupboard for holding books. In the Middle Ages that book sense ruled widely, so that the tenth-century rule of Cluny calls the library itself the armarium. the monk in charge, the armarius or librarian, was usually also the precentor, the choirmaster.

Aelfric's Anglo-Saxon glossary renders the native word for book-hoard as library, armarium, or archive. A proverb current by 1170 likened a library-less monastery to a fortress with no weapons. Because cupboards stored vestments and church plate too, the word also came to mean the sacristy, the room for sacred vessels and robes. In German, the child of armarium, Almerei, still means the sacristy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-balderic-baud:
Balderic, also called Baudry, was a monk of Liege, a writer and teacher of the twelfth century. He was born at Florennes in Belgium, date unknown, and died about 1157. He served as proctor at Pope Eugene III's court and followed him to France when Arnold of Brescia drove him from Rome. At the Paris synod of 1147 he met Albero, Archbishop of Trier, who made him head of Trier's cathedral school.

While Albero lived, Balderic stayed his friend and adviser. After Albero's death he wrote his biography, remarkable for its classical Latin. That life appears in Monumenta Germaniae Scriptores, volume eight, and in Patrologia Latina, volume 154. The Paris meeting thus fixed the course of his later life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baldwin-of-ca:
Baldwin of Canterbury was the thirty-ninth Archbishop, a native of Exeter, who died on 19 November 1190. Ordained priest and made archdeacon by Exeter's bishop, he became a Cistercian at Ford Abbey and its abbot. In 1180 he rose to Worcester's bishopric and was elected primate the same year. Canterbury's monks disputed the election, backing Battle's abbot, then Cardinal Theobald of Ostia.

Henry II stepped in, and Baldwin, who would accept only a monks' election, was installed. Disputes with the monks drew in Richard and the Holy See, though his right to name priors stood. As legate in Wales he held a visitation in 1187 and preached the Crusade in 1188. In 1190 he sailed for the Holy Land with Hubert of Salisbury, funding two hundred knights and three hundred retainers. He died at Acre, leaving all he owned for the Holy Land.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-baptistery:
A baptistery is the separate building where baptism was once solemnly given, or the part of a church later set apart for it. In ancient use the word also meant a basin, pool, or bathing place. Its Latin form, baptisterium, covered both the vessel holding baptismal water and the chapel enshrining it. Name and form seem borrowed from pagan baths: Pliny calls bathing apartments baptisteria, and Pompeii's baths show the same use.

The earliest surviving type is the catacomb chamber with its baptismal pool, as at Priscilla and the Pontian cemetery. Once churches were built, a special, usually circular or polygonal building held the font at its center. A circular walkway gave room for ministers, witnesses, and the many neophytes of Easter and Pentecost. Rome absorbed the baptistery into the basilica earliest, though a small late one still stands by Bergamo's cathedral.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-belfry:
A belfry is the upper part of a church tower holding bells, or a detached bell tower like Italy's campanile. The term also covers the timber frame supporting bells and the loft from which they are rung. Originally it meant a wooden, movable tower where sentinels rang alarm bells or besiegers overlooked a fortified place.

In England the tower usually joins the church, though Evesham, Berkeley, and Chichester have detached examples, and Pembridge's is wholly wooden. In Belgium, belfries expressed new communal independence: the bell right was a first charter privilege, summoning citizens and symbolizing power. Ghent's belfry, begun in 1183 with stonework done by 1337, once bore a wooden spire to 237 feet. Tournay's, the oldest surviving, is much altered by modern additions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-story:
Blessed John Story, a martyr, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in 1504, he died at Tyburn in 1571 after education at Oxford, where he headed Broadgates Hall, now Pembroke College, from 1537 to 1539. Entering Parliament for Hindon in 1547, he was jailed for opposing the Act of Uniformity in 1549.

After Mary's accession he returned from Louvain and served as chancellor to Bishop Bonner, sitting for Wiltshire seats until Elizabeth's displeasure at his outspoken opposition in 1560. Kidnapped abroad and brought to London, he was tried and executed. The entry presents a lawyer whose tongue never learned caution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-blessed-marga:
Margaret of Hungary, daughter of King Bela I, spent her whole life as a Dominican nun. Her parents had vowed their next child to religion when Hungary was freed from the Tatars. Born in 1242, she entered the Veszprem convent in 1245. She took the habit at four. At ten she moved to her parents' convent on Margaret Island near Buda.

She refused her father's plan for a marriage to Ottokar II of Bohemia. She took solemn vows at eighteen. She lived in contemplation, fasting, and hard penance, including a hair garment and an iron girdle. Venerated at once after her death in 1271, she was never canonized. Pius VI allowed her veneration in 1789, and her feast falls on 18 January.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-breviary:
The Breviary, the book holding the whole canonical office, began as an abridgment and grew into a full liturgical library in one volume. Its name first meant a book of rubrics, a sort of Ordo, and the title for a book with the entire office dates from the eleventh century. Gregory VII's abridged Roman Court order gave the name fresh force, since breviary means abridgment.

Six parts organize the entry: definition, contents, the hours, component parts of the office, history, and reforms. It traces early uses by Alcuin and Prudentius of Troyes, the Monte Cassino Ordo of about 1100, and the growth from scattered books, Psalter, Antiphonary, Responsoriary, and Lectionary, into one work. The name itself is illogical today, since such a book should be a Plenarium, not an abridgment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-breviary-hymn:
The Breviary Hymns of the Rosary, four hymns for the feast's proper office granted by Leo XIII on 5 August 1888, compress each mystery into a single stanza. Some critics credited Leo himself, famed for his Latin verse and Rosary devotion, but the hymns trace to the Dominican Office of 1834 and to Eustace Sirena, a devout client of Mary. They later reached Segovia in 1841 and Venice in 1848.

Each hymn holds five four-line stanzas of classical dimeter iambics, apart from the shared doxology. First Vespers sings the Joyful Mysteries, Matins the Sorrowful, and Lauds the Glorious, one stanza per mystery. Second Vespers sums all three sets in three stanzas. A frame stanza gathers them whole, and a closing call bids the singer weave from the rosary a flower crown for the Mother of fair love.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bribery:
Bribery, the payment or promise of money to bend a public trust to private gain, is judged here on moral grounds alone. Judges must serve justice without fear or favor, and those who appoint officers, award contracts, enforce laws, or elect lawmakers must seek the common good. Taking a bribe for such acts betrays the trust and shares guilt for the unfit or crooked men put in place.

Hard cases test the rule, since a voter may see little difference between candidates and feel no injustice in selling his vote. The entry still calls the act immoral and rightly banned by law. A bribe blinds judgment, blunts discrimination, and leaves the voter unable to weigh whether his man is worthy of the post he seeks to fill.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-caius-3rd-cen:
Caius, also called Kay or Key, was a physician and scholar born at Norwich on 6 October 1510 who died at London on 29 July 1573. He entered Cambridge in 1529, took his M.A. in 1535, and studied medicine at Padua under Montanus and Vesalius, earning his doctorate there in 1541. After touring Italy, France, and Germany he returned to England in 1544 and lectured on anatomy in London for twenty years.

His book on the sweating sickness of 1552 stands as the best account of that epidemic, and he also translated and commented on Galen and Hippocrates. With his medical earnings he refounded his Cambridge college, Gonville, in 1558, ever since known as Gonville and Caius College. He served as royal physician under Edward VI and Elizabeth until dismissed in 1568 for his Catholic faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canonical-ere:
A religious house is a fixed home for religious persons, a community in the strict sense, ruled by a superior and keeping its order's rule. It differs from a grange or farm, a villa for recreation, and a hospice for traveling religious. Lawful erection needs the Holy See's permission, certain in countries under the decree Romanos Pontifices, including the United States and England, and required also for Italy.

It also needs the assent of the ordinary, a rule approved at Chalcedon in 451 and restored by Trent after mendicant privileges had worn it down. The bishop must hear those the house might harm, such as nearby orders or the local people, though the parish priest cannot object unless parochial rights are granted. Twelve religious must be provided for, or the house falls under the ordinary. Moving a house within one place needs no Roman permission, since that is transfer, not erection.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-canterbury:
Canterbury served as England's leading archbishopric from 597 until 1558, when Cardinal Pole, the last Catholic archbishop, died. The entry opens with Augustine's mission from Gregory the Great. It tells of his welcome from Queen Bertha of Kent. It recounts the conversion of King Ethelbert with many thousands of Saxons in the year of Augustine's landing.

Gregory had planned archbishoprics at London and York, yet Augustine's success fixed the southern see at Canterbury instead. Later sections trace the archbishops, metropolitan rights, the diocese, the cathedral, and the see's history. Drawing on Bede and a long shelf of local histories, the entry covers a church that shaped English Christianity for nearly a thousand years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-category:
Category began as a Greek legal word for accusation, which Aristotle turned into a logical term for attributing a predicate to a subject. Boethius gave it the Latin name predicament. The categories are the widest classes of predicates that can be said of an individual thing, the highest genera under which narrower ideas fall.

Whether Aristotle meant them as divisions of words, ideas, or things is still debated, and the article shows how they fit each reading. Taken as ideas they belong to logic, as words to grammar, and as things to ontology, where they name the ultimate classes of finite being. The piece defends the scheme as a workable simplification of reality for inquiry.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chambery:
Chambéry is an archdiocese covering the whole arrondissement of Chambéry in Savoy, except eight communes, plus communes around Annecy and Albertville. In 1467 Paul II set up a chapter answering directly to the Holy See. It met in the ducal chapel that Amadeus IX of Savoy and Yolande of France had built for the Holy Winding-Sheet. Sixtus IV joined it to the deanery of Savoy.

Leo X made the deanery an archbishopric in 1515, but Francis I objected. Only in 1775 did Pius VI separate it from Grenoble, creating it a bishopric with its see at Chambéry in 1779. Revolutionary France formed the constitutional Diocese of Mont-Blanc in 1792. The 1802 Concordat set up a Chambéry-Geneva diocese, and a bull of 1817 made Chambéry an archdiocese with Aosta as suffragan. At the close of 1905 it counted 164,424 people.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-changanacherr:
Changanacherry is a Vicariate Apostolic in Travancore, British India, created on 28 July 1896. Its first vicar apostolic in fact, Mathew Makil, Bishop of Tralles in title, was consecrated on 25 October 1896. The vicariate was founded to serve the Syro-Malabar Rite's Native Indian Christians. Five deaneries of Nordist Syrians, descended from native Malabar castes, and two of Sudists, descended from fourth-century immigrant Syrians, belong to it.

Its territory runs south to Purakad, bounded north by the Vicariate of Ernakulam, east by the Ghats, and west by the Gulf of Arabia. Catholics number 140,172 out of 900,000 people, served by 95 churches and 57 chapels and a native clergy of 283. Schools flourish: 418 native parish schools hold 14,328 pupils, and a Malayalam weekly paper speaks for the Catholic press.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chantry:
A chantry endows priests to sing or say Mass for its founder's soul, or for souls named by him. Most also performed other offices: singing in a collegiate church or cathedral choir, curate in outlying districts, chaplain in hospitals and jails, or schoolmaster or librarian. The institution was essentially liturgical, and it needed a place where the incumbent could say Mass.

As a rule, space was screened off between the great pillars of a nave or transept and an altar erected there. Sometimes an addition opening into the choir was built, or a detached building. Detached chantry chapels, in churchyards, outlying districts, or at bridge entrances, often had two stories: the lower for religious uses and the upper as the incumbent's home or schoolroom. Founding a chantry needed the ordinary's consent and a fund large enough for its building.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chartulary:
An entry on the chartulary, a medieval book or roll holding copies of documents about the foundation, privileges, and legal rights of churches, towns, guilds, schools, and families. Also called a cartularium or codex diplomaticus, it sometimes means a bound set of originals rather than copies. Gregory of Tours mentions rolls of charters in the sixth century. The oldest surviving chartularies date from the tenth, and those from the tenth to the thirteenth centuries are very numerous.

Copyists sometimes reproduced originals exactly and sometimes altered wording, modernised names, or even changed the sense to stretch a privilege. A chartulary's worth as history therefore turns on how faithfully it keeps the original meaning, a question for historical criticism. The entry ranks an honest chartulary above a private letter or a chronicler's tale, and points to the great French catalogues and to Gross on English sources.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-children-of-m:
An entry on the Sodality of the Children of Mary Immaculate, a confraternity for young girls that grew from the apparition of the Miraculous Medal. The Virgin appeared to Sister Catherine Labouré, a Paris novice of the Daughters of Charity, in 1830, and trial associations soon formed in houses of the order. A rescript of June 1847 empowered the superior general to erect the confraternity in every Sisters of Charity house for girls in their schools and workrooms.

The same favour was extended in 1850 to boys taught by the Lazarist priests and the Sisters of Charity, and in 1876 Pius the Ninth opened membership to girls outside those schools. Leo the Thirteenth confirmed the privileges in 1897 and 1903. Members wear the Miraculous Medal on a blue ribbon, and by 1897 the sodality counted 100,000 living members worldwide, with 400,000 registered since its first canonical erection at Paris in 1847.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chivalry:
An entry on chivalry, the institution of the medieval knight, viewed from its military, social, and religious sides and traced to its fall. In war, chivalry meant the heavy cavalry that formed the chief force of the age. Its marks were costly arms, from the mail coat of the Crusades to the plate armour of the fourteenth century. A knight needed at least three horses, for battle, travel, and baggage, plus attendants to bear the shield and help him mount.

Socially, chivalry softened into courtly display, with jousts, tournaments, and banquet-hall vows. The Vow of the Swan dates to 1306, and the Vow of the Pheasant to 1454, when 150 knights swore to rescue Constantinople and achieved nothing. Literature first lifted chivalry, then mocked it, from Chaucer to Cervantes. Revived infantry, Swiss pikemen, and at last gunpowder ended the horseman's reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chrismal-chri:
An entry on the chrismal and chrismatory, the vessels that hold the holy oils consecrated by the bishop on Holy Thursday. Those oils are oil of catechumens, oil of the sick, and chrism, which gives the vessels their name. The word chrismal once meant other things too. It named a cloth sheath for relics, a pall or corporal, and a vessel for the Eucharist. It also named the long white hooded robes of the newly baptised, worn from Holy Saturday to Low Sunday.

In present use the two words mean the oil vessels. One set keeps the yearly supply in the cathedral sacristy, the other holds the daily need in the parish church. Both must be gold, silver, tin, or pewter. Longer vessels look like little jars, smaller ones like jointed cylindrical boxes. Each bears a stamped letter for its oil, so the oils are never confused.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-church-histor:
A vast entry on church history, the scientific study and methodical telling of the Church's growth in time. History in general traces how human life changes through facts, events, and situations, and religion's history among peoples is its noblest form. Reason holds there is one true religion, and revelation shows it to be the Christian religion, in particular the Catholic Church, visible and concrete.

Church history therefore studies the institution Jesus Christ founded and the Holy Spirit guides for human salvation. Religion is social by nature, since moral life binds people together, and Christianity all the more aims at organisation. The entry sets out the nature, office, sources, and divisions of the discipline, from its method to its periods. It defends its place as the most important and edifying branch of the history of religion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-clerestory:
A clerestory once meant any traceried opening or window in a church, in an aisle, tower, cloister, or screen. Now it means the windows in an aisled nave, or the wall holding the high windows. Sometimes these windows are very small, mere quatrefoils or spherical triangles. Yet in large buildings they matter greatly for beauty and utility, above all where nave and side aisles allow light to enter from above the aisle roofs into the church body.

Fergusson's theory holds that Greek temple interiors were lit by a clerestory, similar inside to those of great Egyptian temples but adapted outside to a sloping roof. Countersinking into the roof made three ridges where light entered, while the roof's regular shape and ridge lines stayed intact between openings. All surviving remains and ancient descriptions support the theory, the article says, though Simpson regards it as extremely improbable.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-confraternity:
Herbert Thurston's entry treats the Confraternity of the Holy Rosary, following his Rosary article's verdict: no sound evidence places any Rosary confraternity before the last quarter of the fifteenth century. Dominican guilds existed, but proof linking them to the Rosary fails. Through Alan de Rupe's preaching, associations rose shortly before 1475. Cologne's 1474 foundation by Father James Sprenger stands most famous, drawing enrollees worldwide. A 1486 Plumpton letter shows a London priest registering his Yorkshire patron's name with Our Lady of Cologne.

Later forms widen the picture. The Perpetual Rosary organizes day-and-night recitation among associates taking allotted shares. The Living Rosary, begun in 1826 and independent of the confraternity, rings fifteen members who each say one decade daily, completing the whole Rosary together. Another Rosary confraternity dates from the seventeenth century. Thurston thus guards the early history against assumption, while mapping the living devotions that grew from it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
Francesca Steele's entry follows the Congregation of Our Lady of Calvary, founded at Poitiers in 1617 by Antoinette of Orléans-Longueville with Capuchin Father Joseph Le Clerc du Tremblay. Widowed in 1596, Antoinette entered Toulouse's Feuillantines in 1599. After profession the pope made her coadjutrix to Fontevrault's abbess for reform work.
