There she met Father Joseph, her director, fresh from l'Encloître's reform. When Paul V ordered a training seminary, that convent filled with novices. In 1614 Antoinette built a new Poitiers convent to Our Lady of Calvary, cradle of the congregation.

With papal leave she left Fontevrault, taking nuns who sought the strict Benedictine rule. Fontevrault's abbess first consented, then objected. Only after Antoinette's death did Father Joseph set constitutions and win Gregory XV's erecting bull. The Holy See finally approved it on 17 January 1827. Revolution crushed it, restoration revived it, and by 1860 twenty French houses stood, seven surviving.

Sister Mary St. David's entry follows the Presentation of Mary congregation, devoted to educating young girls. Mother Marie Rivier founded it in 1796 at Theuyts, Ardèche. The mother-house stands at Saint-Andéol, Ardèche, under superior general Mother Marie Ste-Honorine. Canada's provincial house, founded 18 October 1853 by Mgr Prince, first Bishop of Saint Hyacinthe, doubles as mother-house, where vows are made.

First six, led by Mother Marie St-Maurice, settled at Sainte-Marie de Monnoir, where pastor Crevier had prepared a convent. They opened a boarding school and a day class, both prosperous. The novitiate moved to Saint Hugues in 1855, then to Saint Hyacinthe in 1858, into a convent lately held by Montreal's Notre Dames. Cramped quarters forced a large new building near the seminary, occupied 1876, the older house an academy. An annex followed, students installed in 1907. Thirty Canadian houses and sixteen American houses educate 13,670 children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregations:
Florence McGahan's entry covers two Mount Calvary congregations, first the Daughters. Virginia Centurione, Genoa's Doge's daughter and Gasparo Grimaldi Bracelli's wife, founded them in 1619. In famine she gathered abandoned children into Monte Calvario's Santa Maria del Refugio dei Tribolati. Associates chose common life, Francis's rule, and service of poor and sick, bound by a solemn promise of perseverance, not vows. Marquess Brignole funded a second house in 1641, earning sisters the Brignole name.

Pius VII invited them to Rome in 1815, and Gregory XVI assigned an Esquiline house near Saint Norbert's in 1833. Hubert Charpentier formed the Missionary Society in 1633, priests honoring the Sacred Passion and spreading the Faith in Huguenot regions. First houses stood at Betharram and Notre Dame de Ceraison. Joined with a Capuchin association on Mont-Valérien at Louis XIII's instance, it won royal confirmation in 1650. Paris pastors joined, pilgrimages flowed there, but Revolution ended it.

The entry surveys Heart of Mary congregations, beginning with Nancy's Sisters. Mgr Menjaud, Bishop of Nancy and Toul, founded them in 1842 to teach girls trades and protect their virtue. Masson's statutes let them own only their houses, sending surplus to poor children and altar decoration. Perpetual Adoration graced the mother-house. Delaplace and Marie-Jeanne Moisan founded Paris's Sister-servants in 1860, teaching children and visiting the sick at hospitals and homes. Canada flourished with about 140 sisters and 2,500 children, plus six American communities.

Kobès founded Dakar's Daughters on 24 May 1858 for native women in Senegambia. Dupuis founded Pondicherry's Congregation at the synod's desire for young Indian girls' education. Pico Heights, Los Angeles, gained Sisters in July 1848. Rennes ladies running an incurables' home took the Daughters name in 1841. Turgeon and Marie Roy founded Quebec's Sister-Servants in 1859, with Monroe, Michigan, holding a sister foundation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cuthbert-arch:
A biographical entry follows Cuthbert, Archbishop of Canterbury, who died on 25 October 758. First heard of as Abbot of Liminge in Kent, he became Bishop of Hereford in 736. He was moved to Canterbury around 740. Journeying to Rome, he received the pallium, the woollen band marking an archbishop, and attended the Council of Clovesho in 742.

At his second Council of Clovesho in 747, called at Pope Zachary's wish, many canons guided monks' lives and bishops' and priests' duties. The council insisted that catechetical teaching be given in English. Its proceedings, sent to Saint Boniface, prompted similar reform in Germany. Cuthbert also won a great change for Canterbury. Archbishops, once buried at Saints Peter and Paul, were henceforth interred at Christ Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-denis-nicolas:
A life of Denis-Nicolas Le Nourry, a Maurist Benedictine writer born at Dieppe in 1647 who died at Saint-Germain in Paris in 1724. Schooled by Oratorians at home, he entered the Benedictines at Jumièges in 1665 and later helped publish Cassiodorus at Rouen and Ambrose at Rouen and Paris. His last forty years were spent in Paris.

His chief work, the Apparatus, appeared in two volumes in 1703 and 1715 as a guide to the Lyons collection of the Fathers. Long dissertations give each writer's life, the aim and genuineness of each work, and the age that shaped it. A 1710 edition argues that a tract on persecutors came from Lucius Caecilius rather than Lactantius, and he also edited Lactantius, Hilarianus, and a fragment on human origins.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-devotion-to-t:
A historical survey of devotion to the Blessed Virgin Mary, read as the Communion of Saints put into practice. Early centuries show no clear trace of Marian cult. The first plain saintly honour goes to martyrs, whose tombs hosted the sacrifice and whose yearly birthdays Christians kept from the second century. Tertullian and Cyprian sharpened the sense that martyrs win graces for others, and direct invocation followed.

Later ages widen the picture. The Collyridians' cake offerings drew Epiphanius's rebuke. Merovingian and Carolingian times fixed feasts such as the Assumption, and after 1000 devotion took organized shape in countless practices. Modern pages highlight the Litany of Loreto, the Lourdes apparitions of 1858, and the miraculous medal of Notre-Dame des Victoires in Paris.

A doctrinal and historical entry on devotion to the Heart of Mary, twin to the Sacred Heart devotion yet distinct from it. True devotion needs two things together. Homage must aim at the physical heart itself. Reading in it means seeing her inner life: joys and sorrows, virtues, and above all her love for God, for her divine Son, and for sinful children. Either element alone falls short.

History links the devotion with that of the Heart of Jesus while keeping its own thread, which the Gospel invites with quiet delicacy. Feast days vary by place: the Sunday after the Assumption octave, the third Sunday after Pentecost, early July, the Eudist feast of 8 February, and Notre-Dame-des-Victoires before Lent. No feast has yet been granted to the whole Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-diocesan-chan:
The diocesan chancery is the office that handles all written papers used in governing a diocese. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry places it under the bishop or his deputy, where documents are drawn up, copied, sent on, and filed. A record is kept of every official writing that goes out or comes in. The officer in charge is called the diocesan chancellor.

In many dioceses the chancellor holds powers that elsewhere belong only to the vicar-general. This is commonest in small dioceses run directly by the bishop, where the vicar-general is called only when the bishop is away or hindered. The entry thus opens a window onto the quiet paperwork that keeps a diocese running.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ecclesiastica:
Members of cathedral or collegiate chapters who hold both a foremost place and a measure of jurisdiction are ecclesiastical dignitaries. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry names the usual dignities as provost and dean, with custos and scholasticus at times. Their nomination and canonical institution rest largely with the pope, under common church law, special legislation such as concordats, and custom.

Dignities differ from personates, whose holders hold only a fixed right of precedence. They differ again from offices such as canon theologian or canon penitentiary, which imply only a charge or duty. The entry cites Wernz, Laurentius, and Sagmuller, giving readers the ranks within a chapter in short compass.

Ecclesiastical heraldry splits into several branches, chiefly the arms of religious bodies and the insignia of church rank and office. It also covers the charges and forms of general heraldry with a religious origin or use. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry adds the emblems of saints and other beings honored by the Church. Through all these runs symbolism, real, suggested, or fancied, and close woven with rank insignia lies the lore of vestments.

The origin of heraldry itself stays shrouded in mystery, a growth from three ideas, none of which alone can explain it. The entry works through corporations, dignities, and saints' devices, citing Woodward, Fox-Davies, and Battandier. For readers of shields and seals, it is a full guide to the Church's pictured language.

An ecclesiastical seminary is a school set up under a decree of the Council of Trent to train the diocesan clergy. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry warns that the bare word seminary means other things, a university circle in Germany or a young ladies' academy in England and America. Qualified by ecclesiastical, it names only the diocesan school, distinct from the novitiate and scholasticate of religious orders.

In the seminary, spiritual and intellectual formation go together, unlike a university faculty of theology, which is not a seminary. The entry surveys seminaries across the English-speaking world, with acts of the Holy See, histories of houses, and essays on training. It points readers to the American colleges at Louvain and Rome among special articles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-embroidery:
Church embroidery is the subject of this entry, which traces needlework on vestments from early times to its high point. For the period before the tenth century no full account survives, and no church embroidery of that age is preserved. The oldest pieces known are a maniple and stole from the early tenth century at Durham, and fragments of an altar cover of the same age at Ravenna.

Magnificent work appears in the eleventh century, such as a chasuble wholly covered with pictures in pure gold at Bamberg, and the coronation mantle of Hungary, once also a chasuble. Gold thread ruled church work until the thirteenth century, though silk was also used, as splendid copes at Saint Paul in Carinthia show. Embroidery reached its fullest flower in the thirteenth, fourteenth, and early fifteenth centuries, using gold, silver, and silk, with stamped disks and enamel spangles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-espousals-of-:
The Espousals of the Blessed Virgin Mary is a feast of the Latin Church. Joseph and Mary certainly contracted a real matrimony. Still Mary is called espoused to Joseph, because the marriage was never consummated. Peter d'Ailly and his disciple Gerson were the first energetic propagators of devotion to Saint Joseph.

Gerson worked many years for a special votive feast of the virginal espousal of Mary and Joseph. His friend Henry Chicoti, canon of Chartres, left money for celebrating this feast in the cathedral, for which Gerson composed an Office. The first definite feast dates from 29 August 1517, when Leo X granted it to the Nuns of the Annunciation. This feast was celebrated on 22 October as a double of the second class. Its Mass honoured the Virgin exclusively and hardly mentioned Joseph, so it did not match Gerson's idea.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ethical-aspec:
In Greek and Roman civilization slavery formed an essential element of the social structure, and ethical speculators and statesmen alike regarded it as just and indispensable. The Greek assumed slaves should normally come only from barbarian or lower races. Roman law in the empire's heyday treated the slave as a mere chattel. The master held power of life and death over him; the slave could make no contract and had no civil rights; in law he was not a person.

Nevertheless natural justice condemned, or at least disapproved, masters who treated slaves with signal inhumanity. Christianity found slavery throughout the Roman world, and in power did not attempt summarily to abolish it. From the beginning, however, the Church pressed steadily for ameliorating the individual slave's condition. It pressed ultimately for abolishing a system hardly reconcilable with the Gospel and the brotherhood of all men in Divine sonship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eudists-socie:
The Eudists, or Society of Jesus and Mary, were instituted at Caen, France, on 25 March 1643, by Jean Eudes. The society's works are the education of priests in seminaries and the giving of missions. The end he assigned to his society made him decide against religious vows. He believed priests, finding in their dignity the means of rising to perfection, could inspire clerics with an idea of the priesthood.

He felt bishops would less willingly give seminaries to priests not subject to them. Father Eudes shared the opinions of Cardinal de Bérulle and Father Olier, who opposed religious vows in the orders they founded. Even Saint Vincent de Paul admitted vows only after hesitation, and on condition that his Priests of the Mission form an ecclesiastical society, not a religious order. The Society is therefore not a religious order, but an ecclesiastical body under the bishops, forming the clergy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eugene-o-curr:
Eugene O'Curry was an Irish scholar, born at Dunaha near Carrigaholt, County Clare, in 1796 and dead in 1862. His father, a modest farmer, was an Irish scholar and a fine singer, steeped in his people's traditions. Eugene grew up amid Irish surroundings and soon learned to read the Irish manuscripts still common among the people. After the fall of Napoleon in 1815, agricultural distress in Ireland broke up the O'Curry farm.

In 1834 Eugene joined the men engaged upon the topographical and historical part of the Ordnance Survey of Ireland, with Petrie, Wakeman, Clarence Mangan the poet, and John O'Donovan. Seeking information on Irish places, he visited the British Museum, the Bodleian, Trinity College Library, the Royal Irish Academy, and other places. But the Government, afraid of the national memories the work evoked, abandoned the survey a few years later and dissolved the staff.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feast-of-the-:
The Holy Name of Mary feast honours Mary and all the graces given through her. It began at Cuenca in Spain in 1513, on the octave day of Mary's Nativity, 15 September. Sixtus V later moved it to 17 September after the Breviary reform. Spain and Naples received it in 1671 under its original title.

After Sobieski's victory at Vienna in 1683, Innocent XI spread it to the whole Church. The feast fell on the Sunday after Mary's Nativity each year. If a higher feast displaced it, the day moved to 12 September. Piarists and Marianists keep it as their own patronal feast today.

The Holy Rosary feast falls on the first Sunday of October each year. It grew from thanksgiving for the great naval victory at Lepanto in 1571. Pius V ordered a commemoration of the Rosary on that day. Gregory XIII let churches with a Rosary altar keep the feast.

Clement X extended the feast to all of Spain in 1671. After Prince Eugene's victory in 1716, Clement XI spread it to the universal Church. Leo XIII raised its rank and added Queen of the Most Holy Rosary. On the feast, Rosary chapels offer a plenary indulgence to visiting pilgrims.

The Maternity of Mary feast honours the dignity of Mary as Mother of God. The Council of Ephesus solemnly ratified that title on 22 June 431. Its hymns also praise Mary as the spiritual mother of all mankind. The Roman Breviary commemorates it on the second Sunday in October.

Portugal first received the feast in 1751 at the petition of King Joseph Manuel. Venice, Naples, and Tuscany followed it across the next fifty years. Rome keeps it at St Augustine's with a solemn octave each year. At Mesagna it marks the great earthquake of 20 February 1743.

The Most Pure Heart of Mary feast honours Mary's joys, sorrows, virtues, and perfections. John Eudes began it as the patronal feast of his priests and nuns. Kept at Caen from 1644, it spread across nearly all France. Its Office, composed by Eudes, was fixed in text by 1672.

French bishops claimed the right to found feasts and compose offices without Rome's leave. Pius VI gave the first papal sanction to Corbeil nuns in 1787. Rome adopted the feast in 1879, though it never reached the whole Church. Ecuador keeps it as patronal feast of the republic to this day.

The Nativity of Mary falls on 8 September in the Latin Church. Its earliest witness is a sixth-century hymn by St Romanus the Melodist. The feast likely arose in Syria or Palestine soon after the Council of Ephesus. Rome took it in the seventh century from the Eastern churches.

The story of Mary's birth comes only from apocryphal gospels and legends. Many Latin calendars were slow to accept this Eastern festival. Sergius I ordered a litany and procession for the feast day. Innocent IV added an octave after the cardinals' vow in conclave.

The Presentation of Mary recalls her being brought to the Temple aged three. Apocryphal gospels say her parents fulfilled a vow in doing so. The feast arose in the East, likely in Syria, its apocryphal home. A Greek canon for it dates from the seventh or eighth century.

Philippe de Mazieres brought the feast to the West at Avignon. Paris kept it in 1373, Metz in 1418, and Cologne in 1420. Sixtus IV entered it in the Roman Breviary for a time. Sixtus V restored it in 1585, and Rome keeps it as a major double.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-feasts-of-the:
The Seven Sorrows feasts honour Mary's spiritual martyrdom standing beneath the Cross beside her Son. One falls on the Friday before Palm Sunday each year. The other falls on the third Sunday in September. Both recall her compassion in Christ's sufferings from Simeon's prophecy to the burial.

The Servites took Mary's sorrows as the chief devotion of their order in 1239. Cologne's synod enacted the feast in 1413 to expiate the crimes of Hussite iconoclasts. Benedict XIII spread the Friday feast to the whole Church in 1727. Pius VII extended the September feast after his exile in 1814.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-florence-conr:
Florence Conry was Archbishop of Tuam, patriot, and founder of the Irish College at Louvain. Born in Galway in 1560, he joined the Franciscans at Salamanca and became Irish provincial in 1588. He sailed with the Spanish Armada and later aided Hugh O'Neill in Tyrone's Rebellion. After Kinsale in 1601 he went to Spain with Hugh Roe O'Donnell and stood by the exiled earls.

Consecrated archbishop at Rome in 1609, he never took possession of his see under penal proclamations. In 1616 he founded St. Anthony's College at Louvain, home of Irish scholars and a busy press. He translated a Spanish catechism into pure Irish, printed at Louvain in 1626. A deep scholar of Augustine, he wrote on grace, free will, and original sin until his death in 1629.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-french-congre:
The French Congregation of the Oratory, founded at Paris in 1611 by Cardinal Pierre de Bérulle, aimed to renew the priesthood in France. Bérulle took Saint Philip Neri's Italian Oratory as his model but changed one thing: where Italian houses stood independent, all French houses answered to a single superior-general. A papal bull of 1613 approved the new institute.

More than fifty houses joined during Bérulle's lifetime, and later the count more than doubled across four provinces. Members took no vows beyond priesthood itself, and their one aim was priestly perfection. Though not a teaching order, the Oratorians ran colleges and were the first to shape French seminaries on the lines of the Council of Trent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gervase-of-ca:
Gervase of Canterbury, an English chronicler born about 1141, wrote the monks' side of Canterbury's quarrels. Of a Kentish family, he took profession from Saint Thomas on February 16, 1163. He was ordained by him and helped bury the saint after his martyrdom on December 29, 1170. He fought Archbishop Baldwin in the monks' disputes of 1185 to 1191, carrying appeals to pope and to Richard I in 1189.

Made sacristan about the time he attended Hubert Walter in 1193, Gervase ceased that office by 1197, when Felix appears as sacristan. He was still writing in 1199, and his Gesta Regum runs to 1210. A sudden change of style and arrangement signals a new chronicler, so his death falls in or soon after that year. His Chronicle of 1100 to 1199 and Acts of Canterbury's Pontiffs to Hubert Walter's death in 1205 appeared in Twysden in 1652. His Gesta Regum and topographical Mappa Mundi appeared in the Rolls Series of 1879 to 1880 under Stubbs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gervase-of-ti:
Gervase of Tilbury, a writer born about 1150, entertained an emperor with the world's wonders. Of Tilbury in Essex, likely kin to English royalty. He served Henry of Guienne, traveled Europe, studied and briefly taught canon law at Bologna, and attended William II of Sicily's court until 1189. Settling at Arles, he became Marshal of the Kingdom of Arles in 1198 under Otto IV, escorting him to Rome's coronation in 1209.

Between 1210 and 1214 Gervase composed Otia Imperialia, also called Book of the World's Marvels, Emperor's Solace, and Description of the Whole World. It ran in three parts on history, geography, and physics. Much read in the Middle Ages and twice rendered into French in the fourteenth century, it divides judges. Leibniz dismissed it as a bag of foolish old wives' tales, while others prize its recognition of papal claims against empire. Leibniz edited it in 1744, and much of Gervase's other writing has perished.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-glory:
Glory is a word of many shades of meaning, which lexicographers struggle to separate sharply. In the English Bible it translates Hebrew terms of the Old Testament and the Greek doxa of the New Testament. A Catholic Encyclopedia article treats it only in its ethical and religious senses, as Scripture and theology use it.

Sometimes it means a visible brightness, as in the glory of the Lord dwelling on Sinai or the Transfiguration on Mount Thabor. Often it means the witness creation bears to its Creator. It can also mean a manifestation of divine majesty through the incarnate Son, as in John 1:14. It also means praise given to God, judgment on personal worth, and finally the blessedness of the future life in union with God.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gregorian-ant:
The Gregorian Antiphonary is an article on the earliest collection of antiphons, groups of antiphons, and their melodies. A primitive Christian antiphonary can no longer be reconstructed completely, but study of the text establishes its existence at a remote date. A Catholic Encyclopedia article distinguishes idiomelodic antiphons, fitted with special melodies, from automelodic anthems adapted to a common type.

The list of melodies was limited. Oral tradition may have sufficed to hand down musical formulas until the chants were coordinated and notation became necessary. From the fourth century singers commonly used a book or page bearing the notation, though many churches had only the words. The oldest trace is an Egyptian papyrus of about the year 300, worn where singers' fingers held it, carrying a Greek text of praise to Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hail-mary:
The Hail Mary, also called the Angelical Salutation or Ave Maria, is the most familiar prayer in honour of the Blessed Virgin. The entry traces its three parts to their sources. Gabriel's greeting in Luke supplies the opening, Elizabeth's words add the blessing on the fruit of Mary's womb. The Church itself framed the closing petition for sinners now and at the hour of death.

No firm trace of the prayer as a set formula appears before about 1050, when its phrases surface in the Little Office of the Blessed Virgin. Synods from Paris in 1196 and Durham in 1217 pressed clergy to teach it beside the Creed and Lord's Prayer. Early users treated it as a greeting, kneeling or bowing as they said it, and saints like Louis of France repeated it fifty times nightly on their knees.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-of-fleur:
Hugh of Fleury, also called Hugo a Santa Maria, was a Benedictine monk and church writer known only through his writings, dead not before 1118. In 1109 he compiled a church history in four volumes reaching the death of Charlemagne in 814. The next year he recast it in six volumes, better arranged, with theological notes added and some matter dropped, reaching 855.

That edition, first printed at Münster in 1638, also carries a preface to King Louis the Fat and a letter to Ivo of Chartres. Hugh also wrote a book on the acts of the Frankish kings from 842 to 1108. He wrote a chronicle of French kings from the legendary Pharamond to Philip I. He also wrote an abridged chronicle for Louis VI, and a work on royal and priestly power for Henry II during the investiture controversy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hungary:
Hungary, the Realm of the Crown of St. Stephen, lay between set longitudes and latitudes in central Europe, joining Hungary Proper and Transylvania with Croatia-Slavonia and the Military Frontier. Its total area was over one hundred and twenty-five thousand square miles, and its 1900 population exceeded nineteen million, just over half Catholic. Budapest, on both banks of the Danube, held about eight hundred thousand people.

The Danube and its tributaries, the Save, Drave, and Theiss, drain the land. Great plains, the Alföld, fill tens of thousands of square miles between Alps and Carpathians. Farming led its industries. The entry then traces Hungary's church history from early conversion through Reformation struggles. Districts beyond the Theiss accepted Reformed religion in 1556, and Catholic revival followed under Archbishop Oláhus, who held a national synod in 1561 and founded a seminary at Tyrnau.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-idolatry:
The word idolatry first meant divine worship given to an image. Now it covers worship of anything at all: divine worship offered to any being or thing other than the true God. For Aquinas it is a kind of superstition, a vice against religion: it offers divine honour to non-divine things, or to God in a wrong manner. Its specific mark is direct opposition to worship's primary object.

In several ways it hands a creature the reverence owed to God alone. Some, by nefarious arts, made images that seemed, through the devil's power, to work effects, and judged them divine and worthy of worship, as Hermes Trismegistus held. Others honoured not images but the creatures they represented. Paul hints at both in Romans, where people changed God's glory into the likeness of corruptible things.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-institute-of-:
Mary Ward's second congregation, founded for the schooling of girls, carries the official title Institute of Mary. After her first congregation was suppressed in 1630 and attacked as “Jesuitesses,” most members left religious life or joined other orders. A loyal group, sheltered at Munich in the Paradeiser Haus with Pope Urban VIII's leave and the Elector of Bavaria's help, kept living under Ward's guidance.

In 1703 Barbara Babthorpe won approval for the institute's rule under this title. She was the fourth successor as chief superior. The title appears in early superiors' signatures and in the first members' formula of vows. In different lands the sisters were known as English Ladies, Dames Anglaises, or Loreto nuns. The entry traces a community that survived suppression by holding fast to its founder's plan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-irish-institu:
Frances Mary Teresa Ball founded this Irish teaching congregation under Dublin's Archbishop Murray, after two years as a novice at St Mary's Convent, York. Ellen Arthur and Anne Therry joined her as the first companions. On 4 November 1822 the three pioneers took possession of Rathfarnham Abbey. The archbishop had bought it as motherhouse and novitiate. Dubliners soon called the sisters Loreto nuns.

Fame for the superior schooling they gave in the Dublin archdiocese drew calls for their help across Ireland. Navan in County Meath took the first offshoot in 1833, with a later filiation at Mullingar, and Dublin houses in North Great George's Street and Stephen's Green followed. The entry traces a teaching order spreading from one abbey to a national network of girls' schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ivory:
Ivory is dentine, the tusk matter of elephants, hippopotami, walruses, and other animals. It is tough and elastic. It holds a creamy white color. It takes a high and lasting polish. Artists have used it since prehistoric times. Early and medieval Christians used it widely for church objects.

Museums in Europe hold carved ivories from many ages. Examples include Egyptian, Assyrian, Greek, and Roman reliefs. They also include statues, diptychs, plaques, and caskets. Classical writers often mention ivory. The Old Testament uses its traits as poetic praise. The Litany of Loreto still calls Mary a tower of ivory. The entry surveys a material prized for beauty and craft.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-andre:
Jacques André Emery led the Society of St Sulpice through the French Revolution. He was born at Gex on 26 August 1732. He died at Paris on 28 April 1811. He studied first with Carmelites at Gex and Jesuits at Mâcon. He then attended St Irenaeus seminary at Lyons. He finished at St Sulpice, Paris, joined the society, and was ordained priest in 1758.

He taught with distinction at Orléans and Lyons seminaries. At Lyons he defended Rome's rights firmly yet courteously before Archbishop de Montazet, a Jansenist-leaning prelate. Partly on that archbishop's advice, he became superior at Angers seminary in 1776. Later he became vicar-general of the diocese. He showed marked governing power in both posts. In 1782 he was elected superior-general of St Sulpice. The entry follows a seminary chief steering priests through revolution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-de-vi:
Historian of the crusades Jacques de Vitry was cardinal bishop of Acre, later of Tusculum. He was born at Vitry-sur-Seine near Paris, probably about 1160, and died at Rome in 1240. After attending Paris university in its infancy, he visited Marie d'Oignies, a Liège mystic famed for holiness. On her advice he became a canon regular. He returned to Paris for priestly ordination and then devoted himself to preaching.

From 1210 to 1213 he ranked among the most noted preachers of the crusade against the Albigenses. His fame spread so widely that Acre's Latin clergy chose him as bishop. He accepted with Honorius III's approval. From Palestine he went to Egypt and witnessed Damietta's capture in 1218 to 1220. He wrote an account of it to the pope. Crusade leaders complained of his imperious temper and ambition. The entry follows a preacher become bishop on crusading frontiers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-joseph-:
Third bishop of Hamilton, Ontario, James Joseph Carbery was born in County Westmeath, Ireland, on 1 May 1823, and died at Cork on 17 December 1887. Early education at Navan seminary led him into the Dominican order at an early age. Philosophy and theology at Viterbo and Rome prepared a return to Ireland in 1849. There he soon became known for learning, eloquence, and zealous labors.

Many important posts in his order followed, including assistant to the master general, and in 1883 he was appointed bishop of Hamilton, consecrated at Rome on 11 November that year. He died while visiting his native country to restore his broken health, a Dominican scholar-bishop whose Canadian episcopate lasted only four years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-mcsherr:
James McSherry served as chief justice of Maryland's highest court from 25 January 1896 until his death, with distinction, among the state's judges of the postwar generation. In 1887 he had become chief judge of the circuit court for Frederick and Montgomery counties, a post that carried a seat on the appeals court. Voters gave him a full term with no rival on the ballot on 8 November 1887.

His father was the author James McSherry. The younger man was born in Frederick, Maryland, on 30 December 1842, and died there on 23 October 1907. Mount St Mary's College in Emmitsburg schooled him until the year before graduation, when his open Southern views got him sent away in 1861. Arrested, he spent a spell confined at Fort McHenry in Baltimore. He then learned law beside his father and qualified as a lawyer on 8 February 1864. Clara Louise McAleer became his wife on 26 February 1866, and they raised six children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-pierre-g:
Jean-Pierre Gury, a French Jesuit moral theologian born in 1801 and dead in 1866. He joined the Society at Montrouge in 1824 and taught moral theology for thirty-five years, mainly at Vals seminary, with one year at Rome. His teaching career shaped generations of confessors.

Gury's Compendium of Moral Theology, first issued in 1850, reached seventeen editions by his death. It spread in German, Belgian, Italian, Spanish, and Austrian versions, with noted editions by Ballerini, Dumas, and Sabetti.. His 1862 Cases of Conscience likewise ran through many editions. Brevity made the book handy, though critics found it thin on scientific depth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-siffrein:
Jean-Siffrein Maury, a French cardinal and statesman born at Valréas in 1746 and died at Rome in 1817, finished theology by nineteen and went to Paris. Ordained in 1769, he won a vicar-general post through a Fénelon kinsman's favour after praising the archbishop.

Maury's 1772 panegyric of Saint Louis at the Louvre drew applause that broke into the speech, winning him a benefice and royal preacher's place. At the 1776 synod he exposed court bishops' faults, and in 1784 his Vincent de Paul sermon rebuked France's ingratitude. Elected deputy for Péronne's clergy in 1789, he led the court and church party against Mirabeau, often losing votes but winning debates.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-barry:
John Barry was an Irish-born captain counted among the founders of the United States Navy. Born at Tacumshane in County Wexford in 1745, he went to sea young, reached Philadelphia at fifteen, and commanded merchant ships in the West Indian trade. On 7 December 1775 he received the first commission sent out by the Continental Congress's Marine Committee, for the brig Lexington.

In April 1776 he captured the British tender Edward off Delaware Bay, the first war vessel brought to Philadelphia by a commissioned Continental officer. Blockaded in the Delaware, he joined Washington's army for Trenton and Princeton, then returned to daring boat expeditions on the river. His later commands and his standing with Washington made him, in the entry's judgment, a father of the American navy, and he died at Philadelphia in 1803.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-curry:
John Curry was a Dublin physician and historian who defended Irish Catholics against the calumnies of their enemies. Born in Dublin early in the eighteenth century, Medicine was his study at Paris and Reims, and he practiced in Dublin. An ardent Catholic, he published in London in 1747 a brief account of the Irish Rebellion of 1641 drawn from Protestant writers.

Attacked by Walter Harris in 1752, Curry answered with his Historical Memoirs. Enlarged in 1775 as a Historical and Critical Review of the Civil Wars in Ireland, it was his best work. It traces Irish history from Elizabeth's reign to the settlement under William III. He helped found the Catholic Committee that met in Essex Street in 1760. He labored for repeal of the penal laws, while also publishing essays on fevers in 1743 and 1774.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-john-of-salis:
John of Salisbury was a twelfth-century philosopher, historian, and churchman, secretary to two archbishops of Canterbury. Born near Salisbury about 1115, he studied at Paris under Abelard, Alberic of Reims, and Robert of Melun, and at Chartres under William of Conches. He studied again at Paris in theology under Gilbert de La Porree, completing his studies in 1145.

Introduced by St. Bernard to Archbishop Theobald at Reims in 1148, he served as Theobald's secretary and crossed the Alps ten times on diplomatic missions to Rome by 1159. Forced seclusion after incurring Henry II's displeasure let him finish his two chief works, the Policraticus on statecraft and the Metalogicus on logic, both dedicated to Thomas Becket. Exiled again in 1163, he worked for peace between king and archbishop. He witnessed Becket's murder in Canterbury Cathedral in 1170, and became treasurer of Exeter before his death in 1180.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-aubery:
Joseph Aubery was a French Jesuit missionary who served the Abenaki people in Canada for nearly half a century. Born at Gisors in Normandy in 1673, he joined the Society of Jesus at seventeen and reached Canada in 1694. Ordained at Quebec in 1700, he revived the mission at Medoctec in 1701.

From 1708 he led the Abenaki settlement at St. François until his death in 1755. A skilled linguist, he lost his manuscripts and mission registers in a fire in 1759, four years after his death. He also wrote memorials and a map defending French claims in Acadia, papers still kept in the Paris archives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-latin-literat:
Latin literature in Christianity from the sixth to the twentieth century treats the church Latin poetry of the Middle Ages. It also covers the classical revival of Renaissance neo-Latinists, alive even today in modest form. Strict chronology would muddle the story, so the article groups poets by kind, tracing each kind's development.

Drama shows the break most sharply. In no field, says Creizenach, did the Middle Ages so wholly suspend classical tradition. Terence was read in schools, but his stagecraft and metres were lost, and comedy, tragedy, and other verse blurred together. Only isolated imitations appear, like the tenth-century nun Hroswitha of Gandersheim, whose spiritual literary dramas, written without any notion of staging, left no mark on later drama.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lectionary:
A lectionary, Lectionarium or Legenda, is a liturgical book term of loose meaning. In the early Middle Ages neither Mass nor Divine Office stood complete in one volume, as in today's Missal and Breviary. Books were bulky and costly, so altar prayers belonged in a different book from choir antiphons.

In its wide sense a lectionary covers any liturgical volume holding passages read aloud in church. That includes continuous Scriptural books with readings marked, Evangeliaria, and Plenaria joining Epistles and Gospels for high Mass. It also includes collections of Fathers' extracts or saints' histories read as Office lessons. More commonly it means one of two books. One holds the Mass readings chanted by deacon, subdeacon, or lector. The other holds the Matins readings after each psalm group, sometimes gathered as extracts, sometimes marked in large volumes of homilies or saints' lives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-little-brothe:
The Little Brothers of Mary, better known as the Marist School Brothers, are a teaching order founded in France in 1817 by Benedict Marcellin Champagnat. He aimed at plain schooling for poor children, and wrote guides and methods to train his brothers as teachers.

Rome gave full approval in 1863. At the founder's death in 1840 the order counted 310 men in 48 schools, all in central France. By 1910 it had grown to about six thousand brothers, running schools from Spain and Belgium to China, Brazil, Canada, and Australia. Its English province dated from 1852, and its North American foothold from 1885.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-llanthony-pri:
Llanthony Priory was a house of Augustinian canons hidden among the Black Mountains of South Wales, some nine miles north-east of Abergavenny. A retainer named William, hunting about 1100, found a ruined chapel said to be St. David's cell, and turned hermit there.

Ernisius, chaplain to Queen Maud, joined him, and Hugh de Lacy founded and endowed a monastery for them in 1107, dedicated to St. John the Baptist. Harsh weather, poor soil, and Welsh hostility drove all forty canons away in 1134 to Hereford, and a second house, Llanthony Secunda, rose near Gloucester. The old church now lies ruined, its towers and nave piers still standing.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lottery:
A lottery is a game of chance in which players buy numbered tickets and prizes fall to numbers drawn, often from a wheel. Some buyers win far more than they paid, some win less, and most win nothing at all.

Judged as gambling for the players, it turns blameworthy when it feeds a gambling habit and pulls people from honest work. Yet without fraud, and with ticket price in fair proportion to the chance of gain, the entry holds it not evil in itself. Law followed suit: Congress barred lottery matter from the mails in 1890, and England long banned lotteries save for chartered art unions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lucas-d-acher:
Lucas d'Achery was a French Benedictine scholar of the Maurist congregation, born at Saint-Quentin in 1609 and dead at Saint-Germain-des-Pres in 1685. He gave his life to hunting, explaining, and printing medieval history and theology from original manuscripts.

Professed at Vendome in 1632, he spent nearly fifty years at Saint-Germain, scarcely leaving its walls, and served as its librarian. Letters to monasteries across Europe made him a first-rank guide to forgotten medieval writers. His Spicilegium of 1655 to 1677, a harvest of texts hidden in French libraries, above all Benedictine ones, remains his chief monument, with editions of Barnabas, Lanfranc, and Guibert beside it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-malmesbury:
Malmesbury was a small, decayed market town in Wiltshire, ninety-five miles west of London. It once held a mitred parliamentary abbey of Benedictine monks. Its origin lay with Maildubh, an Irish monk and teacher who settled there about the mid-seventh century. The place was then a border town between Welsh and English, and between Wessex and Mercia.

Maildubh's school drew many pupils, chief among them Aldhelm, kin to King Ina of Wessex. Later, under King John, a raider named Robert slew monks who failed to flee in 1140. John then gave the abbey the castle site and pulled the castle down to widen its forty-five-acre enclosure. A walled town with four gates, a Knights' preceptory, three churches, a mint, and a merchants' guild marked its prosperity, crowned by a vast abbey church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-manila-observ:
Manila Observatory was founded by the Jesuit Frederic Faura in 1865. Its work grew from one man's long study of typhoons, known in the Philippines as baguio, among the islands' worst foes.

Faura, a professor at Ateneo College, hoped to foretell storms and limit their damage. On 7 July 1879 he predicted a baguio over northern Luzon, and events proved him right. It was the first forecast in the Far East of a typhoon's existence, length, and course. A second correct warning for Manila followed that November. City merchants then funded wider work, and Hong Kong merchants asked for his forecasts once a cable linked the cities in 1880. His Faura barometer of 1886 soon served navigators across Philippine and China seas. Under Father Algue the service grew into a telegraph network, with reports cabled twice daily from Japan, Formosa, China, and Indo-China.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-margaret-haug:
Margaret Haughery, called the mother of the orphans, was born in Cavan, Ireland, about 1814 and died at New Orleans on 9 February 1882. Her parents died at Baltimore in 1822, leaving her untaught in reading and writing. She married Charles Haughery in 1835 and moved to New Orleans, where husband and infant died within a year.

The Female Orphan Asylum of 1840 was largely her work, and she cleared it of debt. In yellow fever years she nursed victims house to house, regardless of race or creed, promising dying mothers to care for their children. She ran a dairy, then a bakery, the South's first steam bakery, driving her own rounds. She braved General Butler in the Civil War to carry flour across lines for her orphans. New Orleans mourned her death as a public calamity, and a monument rose in Margaret Place in 1884.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-masonry-freem:
Masonry, or Freemasonry, is treated in this vast article under name and definition, origin and early history, fundamental principles and spirit, and propagation and evolution. It also covers organisation and statistics, inner work of symbolism and oaths, outer work of achievements and methods, and action of state and Church authorities. 

Modern speculative Masonry dates from England's Grand Lodge constitution of 24 June 1717, uniting four old lodges, though Anderson's 1723 Constitutions history is called little more than fables. Its first Old Charge article sets an unsectarian religion in which all men agree, a principle the article judges anti-Catholic and anti-Christian in character. Grand Lodge statistics count some 262,651 members in Britain and colonies, 60,728 in Canada, and 1,203,159 in the United States. Papal pronouncements from Clement XII's In Eminenti of 1738 onward forbid Catholics, under excommunication, to join.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-matthieu-ory:
Dominican inquisitor Matthieu Ory (1492-1557) entered his order at eighteen, studied at St-Jacques in Paris and the Sorbonne, and took his theology licence in 1527. His learning and eloquence won him the post of grand inquisitor for France in 1534, which he held until death. He preached tirelessly, held several offices in his order, and fought false teaching and wrongdoing.

Asked to judge false charges against Ignatius of Loyola and his Spiritual Exercises, Ory saw through the accusers. Instead of condemning the saint, he praised and assisted him, and kept a copy of the Exercises for himself. Some writers wrongly call him a Spaniard named Ortiz. His only fully proven printed work is the Alexipharmacum of 1544, which turns five words of St. Paul, grace, justification, sin, liberty, and law, against heretics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-memory:
Memory, from Latin memoria, is the mind's power to store conscious processes and bring them back later with some fidelity. Strictly, a revived process counts as remembered only when it is also recognized as something that happened before. Memory thus involves recognition. Voluntary recall of mental processes is often called recollection, and involuntary recall is called recall.

St. Thomas splits memory into sensory and intellectual kinds. He excludes mere storage of mental images from sensory memory and assigns it to imagination. Sensory memory keeps what the special senses cannot take in yet stays individual. Examples are an object's use and its place in past time, meaning only the sensory lesson that certain things help or harm. It sits in the bodily organism. Intellectual memory takes in and stores the abstract and universal, seated in the passive intellect's division, or perhaps only an aspect of understanding, paired with the active intellect.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-missionaries-:
Blessed Louis-Marie Grignion de Montfort established the Company of Mary in 1713. Montfort had already dreamed of a missionary society by 1700. Five months after his ordination in November 1700 he wrote of praying continually for a poor and small company of good priests. They would preach missions and retreats under the standard and protection of the Blessed Virgin.

For years he prayed, fasted, and had others pray for his project. In 1713 he went to Paris to recruit members, and the director of the St-Esprit seminary promised to send him young priests. Montfort died in 1716, but his company, the Montfortians, lived on, preaching parish missions and spreading devotion to Mary, especially through the rosary and total consecration.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mount-calvary:
Mount Calvary is the place of Christ's Crucifixion, a name from Latin calvaria, meaning a skull. That matches Greek kranion and the original Golgotha. The Gospels call it merely a place. The Pilgrim of Bordeaux joined the diminutive monticulus, little mount, to it in 333. Rufinus spoke of the rock of Golgotha near the fifth century's start. Since the sixth century usage has treated Calvary as a mountain.

Why it bears the name is debated. It may have been a public execution ground strewn with skulls, or named from a cemetery nearby. That would also explain the thin population of the district and Joseph's tomb standing there. The entry weighs the theories, traces the site's identification and the churches raised over it, and sets out the topography pilgrims and scholars have argued over.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mystery:
Mystery, from Greek mysterion, rooted in a verb meaning to shut or close, signifies in general what is unknowable or valuable knowledge kept secret. In pagan antiquity it named esoteric doctrines such as Pythagoreanism and private rites like the Eleusinian ceremonies, known only to the initiated. Early Christians used it for teachings carefully guarded from the profane.

Scripture's versions render Hebrew sod, secret, by mysterion. The New Testament applies the word chiefly to the Gospel's sublime revelation, the Incarnation and life of the Saviour proclaimed by the apostles. Theologians therefore call mysteries revealed truths surpassing natural reason, not merely the incomprehensible, since all knowledge is partly beyond full grasp. The entry sorts mysteries of faith from those of nature and grace.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-northern-terr:
The Northern Territory of Australia, a prefecture apostolic larger than many nations, lay almost empty in the early twentieth century. Bounded by ocean, South Australia, Queensland, and Western Australia, it spans 523,620 square miles, mostly within the tropics.

Some 25,000 to 30,000 people lived there, under a thousand Europeans, about 4,000 Asiatics, and the rest Aboriginal peoples. Palmerston at Port Darwin and Southport were its only towns, linked to Adelaide by a telegraph of over 2,000 miles but by rail for just 146. Droughts, cattle disease, and the 1891 financial crisis slowed the country’s growth. Port Darwin probably ranks second only to Sydney Harbour as a deep-water port.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-odo-of-canter:
Odo of Canterbury, abbot of Battle who died in 1200, served Thomas Becket and Christ Church through the Becket quarrel. A monk of Christ Church and subprior by 1163, he carried Becket's appeal to Pope Alexander III against the archbishop of York's carrying his cross in the south.

Prior by 1167, Odo wavered between king and archbishop until Becket's murder fixed him for church authority. Monks put him forward for Canterbury in 1172, Henry stalled, and Richard of Dover won the see, with Odo writing in his support. In 1173 a great fire struck Christ Church, and Odo later attended the Council of Woodstock in 1175.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-offertory:
The Offertory, in the Mass, presents bread and wine to God before consecration, with prayers and chant to match. Justin Martyr already describes bread and a cup brought to the president, and soon a prayer asked God to accept, bless, and change the gifts into Christ's Body and Blood.

Eastern rites prepare the gifts before the liturgy in the proskomide, elaborately in Byzantine use, while Rome keeps the offering within the Mass. The entry traces that split, the offertory chant, and the prayers of priest and people across ancient and medieval rites.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oratory:
An oratory, from Latin for prayer, is technically a place set aside by church authority for prayer and Mass, other than a parish church. Early oratories rose over martyrs' tombs and in country districts where churches proper stayed in cathedral cities, then spread to bishops' houses, convents, and noble homes.

Canon law sorts them as public, semipublic, and private. Public oratories, erected by the bishop with a street entrance, serve divine worship perpetually, while semipublic and private ones carry narrower rights for Mass, reservation, and indulgences. A public oratory needs an entrance and an exit onto the public road.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ordinary:
An ordinary, in church language, holds jurisdiction joined stably to an office, whether by divine law, as with popes and bishops, or by church law. Ordinary jurisdiction stands against delegated jurisdiction, a temporary grant from a superior to an inferior for particular acts.

Full and real in the external forum, an ordinary's power covers legislating, judging, and governing, while jurisdiction in the internal forum alone does not make an ordinary. Parish priests, therefore, though they guide consciences, are not ordinaries, and the entry sorts the classes of ordinaries. A person may be an ordinary in his own sphere while holding delegated powers for special acts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ossory:
Ossory is an Irish diocese in Leinster, bounded by the Suir in the south, the Barrow in the east, and Tipperary, King's County, and Queen's County on the other sides. It spans 600,000 acres and matches the old Kingdom of Ossory, whose first king, Aengus Osrithe, flourished in the second century. His heirs widened its bounds into Tipperary, lost South Ossory to the Deisi for a century, and won much of it back in the seventh century.

Saint Kieran, apostle and patron of the diocese, was born near Cape Clear in the fourth century and, by tradition, was ordained at Rome. Saint Patrick gave him a bell and told him to found a monastery where it first rang. The entry follows the diocese through Danish wars, Norman changes, and later bishops, schools, and religious houses down to its modern shape.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-papal-consist:
A papal consistory is the senate of the Roman pontiff, the gathering of cardinals in council round the pope. The word comes from the imperial consistorium, the emperor's sacred council, and Innocent III used it in 1212 for the cardinals' assembly. Its roots lie in the old Roman presbytery, the city's clergy of deacons, priests of titular churches, and nearby bishops.

Today's cardinals, in the same three orders, inherit that presbytery's offices and, above all, its task of aiding the pope in church government. From the earliest Christian times popes consulted the presbytery on church affairs, as a letter of Pope Cornelius to Cyprian in 254 shows. Later pages trace the consistory's forms, public, secret, and semi-public, and its role in creating cardinals and settling great causes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-patrick-barry:
Patrick Barry was a horticulturist born near Belfast in May 1816 and dead at Rochester, New York, on 23 June 1890. After teaching in Ireland he emigrated to America in 1836 and worked for a Flushing, Long Island, nurseryman. In 1849 he partnered with George Ellwanger at Rochester, and their firm led in importing or breeding improved flowers, fruits, and hardy exotics, and in bringing wild shade trees into cultivation.

Their nurseries grew into the country's largest. Barry wrote widely on fruit and flower gardening, editing the Genesee Farmer from 1844 to 1852 and the Horticulturalist from 1852 to 1854. His books include a Treatise on the Fruit Garden, printed in 1851 and reissued in 1872, and a catalogue of the American Pomological Society.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paul-de-barry:
Paul de Barry was a French Jesuit born at Leucate in 1587 and dead at Avignon on 28 July 1661. He served as rector of Jesuit colleges at Aix, Nimes, and Avignon, and as provincial of Lyons. He wrote many devout works on the Blessed Virgin, Saint Joseph, and the saints. Above all stands his Pensez-y-bien, or Think Well On It, which circulated widely and was translated into several tongues.

Only three of his works reached English. They are Pious Remarks upon the Life of Saint Joseph, printed in 1600, the Glories of Saint Joseph of Dublin 1835, and Devotions to Saint Joseph, edited by Tickell in London. His Pensez-y-bien travelled farther than his larger works, reaching readers in several tongues.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-perjury:
Perjury is the crime of swearing falsely, and this Catholic Encyclopedia entry weighs it as both sin and crime. A proper oath counts as worship, since it calls on God as all-knowing witness to truth. Invoking that witness for a lie therefore joins the guilt of lying to an offence against religion, and, apart from ignorance or rashness, the sin is always mortal.

The entry works through hard cases with care. Doubt bars swearing to a thing as certain, while a lawful mental reservation may still be confirmed by oath for good cause. Demanding an oath from someone known to lie is grievous, except where justice or necessity requires sworn testimony, as a judge may require it. Canon law classes perjury as a mixed crime, open to church or civil courts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pluscarden-pr:
Pluscarden Priory is a Scottish monastery founded in 1230 by King Alexander III six miles from Elgin for monks of the Valliscaulian Order. That order's mother-house stood at Val-des-Choux in Burgundy. It was the first of three Scottish houses of the order, whose observance blended Carthusian and Cistercian rule.

In 1454 the two surviving monks of Urquhart's Benedictine priory joined the six of Pluscarden, which then took Benedictine rule and became a dependency of Dunfermline Abbey. The last prior died in 1560, yet the monks were never dispersed. The buildings, partly restored by the Marquess of Bute, still show an aisleless choir and transepts. They also keep a chapter-house and cloister garth amid lovely surroundings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pondicherry:
Pondicherry, an archdiocese of India on the Bay of Bengal, spans French holdings plus nearby British districts. Beyond the town itself it takes in Karikal, Yanaon, and Mahe, two on the east coast and one on the west, plus Chandernagore in Bengal. Catholics there number 143,125, with 78 churches, 210 chapels, and 102 priests.

The archbishop lives at Pondicherry, where the cathedral and seminaries stand, and Paris Foreign Missions priests direct the diocese alongside four sisterhoods. The town stayed a mere village until Francis Martin's shipwrecked Frenchmen made their home there in 1674. Capuchins came first, then Jesuits, and the Carnatic mission spread outward from Pondicherry until the Paris seminary assumed the whole territory in 1773.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pontefract-pr:
Pontefract Priory was a Cluniac monastery in Yorkshire dedicated to Saint John the Evangelist. It was founded about 1090 by Robert de Lacy as a dependency of La Charité-sur-Loire, which supplied the first monks. A bull of Pope Celestine confirmed its gifts and privileges.

Visitations counted sixteen monks in 1262 and twenty-seven in 1279, under a prior who cut the house's debts from 3,200 marks to 350 in twelve years. The priory church held the body of Thomas, Earl of Lancaster, beheaded at Pontefract in 1322 and rumoured a worker of miracles. The last prior surrendered the house to Henry VIII in 1540, and church and buildings are now wholly destroyed, the site marked only by Monk-hill.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pope-st-zacha:
Zachary, also called Zacharias, reigned from 741 to 752 and died in March 752. He sprang from a Greek family in Calabria, son of Polichronius. Probably a deacon, he signed the Roman council's decrees of 732. After Gregory III's burial on 29 November 741, he was elected at once and unanimously, then consecrated and enthroned on 5 December. His biographer calls him gentle, conciliatory, and charitable to clergy and people.

Soon after his elevation he notified Constantinople, addressing his letter to the church there rather than the iconoclast patriarch Anastasius. His envoys found Artabasdus ruling after revolting against Constantine V in 742, and papal letters dated by Artabasdus's reign in 744. In 743 he held a Roman synod of sixty bishops issuing fourteen canons on discipline. He kept close correspondence with Boniface, who organized Germany's church in touch with Rome. In 749 Ratchis abdicated with wife and daughter to take monastic vows before the pope.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-presbytery:
The presbytery is the part of the church set aside for the higher clergy. In antiquity it bore many names, since priests attached to a church stood there in a half circle round the bishop during liturgical functions. It was called apsis, exedra, and concha, from its shape. It was called bema, since it stood raised above the nave and was reached by a few steps. It was called tribuna, from its place and likeness to the tribunal in civil basilicas, where magistrates gave justice.

In the Middle Ages these names mostly gave way to choir, which in turn gave way to the modern word sanctuary. Rails, cancelli, cut the presbytery off from the rest of the church. Eusebius, in his dedication speech at Tyre, tells how the Holy of Holies, the altar, was ringed with wooden lattice, finely carved, to bar the multitude.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-priory:
A priory is a monastery whose superior is a prior. Dominicans, Augustinian Hermits, Carthusians, Carmelites, Servites, and Brothers of Mercy name every house a priory. Benedictines and their offshoots, Premonstratensians, and military orders mark two kinds: conventual priories and simple, or obedientiary, ones. Conventual priories are self ruling houses with no abbots, either since twelve monks, the canonical number, are not yet reached, or for some other cause.

Cluny's congregation held many conventual priories. In England all houses tied to cathedral churches were called cathedral priories. Nearly all houses of the famed Maurist Congregation in France, in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, were called priories. Today the Benedictine Order counts twenty-seven conventual priories. The simple, or obedientiary, kind stands as abbeys' dependencies, and their superior, subject to the abbot in all things, is called a simple or obedientiary prior.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-purgatory:
Purgatory, from the Latin purgare, to make clean, is treated here under the heads of doctrine, errors, proofs, duration, nature, aid for the dead, indulgences and invocation. Catholic teaching calls it a place or condition of temporal punishment. It holds those who die in God's grace yet still carry venial faults, or owe satisfaction still unpaid for their wrongs. The Council of Florence stated the faith in its Decree of Union, and the Council of Trent defined it in its twenty-fifth session.

Passages quoted against purgatory, it argues, either miss the question or lack the clarity to outweigh the open testimony of the very writers cited. Purgatory passes, since its pains cleanse rather than condemn. Prayers, Masses and indulgences offered by the living form the practical heart of the entry, closing with a meditation on the unfailing lamp of ancient piety before the tombs.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reform-of-the:
Reform of the Roman Breviary came by the Apostolic Constitution Divino Afflatu of Pius the Tenth, dated 1 November 1911, changing the psalter of the Roman Breviary. This encyclopedia entry explains the new shape. Portions needing rubrics, such as the invitatory, seasonal hymns, blessings, absolutions, chapters, suffrages, dominical prayers, Benedictus, Magnificat and Te Deum, are now printed together under the title Ordinary. The psalms stand together under the title Psaltery.

They are arranged so the whole psalter may be chanted or recited each week. They are distributed or, when too long, divided, so that each day's Office holds roughly the same number of verses. The change aims to restore the liturgy's original use, the weekly recitation of the entire psalter. Feasts with proper lessons keep them, responsories come from the Common or Proper, and precedence turns on rite, classification, personal dignity, external solemnity and local importance, with provision for transferring displaced feasts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-religious-of-:
The Religious of Jesus Mary were founded at Lyons in France in October 1818 by Claudine Thevenet, known in religion as Mother Saint Ignatius. Their constitutions won approval from Pius the Ninth on 31 December 1847. Their aim is a Christian education suited to young ladies' social position, given through boarding schools and academies, and, in large cities, through residences for ladies of the literary profession.

Before the expulsion of 1901 their French houses stood at Lyons, Le Puy, Rodez, and Remiremont. Persecution then moved the mother-house to Rome in September 1901, to the Via Flaminia, with a college called Stella Viae. In New York they kept a house on Fourteenth Street, an academy at Kingsbridge, and a day school for poor Italian children. The Fourteenth Street house, Our Lady of Peace, sheltered literary ladies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-de-bu:
A fourteenth-century English bishop remembered above all as a lover of books is the subject of this encyclopedia entry. Richard de Bury, born near Bury St Edmund's in 1286, studied at Oxford, became a Benedictine, and tutored the future Edward III. Once his pupil took the throne, he rose swiftly to Bishop of Durham and to high offices of state. He travelled on embassies to Avignon, where he met the poet Petrarch.

Book collecting shaped his lasting fame far more than court service. He gathered manuscripts through a lifetime of searching and founded Durham College at Oxford. He left most of his volumes to its library. They were scattered when Henry VIII closed the college. His own treatise on the love of books, the Philobiblon, praises learning, defends his spending on manuscripts, and urges clergy to cherish reading. First printed in 1473, it has appeared in many editions and translations since.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-richard-mcshe:
Richard McSherry was a Maryland physician who served as a surgeon in both the army and the navy before settling into Baltimore practice. Born at Martinsburg in 1817, the son of a doctor, he studied at Georgetown College and the University of Maryland. He took his medical degree at the University of Pennsylvania in 1841, after already joining the army medical corps.

His service took him to the Seminole War under General Taylor, and later to thirteen years as a navy assistant surgeon. From 1856 he practised in Baltimore until 1883. He helped found the Baltimore Academy of Medicine and served as its first president. He also wrote for medical journals and published books, including a Mexican travel sketch called El Puchero and a popular health guide, Health and How to Promote It. He died at Baltimore in 1885.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rohault-de-fl:
Rohault de Fleury was a nineteenth-century family of French architects and archaeologists. Its most distinguished member was Charles Rohault de Fleury, born at Paris in 1801 and died there in 1875. After a scientific course at the Ecole Polytechnique, he studied sculpture, then turned to architecture in 1825. He designed public and private buildings in one of the most artistic parts of Paris. He wrote the first edition of the Manuel des lois du batiment for the Central Society of Architects in 1862.

His last years went to religious archaeology. These included Les instruments de la Passion in 1870, L'evangile in 1874, and La Sainte Vierge in 1878. A study of a fifth-century Christian tabernacle followed in 1880, and La Messe in 1883-98. Some appeared after his death through his son George, himself a noted writer on Italian art, whose works cover Pisa, Tuscany, and the Lateran in the Middle Ages.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salisbury:
Salisbury, anciently Sarum, is an English diocese whose roots reach back to Birinus, who set his see at Dorchester in Oxfordshire in 634 and preached to Wessex. From that start sprang Winchester, Sherborne, Ramsbury, and Salisbury itself. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia unwinds a tangle of moves and divisions across four centuries.

Under Headda the see moved to Winchester, then split in 705 into Winchester and Sherborne, where Aldhelm became first bishop. Ten successors later, Wiltshire and Berkshire broke away as Ramsbury in 909, until Herman reunited Sherborne and Ramsbury in 1058 and shifted his chair to Old Sarum in 1075. His successor Osmund built a cathedral there and drew up the Sarum ordinal of services that shaped English worship.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sanctuary:
Sanctuary means the space in a church set aside for the high altar and the clergy. It has borne many names: apse or concha, from its shell-like half-dome, choir since the Middle Ages, from the singers stationed there, and presbyterium, tribuna, hagion, and sanctum. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia traces how that space changed shape across Christian antiquity and the Middle Ages.

Early sanctuaries centred on the apse, where stone benches for clergy ringed the wall like an amphitheatre and the bishop's chair rose in the middle. Yet the apse was not always semicircular: digs, above all in the East, have found over a dozen shapes. In Syria the curve barely projects from the outer wall, flanked by two side rooms with their own uses, and the entry maps those variations.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-savary:
Savary names a noble French family of the seventeenth century devoted to trade and to commercial writings of lasting authority. Its brightest member, Jacques Savary, was born at Doué in Anjou on 22 September 1622 and died on 7 October 1690. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a merchant turned lawmaker.

Destined for trade, Jacques studied law in Paris with a procureur, then joined the wholesale haberdashers and made his fortune by 1658. Ties with Superintendent Fouquet brought him the contract for crown-land revenues. After Fouquet's fall he won Chancellor Séguier's favour, and arbitrations in commercial disputes built his standing daily. In 1670 he joined the commission revising trade laws, work that made his name a byword in French commerce.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-school-of-der:
The School of Derry was Columba's first foundation, raised by the great apostle of Scotland and one of Ireland's three patron saints. When the Yellow Plague of 544 scattered Glasnevin's monks, Columba turned homeward to his own kin, intent on founding a monastery among them. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia tells how an oak grove became a school.

His princely cousin Aedh, son of Ainmire, offered 200 acres, and his master Mobhi Clarainech gave leave with his dying breath. A few miles from Ailech, the stone fortress of the Hy-Neill, stood a fair oak wood that gave the place its name, Doire Colgaigh, Colgagh's oak wood. Beside it Columba built a church and cells for his first monks. The Annals of Ulster date it to 545, corrected to 546, and students clerical and lay soon flocked there.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-shrewsbury:
Shrewsbury, one of thirteen English dioceses created by Pius IX on 27 September 1850, first covered Shropshire and Cheshire plus seven Welsh counties. When Leo XIII formed the Vicariate of Wales in 1895, the Welsh counties were separated, leaving only Shropshire and Cheshire under the bishop of Shrewsbury. Before the Reformation, Cheshire and northern Shropshire fell under Coventry and Lichfield, and the rest of Shropshire under Hereford.

Henry VIII's creation of Chester took Cheshire from Coventry and Lichfield. Innocent XI's four vicariates of 1688 put Shropshire in the Midland district and Cheshire in the Northern, and Gregory XVI's eight vicariates of 1840 split them between the Central and Lancashire districts. The diocese takes its name from Shrewsbury, county town of Shropshire, under the patronage of Our Lady Help of Christians and Saint Winefride, whose body was translated to Shrewsbury in 1138.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-of-sudb:
Simon of Sudbury, Archbishop of Canterbury, was born at Sudbury in Suffolk of middle-class parents and died at London on 14 June 1381. After a law degree at Paris, he went to Rome and became chaplain to Innocent VI. Sent to England as nuncio in 1356, he became Bishop of London in 1361. He worked with John of Gaunt on French negotiations in 1372 and 1373, and enriched his native town with a collegiate church on his father's old house site.

Sudbury succeeded Langham as Archbishop of Canterbury in 1375. Friendship with John of Gaunt set him against Courtenay of London and William of Wykeham. Amiable but not strong, he shrank from proceeding against Wyclif, whom Gaunt backed, though Courtenay forced a summons in 1377 that ended without condemnation. Made lord chancellor in 1380, he paid for the office with his life in the peasants' rising a year later, when rebels seized and beheaded him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sir-thomas-ma:
Thomas Malory's life is almost wholly conjecture. We know he was a knight, his book was finished in the ninth year of Edward IV's reign, and Caxton first printed it in 1485. Long taken for a Welshman on an unsound derivation of Bale's, gratified by matching the romancer's birthplace to Arthurian scenes. He is now more probably judged a gentleman of an ancient Warwickshire house. He served young in France with Richard Beauchamp, Earl of Warwick.

The author's obscurity contrasts dramatically with four centuries of unfailing appreciation for his Morte Arthure. Though a compilation, a mosaic of French romances of Merlin, Lancelot, and Tristan and the English Morte Arthure from Geoffrey of Monmouth. Malory turned episodic matter and clashing racial viewpoints into steady ideals of conduct in epic conflict with fate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-ch:
The Sisters of Charity of Jesus and Mary were founded in 1803 by Canon Triest, called the Saint Vincent de Paul of Belgium. He also founded the Brothers of Saint John of God and the Sisters of the Infant Jesus. As curé of Lovendeghem he laid the congregation's foundations and gave up his living to train members. He won first papal recognition in 1806 and final approbation on 9 September 1816 after going to Rome.

The mother-house stands at Ghent, with forty branch houses, and the congregation ranks among Belgium's largest, counting over a thousand members. In 1889 sisters went to the Congo missions and founded several houses there. In 1895 they went to India, opening schools in the Punjab and Ceylon. Their chief work is teaching in training colleges, schools, and orphanages, plus nursing the infirm. They are enclosed, with no lay sisters, in a spirit of simplicity, devotion, and zeal.

The Sisters of Charity of the Blessed Virgin Mary began with five young women in Dublin on 8 December 1831, devoted to teaching children. Their first Dublin school opened in North Ann Street on 19 March 1832. Mary Frances Clarke became first superior, with Margaret Mann as assistant and mistress of novices. On 1 November 1833 they received their present title.

In 1843 the congregation accepted Bishop Loras of Dubuque's invitation and moved to Iowa for pioneer work. The mother-house has stood at Dubuque ever since. Their rules won approval in 1877, confirmed by Leo XIII on 26 April 1885. Education is their only work, and by September 1907 they counted one thousand members teaching 25,000 children.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sisters-of-th:
The Sisters of the Holy Childhood of Jesus and Mary cover two congregations described in this entry. The first began in 1835 in the Diocese of Fréjus for educating girls and caring for the sick, with its mother-house at Draguignan and government authorization in 1853. The second began at Sens in 1838 for teaching and nursing the sick in their homes.

In the fuller account, the religious divide into choir sisters, who staff higher schools, industrial schools, and orphanages, and lay sisters, who handle domestic care. Vows run annually for ten years before final vows. Papal approval came in 1888, with statutes approved in 1899. A Boston diocese branch taught 2,400 pupils, with a novitiate at Salem, Massachusetts, and the congregation counts about 1,400 sisters.

Founded at Dommartin-sous-Amance, France, in 1855 by John Joseph Begel, pastor of Laitre and Dommartin, the Sisters of the Holy Humility of Mary teach poor children in country districts and small towns. Three women offered their services in 1854, and Begel drew up a rule approved by the Bishop of Nancy in 1858. The congregation also trained orphans, nursed the sick, and decorated parish altars.

Begel's open condemnation of Napoleon III's policy toward the Church brought official disfavour, and the sisters were refused diplomas and barred from opening schools. In 1862 Father Louis Hoffer of Louisville, Ohio, asked for four sisters, and Bishop Rappe of Cleveland invited the whole community to his diocese. They sailed on 30 May 1864 and settled on a 250-acre farm near New Bedford, Pennsylvania, named Villa Maria. By 1909 they counted about 200 members running 15 parish schools, 2 academies, and an orphan asylum.

Founded at Longueuil, Quebec, on 8 December 1844 under Bishop Bourget of Montreal, the Sisters of the Holy Names of Jesus and Mary teach young girls. Three Canadian aspirants trained under John Allard after the Marseilles institute of Eugene de Mazenod, then took simple vows as Sisters Marie-Rose, Marie-Madeline, and Marie-Agnes. Bourget gave diocesan approval and named Mother Marie-Rose general superior for life.

Marseilles supplied the title, habit, and rule, with modifications, and under Mother Marie-Rose the congregation grew fast. A course of study served English and French pupils alike, and missionary need later brought boys' teaching under temporary Holy See permission. By 1910 the institute counted 1,257 professed sisters, 110 novices, and 81 postulants, running 99 schools with 24,208 pupils, 48 of them in the United States.

Founded in England in 1877, the Sisters of the Little Company of Mary honour the Blessed Virgin's maternal heart, above all in the mystery of Calvary. The sisters consecrate themselves wholly to her and imitate her virtues. Their chief outward work is nursing the sick and dying, at home and in hospitals and nursing homes linked to their convents.

They serve every class, nationality, and creed alike, and charge nothing, accepting only free offerings. Besides nursing, they pray continually for the dying, keeping watch before the Blessed Sacrament day and night in the novitiate. Leo XIII gave final approbation to their rules in 1893. Houses stand in Italy, England, Ireland, Malta, Chicago, Australia, and South Africa, with a black habit and blue veil.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-adrian-of-:
St. Adrian of Canterbury was an African by birth who died in 710, and this entry tells how humility rerouted his career. Made abbot of Nerida, a Benedictine house near Naples. While very young, he was Pope Vitalian's first choice to succeed Deusdedit as Archbishop of Canterbury. But judged himself unworthy and begged the pope to name the Greek monk Theodore instead.

Vitalian agreed on one condition, that Adrian travel with Theodore to England as his adviser in running Canterbury.
