They left Rome in 668, but Ebroin, Mayor of the Palace in France, detained Adrian for two years on suspicion of a secret mission from Emperor Constans II. Cleared at last, he reached England, where Theodore made him abbot of St. Peter's, the monastery founded by St. Augustine.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-augustine-:
St. Augustine of Canterbury was the first archbishop of Canterbury and apostle of the English. His date of birth is unknown, and he died on 26 May 604. This entry follows a man probably Roman of the better class, who early in life became a monk in the famous monastery of St. Andrew. Gregory had erected that monastery out of his own patrimony on the Caelian Hill.

It was in the close religious life of the Benedictine rule, and the bracing air of a recent foundation, that the future missionary's character was formed. Chance is said to have furnished the opportunity for the enterprise that would join his name forever with his friend and patron, St. Gregory. Augustine became the true founder of one of Christendom's most important churches, and the channel by which Roman authority was established over the English.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-elizabeth-:
Elizabeth of Hungary, married at fourteen and dead at twenty-four, became one of the Middle Ages' most beloved saints. Daughter of King Andrew II, she was sent to Thuringia as a child bride in a political alliance against Emperor Otto IV. In 1221 she married Ludwig IV, a capable ruler who protected her charities, vigils, and penances. The Catholic Encyclopedia article of 1913 dates her death at Marburg to 17 November 1231.

When flood, famine, and plague struck Thuringia in 1226 while Ludwig served the emperor in Italy, Elizabeth took charge and distributed alms on a grand scale. Widowed soon after, she bore a third child after her husband's death. Her family web runs through the age: her brother became Bela IV, her aunt was Hedwig of Silesia, and her great-niece was Elizabeth of Portugal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eucherius-:
Eucherius, bishop of Lyons until about 449, chose the hermit's island before the Church chose him for a see. Born late in the fourth century, he withdrew after his wife's death to Lérins, where his sons Veranius and Salonius lived, then to neighbouring Lerona, now Sainte-Marguerite, for study and mortification. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 follows his correspondence with John Cassian about Egypt's desert hermits.

Cassian answered with his Collationes on the Thebaid's daily life, and Eucherius wrote his letter De laude Eremi to Hilary of Arles about 428. He kept touch with learned and pious friends, including Honoratus and Valerian, while imitating Egyptian solitaries. Fame across southeastern Gaul carried him to Lyons, probably in 434. The entry joins desert longing to episcopal duty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-gery:
Gery, bishop of Cambrai-Arras, shepherded a diocese still recovering from barbarian invasion. Born of Roman parents Gaudentius and Austadiola at Eposium, now Carignan, about the middle of the sixth century, he led a pious youth that prepared him for zeal and devotion. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death to 11 August, between 623 and 626.

His see was young beside ancient Tongres, and the invasion of 406 had wrecked church organization across Belgium. Under Merovingian recovery, Vaast restored Arras early in the sixth century, and Gery ranked among his earliest successors. The entry sets one bishop's career inside a larger rebuilding: Christians scattered, bishops displaced to Reims, then dioceses slowly knit together again under men like Vaast and Gery.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-lawrence-o:
Lawrence of Canterbury, second archbishop after Augustine, carried news of Kent's conversion to Rome and back. He died on 2 February 619. For his life and rule the entry relies on Bede, with medieval additions lacking proof, though possibly preserving old tradition. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 follows Bede's account closely.

Lawrence was among the original missionaries who left Rome with Augustine in 595 and landed at Thanet in 597. After Augustine's consecration, he was sent back to Rome as a priest, distinct from Peter the monk. He bore news of Ethelbert's conversion, announced the consecration, and asked direction on questions. Gregory decided those questions, and Lawrence returned bearing replies, remaining with Augustine thereafter. Whether he was a parish priest or monk remains disputed by later writers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-patrick-s-:
St Patrick's Purgatory, the celebrated sanctuary on Lough Derg in Donegal, draws pilgrims to Station Island still. The lake covers about 2200 acres, thirteen miles round, with eleven islands, chiefly Saints Island and Station Island. Tradition ties the place to Patrick himself, a link the Bollandists accept on historical evidence.

Canons Regular of St Augustine took charge about 1130 or 1134, making it a dependent priory of Armagh. Its fame turned European after the knight Owen's visit in 1150, and accounts of foreign pilgrimages fill the thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth centuries. The entry traces sanctuary lands, stewards, and pilgrim rites, offering a compact history of Ireland's sternest place of penance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-josep:
Stephen Joseph Perry, a Jesuit astronomer, directed Stonyhurst Observatory and led eclipse expeditions. Born in London in August 1833 to a well known Catholic family, he was schooled at Gifford Hall and Douai's Benedictine college, then went to Rome for the priesthood. Resolving to join the Jesuits, he entered the novitiate in 1853 to 1855 at Hodder and Beaumont Lodge, studying later at St Acheul near Amiens and at Stonyhurst.

His bent for mathematics sent him to De Morgan's lectures in London and to Bertrand, Liouville, Delaunay, Cauchy, and Serret in Paris. Recalled to Stonyhurst in autumn 1860, he taught physics and mathematics and took charge of the observatory. Ordained in 1866 after theology at St Beuno's, he resumed those duties for life, save for scientific engagements. With Sidgreaves he surveyed magnetism in France and Belgium, and led government eclipse parties. He died on 27 December 1889.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-russe:
Stephen Russell Mallory was born in Trinidad in 1813. He grew into a Florida lawyer, then a United States senator, then the man who built the Confederate navy from nothing. This entry traces that rise, from his schooling at a Jesuit college in Mobile to his Florida judgeship and customs post at Key West.

Davis named him navy secretary in February 1861. He took over a department with no ships and no stores, yet he pieced a fleet together from raw materials. After Richmond fell in April 1865, he fled with Davis, was jailed ten months at Fort Lafayette, and won parole in 1866. He then practised law at Pensacola until his death in 1873.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-syon-monaster:
Syon Monastery in Middlesex was founded in 1415 by Henry V at his Isleworth manor. Dedicated to St Saviour and St Bridget of Syon, it was England's only house of Bridget's reformed Augustinian order, counting thirteen priests, four deacons, eight lay brothers, and sixty nuns. Its land ran half a mile along the Thames, and prayer for the founder's soul was its chief duty.

Martin V confirmed the house in 1418, novices were professed in 1420, and the chapel's first stone was laid six years later. Income grew to an estimated 1,730 pounds a year, and even Henry VIII's commissioners found little fault with its observance. Expelled in 1539, the nuns wandered through Flanders, France, Spain, and Lisbon, returning to England in 1861, while Northumberland's descendants still hold Isleworth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tapestry:
Tapestry, a French word, names a fabric where weaving and embroidery join. Instead of throwing the woof by shuttle, the worker adds it to the warp with a needle. The needle carries a short coloured thread, producing a mosaic of dyed threads rich in colour and shading. Such cloth serves for wall hangings and for floor and furniture coverings.

Egyptians used it first, and the art passed through western Asia to Europe. It reached perfection in the later Middle Ages and Renaissance, above all at Arras. Arras gave its name to all tapestry, wherever made. In pre-Reformation England, monastic houses made it for reredoses, altar frontals, hearse cloths, and choir hangings. It pictured Bible scenes, saints' lives, historic events, and points of faith in symbol.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-aberdeen-:
The Aberdeen Breviary is the Sarum Office in Scottish form. The Salisbury use was adopted in Scotland and Ireland during the Middle Ages, for Mass and hours. Its Scottish introduction is sometimes wrongly credited to Edward I in 1292, but evidence puts it earlier. Herbert, Bishop of Glasgow from 1147 to 1164, adopted Sarum for his church with papal sanction. Father Innes, who died in Paris in 1744, asserted that every Scots missal or breviary he saw followed Sarum use.

Moray's bishop, dean, and chapter received and approved Salisbury's Ordo in 1242, and Moray bordered Aberdeen. Scots preference for Sarum reflected resistance to York's jurisdictional claims over Scotland, which adopting York use might have seemed to justify. The Aberdeen Breviary was the work of William Elphinstone, Bishop of Aberdeen from 1483 to his death in 1514. He gathered the materials and composed lessons, notably for Scottish saints, whose festivals devote all nine Matins lessons to their lives.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-alexandri:
The Great Library of Alexandria, distinct from the smaller Serapeum library, was a foundation of the Ptolemies to sustain Greek civilization in Egypt. If Demetrius of Phalerum's move to Alexandria in 296-295 BC concerned the library, its plan formed under Ptolemy Soter, who died about 284 BC. Completion and its Museum link belonged to his successor, Ptolemy Philadelphus. Since Strabo omits the library from his harbour buildings, it stood elsewhere, likely in Brucheion.

Books came strikingly. Ships entering harbour surrendered manuscripts. Athens' copy of the three tragedians was kept by forfeiting a 15-talent deposit for return. Rivalry with Pergamon grew keen that papyrus export was banned to cripple it, driving the perfection of skins, charta pergamena, our parchment. Rivalry bred spurious works, false antiquing, and hasty copying. Roll counts vary by period: Demetrius counted 200,000 rolls and hoped for more. The entry weighs the library's destructions, including the preposterous fuel tale.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-annunciat:
Luke's Gospel, chapter 1, verses 26 to 38, supplies the event at the centre of this entry: the angel Gabriel's visit to Mary at Nazareth. Six months after Elizabeth conceived John the Baptist, Gabriel came to a young woman of David's house, espoused to Joseph but still living in her mother's home. His greeting, Hail, full of grace, troubled her, since she did not know the visitor or his errand.

Gabriel told her not to fear, for she had found grace with God, and that she would bear a son. Mary's questions and her consent follow, with notes on the words of the greeting and on early art and devotion. Readers find both the Gospel narrative retold with care and the Church's reading of what the moment meant.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-blessed-v:
Mary, mother of Jesus Christ and mother of God, is the subject of this vast entry, which follows theology and history through their sources in order. Old Testament prophecies and types open the account, above all Genesis chapter 3, verse 15, where the woman and her seed face the serpent. Hebrew wording, Septuagint renderings, and later translations are weighed with care.

New Testament narratives follow, from Annunciation to Calvary and beyond, then early Christian and Jewish witnesses, councils, liturgy, art, and devotion. Apparitions, feasts, and doctrines such as the Immaculate Conception receive their own sections. Few entries in the encyclopedia range so widely across Scripture, history, and popular piety.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-monk-of-m:
A phantom author dissolves under scrutiny in this short entry. A chronicle among the Cottonian manuscripts in the British Museum, Vespasian D IV 73, bears the name Godfridus de Malmesbury. Tanner judged it a mere copy of Alfred of Beverley's twelfth-century chronicle, while Sir Thomas Hardy traced it almost wholly to Geoffrey of Monmouth.

Worthless as history, it runs from the Saxon invasion to 1129. Godfrey of Malmesbury, a Jumièges native who became abbot in 1081 and founded the abbey library, once seemed its author. His death by 1107, when Edulf succeeded him, disproves the guess. The signature likely marks ownership, not authorship, a warning against trusting a name on a page.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-name-of-m:
Mary's name, in Scripture and Catholic use, is the puzzle at the heart of this entry. New Testament texts give Mariam and sometimes Maria, and scholars cannot yet say whether Evangelists reserved Mariam for Christ's Mother and Maria for others of the name. Mariam surely renders Hebrew MRYM, borne by Moses and Aaron's sister.

Chronicles chapter 4, verse 17, may even give it to a man, though the Septuagint reads Maron there. Two roots compete for Miriam's sense: MRH, to rebel, tied by some to Moses's sister murmuring against him, and MRA, to be fat, which Semitic minds linked to beauty. Lady, the reading most Fathers favoured, closes the debate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-rosary:
Fifteen decades of Hail Marys, each ten framed by an Our Father and a mystery of redemption held in meditation, make up the Rosary as the Roman Breviary defines it. When Albigensian heresy ravaged Toulouse, Dominic besought Our Lady's help and, so tradition asserts, was told to preach the Rosary as an antidote to heresy and sin.

From that hour the prayer spread wonderfully, published abroad and developed by Dominic, whom popes in many ages called its institutor and author. History, mysteries joyful, sorrowful, and glorious, indulgences, and confraternities follow. For readers new to the devotion, the entry joins legend, liturgy, and practice in a single thread.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodore-arch:
Canterbury's seventh archbishop, Theodore of Tarsus, gave the English Church order after years of drift. Born at Tarsus in Cilicia about 602, he died at Canterbury on 19 September 690. A monk at Rome in 667, he was picked by Pope Vitalian for Canterbury when Wighard died before he could be consecrated.

The pope himself consecrated Theodore on 26 March 668, and he reached Canterbury in May 669. He found sees too large, many with no bishop, and old bitterness from the Easter date row still rankling. He toured the whole island, filled empty sees, put Chad's rank in order, and curbed abuses, giving English faith a shape it had lacked.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tomb-of-the-b:
The Tomb of the Blessed Virgin Mary is venerated in the Valley of Cedron, near Jerusalem, yet many modern writers hold that Mary died and was buried at Ephesus. The entry sets the two traditions side by side. Apocryphal works of the second to fourth centuries favour Jerusalem, placing her tomb at Gethsemane. Pilgrims from the fifth century onward visited a basilica in the Valley of Josaphat holding her sepulchre.

Writers from Gregory of Tours to Sophronius and Germanus of Constantinople repeat the Jerusalem tradition. The Ephesus claim rests on later reasoning about John's residence there, and on the silence of early Ephesian sources. Since 1187 the tomb has belonged to the Muslim government, which still allows Christians to officiate there, and the church keeps frescoes and marble slabs from its long history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tynemouth-pri:
Tynemouth Priory stands on the Northumberland coast of England, on Saxon church ground. That church was built first in wood and then in stone in the seventh century. It won fame as the burial place of St Oswin, king and martyr, before Danish raiders plundered and burned the site again and again. In 1074 the place passed to Benedictine monks from Yarrow, and with them it joined Durham Abbey. Later it became a cell of St Albans under Earl Robert de Mowbray.

The entry traces the priory's buildings as they grew: a Norman church raised about 1100, a choir lengthened some 120 years later, and a Lady chapel added around 1320. It notes the monks' life, the priory's lands and troubles, and its end at the Dissolution, when monastic life there ceased. Ruins and memory remain the theme of a coastal house battered by raiders and rebuilt by Normans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-usury:
Usury is the taking of interest on money lent, and this long entry asks when, if ever, it is lawful. It begins with usury as condemned by all honest men. Plato and Aristotle held interest contrary to nature, Aristophanes mocked it, and Cato likened it to homicide, as did Seneca and Plutarch. Greek and Roman writers knew little economics, yet ruinous lending rates explain their severity.

Roman and Greek law still allowed the loan for consumption, and the entry follows the church's teaching from Scripture and the fathers through medieval schoolmen to modern moralists. It distinguishes interest that pays for loss or risk from sheer gain on a loan, and weighs modern banking against old bans. Readers get a full history of a moral question that shaped finance for centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vatican-obser:
The Vatican Observatory now bears the official title Specola Astronomica Vaticana. Its name needs a note: osservatorio or specola can mean any high place for watching sky phenomena, not only a star observatory. From that view the Specola Vaticana passed through four stages. The first began when Gregory XIII ordered a tower raised in a handy part of the Vatican and fitted with the finest instruments of the day.

There Gregory held meetings of the learned men charged with reforming the calendar, and the tower still stands as witness to his generosity. Later stages brought the observatory's refounding under Leo XIII, its new instruments, and its work in star mapping and meteorology. The entry traces the Specola from a calendar tower to a modern observatory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ven-robert-dr:
Robert Drury was a martyr of 1567 to 1607, born of a good Buckinghamshire family, taken into the English College at Reims on 1 April 1588. On 17 September 1590 he went to the new college at Valladolid, where he finished his studies, was ordained priest, and returned to England in 1593. He worked chiefly in London, where his learning and virtue won him much respect among his brethren.

He joined the appellants against the archpriest Blackwell, and his name stands on the appeal of 17 November 1600, dated from the prison at Wisbech. A government invitation asking these priests to acknowledge allegiance and duty to the queen, dated 5 November 1602, produced the famous loyal address of 31 January 1603. Dr William Bishop drew it up, and thirteen leading priests signed it, including Drury. The entry follows Drury to his execution in 1607.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vincent-houdr:
Vincent Houdry was a French Jesuit preacher and writer on the spiritual life who lived from 1631 to 1729. Entering the Society at Paris in 1647, he studied philosophy for three years and theology for four, then taught classics for six years, rhetoric for one. Philosophy for four, before becoming a celebrated pulpit orator preaching for twenty-five years in France's chief cities.

His remaining years were given to writing sermons, and his obituary praised his tireless industry as speaker and writer and his faithful observance of the rules even into his ninety-ninth year. He left two major homiletic works: collected sermons on every subject of Christian morality, five parts in twenty-two volumes published at Paris between 1696 and 1702 and reprinted several times. A library of materials for preachers, supplemented by a scrupulously compiled index volume.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-visitation-of:
The Visitation is Mary's journey from Nazareth to her cousin Elizabeth at Hebron, south of Jerusalem, related in Luke 1:39-57. Assuming Annunciation and Incarnation fell about the spring equinox, Mary left at March's end and crossed the mountains, because her presence. Still more the divine Child in her womb, was to bring great graces to John, Christ's forerunner.

At Mary's arrival John leaped in Elizabeth's womb, was cleansed from original sin, and filled with God's grace. Mary first exercised the office of Mother of God made man, that he might sanctify and glorify us through her mediation. Joseph probably accompanied her, returned to Nazareth, and came again after three months to take her home. The angel's appearance in Matthew 1 may have ended his tormenting doubts about her maternity. As a feast it was adopted by the Franciscan chapter in 1263 on Bonaventure's advice.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-voluntary:
Voluntary, or wilful, describes what proceeds from the will following actual knowledge, formal or virtual, in a rational agent. It is not quite the same as free, since a free act supposes self-determination, an agent able at the time to determine himself or not as he chooses. Moralists commonly use the terms interchangeably, because nearly every specific voluntary act in this life is also free.

A thing may be voluntary in itself, falling directly under the agent's efficacious determination, or voluntary in its cause. Requiring at least virtual foreknowledge of the effect and production by the will's efficiency in willing the cause. The moralist distinguishes effects a cause is naturally destined to produce, for which it is the sole adequate cause. From effects it is not so destined to produce, a distinction that decides how far responsibility for unforeseen consequences extends.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-walsingham-pr:
Walsingham Priory stood a few miles from the sea in northern Norfolk. Its chapel of Our Lady founded in Edward the Confessor's time, confirmed to Augustinian Canons a century later, and enclosed within the priory. From the first it was a famous pilgrimage shrine, drawing the faithful from all England and the continent until Henry VIII destroyed the priory in 1538. The pilgrims' main road through Newmarket, Brandon, and Fakenham is still called Palmers' Way.

Gifts of lands, rents, and churches flowed to its canons, and many miracles were reported at the shrine. Kings came on pilgrimage: Henry III in 1241, Edward I in 1280 and 1296, Edward II in 1315, Henry VI in 1455, Henry VII in 1487. Henry VIII in 1513, while Erasmus, fulfilling a vow, came from Cambridge in 1511 and left Greek verses, later writing a colloquy rationalizing some reputed miracles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-whithorn-prio:
Whithorn Priory stood in Wigtownshire, Scotland, founded about the mid-twelfth century in David I's reign by Fergus, Lord of Galloway, for Premonstratensian, or White, Canons. Its canons formed the chapter of Galloway diocese, re-established about the same time also by Fergus, the old episcopal succession having died out about 796. The prior ranked next to the bishop, as an early thirteenth-century charter's signatories show, and his community held the right of electing the bishop.

York's archbishop, to whom Galloway was long suffragan, sometimes overruled it for secular clergy. The full prior list is lost, but among them were Maurice, who swore fealty to Edward I in 1296, Gavin Dunbar, later Archbishop of Glasgow in 1514. James Beaton, successively archbishop of Glasgow and St Andrews and chancellor of the kingdom. Whithorn long drew pilgrims through St Ninian's venerated memory, Scottish sovereigns Margaret, queen of James III, James IV.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-ma:
William of Malmesbury was a twelfth-century monk historian whose works remain the backbone of early English history. Born about 1090, he died about 1143. Schooled at Malmesbury, he became a monk there and bent early toward history, writing, in his own words, because old writings left him unsatisfied. By 1125 he had finished Gesta Regum and Gesta Pontificum, then spent ten years gathering materials now at the Bodleian and writing on Glastonbury and its saints.

Though he might more than once have become abbot, he stayed content as librarian. About 1140 he revised both great works and began Historia Novella, a sequel for 1125 to 1142, left as a first draft rather than a finished book. His record of Stephen's reign is priceless, his Norman kings rest on knowledge or direct hearsay, and his cause-and-effect method, learned from Bede, advanced history beyond his predecessors.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-of-st:
William of Saint-Thierry was a theologian and mystic, abbot of the house that gave him his name. Born at Liège about 1085, he died at Signy about 1148. Of noble stock, he studied with brother Simon at Saint Nicaise, Reims, where both took religious life; Simon led Saint Nicolas-aux-Bois and William led Saint-Thierry near Reims from 1119. He knew Bernard closely and longed for Clairvaux, but Bernard bade him stay with his charges.

William later withdrew to the Cistercian abbey at Signy, dividing suffering days between prayer and study. His writings span the solitary life, contemplation of God after Augustine, and the nature and dignity of love. Mirrors and enigmas of faith, the Eucharist against Rupert, commentaries on the Song of Songs and Romans, and a life of Bernard complete the list. He first exposed Abelard's errors and spurred Bernard against him, with tracts later condemned at Sens.
confession-or-the-blind-heart-a-domestic:
Confession, or The Blind Heart, a domestic story by W Gilmore Simms, opens under a motto from Goethe's Faust about those who knew and felt, and were crucified or burnt for telling. Simms begins by repeating the quotation and turning it into an essay. The pains and penalties of folly, he argues, are not necessarily death. The old texts threatened as much, but life is subtler. The blind heart of his title is the organ that refuses its own knowledge.

From that somber porch the tale enters Southern domestic life, where a confession withheld or mistimed poisons a household. Simms works here in the domestic vein: marriage, conscience, family honor. What one person knows about another comes out slowly. The Faust epigraph is a warning the characters will spend the book fulfilling, that knowledge shared blindly and knowledge buried can ruin in equal measure.
cow-country:
B M Bower follows Buddy in Cow-Country from ambitious man-child through trail herds and Indian lore to manhood as Bud. The chapter list promises the Muleshoe ranch, a lost boy at Little Lost, the Sinks, the Catrock gang, and Bud meeting the woman. Buddy gives warning and runs true to type before the young eagle must fly.

Bud rides through Catrock and loses Marian, picks his footing in a horse race where Jeff is accused of taking a boy's money unfairly, and faces rustlers with guardian angels riding point. Bower's own Montana years supply the brands, ranges, and talk. The novel is a Western bildungsroman, its hero educated by cattle, horses, and one honest girl.
criticisms-on-the-origin-of-species-from:
Thomas Henry Huxley published this long review essay in the Natural History Review in 1864, five years into the Darwinian controversy. Its occasion is foreign commentary on Darwin's Origin of Species. Huxley notes the support of the linguist Schleicher and of Haeckel, then turns to two substantial attacks, by the Wurzburg anatomist Kolliker and by Flourens of the French Academy.

Kolliker's rival Theory of Heterogeneous Generation gets the closer handling, first in its objections and then in its construction. Huxley charges him with mistaking Darwin for a teleologist, a thinker who builds purpose into nature. Varieties, Huxley insists, arise by general laws whether useful, hurtful, or indifferent. The essay is Darwin's bulldog at work in print: part summary, part cross-examination, part counter-attack.
danny-s-own-story:
Don Marquis lets Danny tell Danny's Own Story in his own unlettered voice, starting with why he has no last name. Found in a basket on the Walters family's steps, he grows up between a drunken Hank and a quarrelsome Elmira. The comedy of his telling softens a hard childhood.

Danny runs away, works farms and lumber yards, falls in with tramps and small-town sharpers, and keeps his shrewd good humor through every beating and betrayal. Marquis, later famous for archy the cockroach, here masters American vernacular storytelling. The novel follows its hero toward the Klondike and manhood, and readers hear Danny thinking in every misspelled, perfectly chosen sentence.
discourses-on-satire-and-on-epic-poetry:
John Dryden wrote his Discourses on Satire and on Epic Poetry in his last years, and this 1888 Cassell edition reprints both with an introduction. Dryden's discourse on satire, inscribed to the Earl of Dorset, traces the form from Horace and Juvenal and settles what makes a fine satire: not mere railing, but art. The epic discourse weighs Homer against Virgil and asks how a heroic poem should be built, judged, and translated.

The introduction contrasts these mature essays with his youthful Essay of Dramatic Poesie, written as Dutch guns sounded in 1667. Dryden reasons from wide reading in the French and classical critics yet trusts his own judgment. English criticism begins in earnest here, in prose as masculine and quotable as his verse.
divine-comedy-cary-s-translation-purgato:
Dante Alighieri's Purgatory, the Purgatorio, forms the second canticle of the Divine Comedy in H F Cary's translation. Its first canto lifts the sail of Dante's genius over better waves, glad to leave hell's cruel sea behind. A mountain island rises from the southern ocean, where souls climb toward heaven.

Virgil leads Dante up seven terraces, one for each deadly sin. The proud bend under stones there. The envious, who hoped a neighbor's fall would raise them, have their eyes sewn shut. Statius joins the climb, and the Earthly Paradise crowns the mountain. Cary's blank verse keeps the middle canticle's mood, harsher than paradise, gentler than hell, full of music and morning light.

doe-osti-3415860-a-synthetic-photonic-do: When blasts throw dust and debris through the air, clocking their speed is brutally hard. This work builds a synthetic testbed for photonic Doppler velocimetry — a laser method that reads velocity — tuned for particle-filled flows. The numerical framework lets researchers check their instruments against known answers.
dream-life-and-real-life-a-little-africa:
Olive Schreiner called Dream Life and Real Life a little African story, dedicating it to her brother Fred, for whose school magazine its first tiny tale was written years before. The 1893 Eastbourne dedication dates the collection. A glossary first explains the karoo landscape. Kopjes rise like ruined castles there. Kraals, krantzes, and sluits carrying storm water complete the picture.

Three stories follow. The title tale concerns a child on a karoo farm. The Woman's Rose remembers white acacia flowers gathered by a man's strong hand on a sultry afternoon. A piece on protection policy closes the set. Schreiner's South African childhood supplies the heat, stones, and loneliness. These early pieces show her allegorical gift forming.
eben-holden-a-tale-of-the-north-country:
Irving Bacheller dated his preface April 1900 and built this tale from the Vermont settlers who crossed into the Adirondack wilderness of northern New York. The preface sketches their world: stumpy farms, coon-skin coats, and sons raised on honour, industry, and the hope of being president. The story itself opens with a ruined Vermont home and a strange little expedition west.

A small boy rides in a basket on the back of a jolly old man, Eben Holden. Holden carries a cane in one hand and a rifle in the other, with a black dog for scout. The boy narrates their life in the north country as he grows. Newspaper editor Horace Greeley enters the tale in its later chapters, from files and memories Bacheller acknowledges in his preface.
from-wealth-to-poverty-or-the-tricks-of-:
Austin Potter's From Wealth to Poverty, or The Tricks of the Traffic, is a temperance story subtitled A Story of the Drink Curse. Potter dedicates it to prohibition's friends around the world. His preface names two motives: hatred of the rum traffic, and a desire to expose the liquor party's measures against the Dunkin Act.

Potter writes from personal experience and observation, having lived in three counties where drink brought hardship to himself and those dear to him. The story follows a family's fall from wealth to poverty, showing how the traffic's tricks ensnare its victims. Readers interested in the temperance movement, or in Victorian moral fiction with a reforming edge, will find Potter earnest and unsparing.
geronimo-story:
Geronimo, the Apache war leader, dictated his life story in 1906 while held as a prisoner of war at Fort Sill. S. M. Barrett, a local school official, took down his words with his permission. Geronimo said he wanted the truth told at last.

He recalls his youth in the Southwest, Mexican raids that killed his family, and his long wars against Mexico and the United States. His surrenders, escapes, and final capture in 1886 close the tale. The book gives the Apache wars from the Apache side, in a voice both proud and bitter. Geronimo died still a prisoner three years later.
glengarry-school-days-a-story-of-early-d:
Ralph Connor wrote Glengarry School Days as a novel of pioneer schooling in Glengarry, a Scottish settlement district in eastern Ontario, Canada. Its setting is the Twentieth school, a log building ringed by deep forest. Master Archibald Munro rules the room with a lame knee, a firm hand, and surprising fairness. Hughie Murray, the minister's lively son, stands near the center of the children's world.

Chapters move from a Friday spelling match to examinations, a new master, and a bear hunt in the woods. Pranks, fights, and loyalty tests fill the school year. Foxy and his partner scheme, Hughie wins a measure of freedom, and two hard rounds settle old scores. Connor gives readers a warm, rough picture of settlement childhood, where lessons in books mattered less than courage, honesty, and standing by friends.
god-s-good-man-a-simple-love-story:
Marie Corelli dedicated God's Good Man to the living original of her hero. The Reverend John Walden and his wife receive the book as a simple love story, affectionately given. Her epigraph runs that there was a man sent from God whose name was John. The novel opens in an English May after a cruel winter.

Walden, a saintly country parson, loves Maryllia, a wealthy woman who returns to her ancestral village. Church politics, a scheming squire, and village gossip oppose their union. Corelli contrasts Walden's pure ministry with worldly clergy who serve fashion. Spring blossom, cowslips, and bluebells frame her sermons in story form. The book was among her best loved, read as both romance and rebuke. Her good man stands against an age she thought faithless and greedy.
govdocs-archive_org-JonBenetRamseyCaseSu:
Chapter twenty of David McGowan's Programmed to Kill, titled Boulder, treats the murder of JonBenet Ramsey, the six-year-old found dead in her Boulder, Colorado home in 1996. McGowan's book argues that many notorious crimes hide organized abuse networks. The Ramsey chapter applies that thesis to America's most debated unsolved case.

McGowan reviews the ransom note, the family's conduct, the police work, and the media storm, reading each through his characteristic conspiratorial lens. His account is argument, not established fact; the case remains officially unsolved and widely disputed. The chapter is held as true-crime writing from the archive, for researchers who study the case and its literature.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HaapinenLarry_H:
Larry Haapinen wrote an article titled Oswald and the U-2, pegged to Francis Gary Powers' book Operation Overflight. Powers was the U-2 pilot shot down over the Soviet Union in 1960. Haapinen's piece discusses Lee Harvey Oswald in connection with the U-2 affair.

Oswald had served as a Marine radar operator and later defected to the Soviet Union, which long fed questions about what he knew. Tying his name to the spy plane story placed the assassin inside Cold War intelligence history. The article preserves that line of speculation as it was argued in print.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HurtHenry_Hurt_:
Chapter Eleven of Henry Hurt's book on the Kennedy assassination takes up the Cuban question. Its title asks the book's central choice: coincidence or conspiracy. In the chapter Hurt quotes the Schweiker Report, a Senate product, and President Lyndon B. Johnson himself.

Cuba sat at the crossroads of the case: Castro's enemies, Oswald's pro-Castro acts, and exile raiders all met there. Hurt weighs whether those crossings were chance or design. A senator's report and a president's words give the chapter its spine, and the excerpt preserves his argument at its most pointed.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PetersenHenry_P:
FBI official A. Evans sent this memorandum to Mr. Belmont on December 17, 1963. Its subject is Henry Petersen of the Justice Department. Petersen worked in the department's Organized Crime and Racketeering Section. He had been asked to serve on the Presidential Commission investigating the Kennedy assassination, the body soon known as the Warren Commission.

Staffing the commission was sensitive work. A Justice Department organized-crime man brought one kind of expertise and one kind of suspicion. The memo records the bureau noting the appointment for its own files. It is a small dated trace of the commission being assembled, less than a month after the assassination, while the FBI watched who would judge its work.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-StoneGregory_St: Los Angeles police oversight took place in public, and the meeting of March 4, 1986, was written down word for word. The transcript covers item 3-A on the agenda of the LAPD Board of Police Commissioners. Verbatim records like this one show how civilian commissioners questioned and directed one of the largest police departments in the country during the 1980s.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-Treasury_Treasu: Picture Scoop magazine previewed its contents on a single page, and one item stands out: Henry Morgenthau Jr. writing on Your Money. Morgenthau had been Franklin Roosevelt's Secretary of the Treasury. A contents page is only a promise of articles, but it shows how a photo magazine sold financial advice from a famous name. The November page survives as a small piece of magazine history.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-UnderhillGary_U: J. Garrett Underhill, a former intelligence agent, told friends he knew who killed President Kennedy. Shortly afterward he was shot dead. The article reporting his death treats it as part of the assassination mystery rather than a closed case. Underhill's story became one of the most repeated in assassination research. The piece preserves the claim and the grim end that made it famous.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WPAFilmLibrary_: A Christmas card from MPI Media Group reached Harold Weisberg from his friends at the company. MPI worked with film libraries, including the WPA Film Library named in the file. The card is a small, warm item in a research archive mostly filled with conflict and suspicion. It shows the friendly business ties behind Weisberg's later work in film and publishing.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WegrockiHenry_W: A Baltimore Sun article by Isaac Rehert profiles a young researcher named Henry Wegrocki. Its headline states his belief plainly: the CIA was behind Kennedy's death. Few newspapers gave young critics of the Warren Commission that kind of space in those years. The article shows a mainstream paper presenting a heretical claim through the person who held it, rather than endorsing or crushing it.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_colombia:
A Colombian taxi driver carried secret cash from Chiquita Brands to a right-wing paramilitary group, and in 2023 he received a thirty-six-month prison sentence. This briefing book, posted that April, draws on internal documents from the Archive's Chiquita Papers. They show his role was larger than earlier reports said.

During the 1990s the driver served as a key go-between for the fruit company. He dealt with practically every major armed actor in Colombia's conflict, not just one group. His case turns an abstract corporate crime into a human chain of payments, one bag of cash at a time.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va: The United States and Cyberspace: Military Organization, Policy - the National Security Archive briefing-book page capture. The archivists capture, complete. A single capture. Dated material. From the archive's collection, for researchers of the records and readers.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_indonesi:
East Timor voted on independence from Indonesia in a historic 1999 referendum. Brad Simpson edited this briefing book, number 682, marking twenty years since that vote. Declassified documents show what the United States knew in the run-up, and what it chose to protect.

Washington knew the Indonesian military had created, directed, and armed the militias terrorizing East Timor. Their plan was to kill, drive out, or silence independence activists before the vote. Even so, the United States sought to preserve close ties with that military. The gap between knowledge and policy is documented here in the government's own paper.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Anatoly Chernyaev worked inside the Soviet Central Committee and kept a diary that recorded the system talking to itself. Anna Melyakova translated and Svetlana Savranskaya edited this volume, number 830, published in May 2023. The diary covers the year 1983.

Chernyaev complained of his humiliating role, dressing a naked, completely naked king. On the KAL airliner shootdown that year, he wrote that it showcased the power of the military complex over Soviet life and politics. On nuclear war he reflected that a world of human achievement could vanish in a few short minutes. Few sources put a senior insider's private honesty on paper this plainly.

Anatoly Sergeyevich Chernyaev wrote one of the great insider diaries of the late Soviet Union. The Archive published his diary for 1978 in English for the first time in May 2018, on what would have been his ninety-seventh birthday. Svetlana Savranskaya edited the edition.

Chernyaev wrote from inside the Central Committee of the Communist Party, where he then worked. A daily diary at that level records meetings, moods, and doubts that official minutes hide. The 1978 volume predates his years as Gorbachev's aide, which makes it a baseline: the same sharp observer, watching a system that did not yet know it was entering its final decade.

President Bill Clinton traveled to Moscow in January 1994 for a summit with Russian president Boris Yeltsin, barely two years after the Soviet Union collapsed. The National Security Archive briefing book on that meeting publishes declassified transcripts of what the two leaders said to each other behind closed doors.

The talks show close work together on nuclear safety and on regional security problems left over from the Cold War. At the same time, worry grows in the record about Russia's troubled shift to a market system, which was bringing hardship and political strain. Readers see a hopeful partnership in plain language, along with the early signs of the troubles that would later strain it.

Anatoly Chernyaev's diary for 1980 records life inside the Soviet Central Committee while Leonid Brezhnev still ruled. Briefing Book number 706, published in May 2020, presents the diary in Anna Melyakova's translation, edited by Svetlana Savranskaya. The Archive calls its author irreplaceable as a witness to that closed world.

One entry asks who is supposed to answer for Afghanistan, where Soviet troops had invaded the year before. Another notes that most work was done to please one man, Brezhnev, and to disturb him as little as possible. Lines like those show a system run for the comfort of an aging leader. The diary gives readers a rare insider's daily record from behind the Kremlin's walls.

Anatoly Chernyaev wrote his 1984 diary while still waiting for a leader who would change the Soviet Union; Mikhail Gorbachev would take power the next year. Briefing Book number 860 presents that diary, translated and edited by Svetlana Savranskaya with help from Anna Melyakova, as part of the Archive's long project of publishing Chernyaev's private record.

Entries quoted from the diary ask what would happen if the weapons were simply destroyed, full stop. Others call the Afghan war an effort to make a country happy that cost thousands of lives and brought global shame. Chernyaev mocks his own idealism, then sizes up Gorbachev as lively, quick, and able to grasp the essence of things. Few sources show the mood inside the Soviet elite so plainly on the eve of reform.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_colombia-chiquita: Chiquita, the banana company, was found liable in an American court for killings carried out by a Colombian paramilitary group it had paid for years. A National Security Archive briefing book page carries that verdict under a plain headline naming the company and the crime. The case grew from payments Chiquita admitted making to the United Self-Defense Forces of Colombia, a group on the United States terrorist list. Only the page capture survives in this entry's evidence, marking the Archive's record of a landmark corporate accountability judgment.
govdocs-nsarchive-News_foia-human-rights:
In a forced disappearance case from Bolivia, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ordered the state to open its military archives and guarantee the right to truth. A National Security Archive news post from January 2023 reports the ruling and what it requires of the Bolivian government.

Forced disappearance works by erasing records: the victim vanishes and the state denies everything. An order to open military files attacks that erasure directly, because the archives are where orders, rosters, and reports survive. The court's demand also sets a standard other countries in the region can be measured against. Readers interested in how international courts turn human rights language into concrete duties will find a clear, compact example here.
haste-and-waste-or-the-young-pilot-of-la:
Oliver Optic's Haste and Waste is a story for young people about a young pilot on Lake Champlain. Optic was the pen name of William Taylor Adams, a Boston schoolteacher. He spent twenty years among boys and became one of America's most prolific writers for the young.

The tale belongs to the world of boats, lakeside towns and boy heroes that made Optic's name. Its hero's hurried choices, as the title warns, bring waste and trouble in their train. Adams wrote it in the same plain, energetic style as his Boat Club series, aiming to hold a young reader's attention while rewarding steady character. The front matter sketches Adams's life and long list of books, a reminder of how widely his stories travelled in their day.
hero-tales-from-american-history:
Henry Cabot Lodge and Theodore Roosevelt divided Hero Tales from American History between them, dedicating the book to the friend who suggested it. Their purpose, stated in the preface, is to tell in simple fashion of Americans whose deeds proved their truth in life and in death. Plato's Menexenus supplies the motto about fighting for liberty.

Lodge takes Washington, Trenton, Bennington, Gouverneur Morris, and the burning of the Philadelphia. Roosevelt answers with Daniel Boone, George Rogers Clark, King's Mountain, Stony Point, and the cruise of the Wasp. David Crockett's journey south to Texas fills a later chapter. Two future statesmen wrote these tales for boys, and their idea of heroism, strenuous and patriotic, shaped a generation.
hunter-quatermain-s-story:
H. Rider Haggard built this short tale around his famous white hunter, Allan Quatermain. It opens at the Yorkshire home of Sir Henry Curtis, where the talk turns to the great diamond treasure the men found in Africa. Curtis and Captain Good refuse to tell that story again and call on their old companion instead.

Quatermain, lately back from Africa, obliges with a hunting story from his years on the frontier. The adventure he chooses is a single dangerous stalk that nearly ends him, told plainly and without swagger. Haggard keeps the frame snug and lets the tale stand on close calls, bush craft, and the hunter's dry way of judging men and beasts. Readers who know Quatermain from the novels meet him here at fireside scale, in one evening's telling.
icelandic-primer-with-grammar-notes-and-:
Henry Sweet's An Icelandic Primer, in its second edition of 1895, teaches Old Icelandic with grammar, notes, and a glossary. Sweet's preface says the want of a short, easy introduction had been felt from the beginning of the study in England. Vigfusson and Powell's Icelandic Reader left room for an elementary book. Sweet modelled his on his own Anglo-Saxon primer.

The grammar leans on Noreen's Altisländische Grammatik, which Sweet calls by far the best yet written. His spelling keeps traditional normalized forms, with diacritics supplied where manuscripts are defective. Texts chosen are easy, interesting, and representative, his preface promises. Sweet, the great phonetician, built the primer to lure students of Old English northward. Generations learned their first Icelandic from it. Its clarity made a saga language approachable in a school term, which was precisely the revolution Sweet intended.
in-the-pecos-country:
In the Pecos Country, by Edward Sylvester Ellis writing as Lieutenant R H Jayne, is a frontier adventure set in New Mexico and Texas. Ellis opens in the valley of the Rio Pecos, where New England families under Caleb Barnwell have planted a settlement they christen New Boston. Their leader, part dreamer and part Don Quixote, passed richer and safer land by to settle where the government could barely protect its own citizens.

Barnwell held odd social theories, and rumors of gold and silver along the river may have helped persuade his followers. Chapter headings then tighten the trap: Fred goes on guard, faces Lone Wolf, and the Apaches are coming. The Pecos country, Ellis warns, was then among the most dangerous ground in Indian country. A boy's watch duty, a settlement's stores, and a war party's approach drive this dime novel machinery at full speed.
in-the-sweet-dry-and-dry:
Christopher Morley and Bart Haley's In the Sweet Dry and Dry is a comic novel of Prohibition, signed from Philadelphia ten minutes before midnight on June 30, 1919. That was the last hour before wartime prohibition fell on America. The authors wish their readers a Merry Abstinence and dedicate the book to G. K. Chesterton, most delightful of modern Decanterbury pilgrims. Their foreword begs that no deductions be made about their private habits. The story leaps into a dry future of mysterious juleps and thirsty secrets.

Inside, Morley's Bishop of the future and his flock scheme for liquor in a republic of raids, passwords, and medicinal fictions. The satire is gentle and thirsty rather than angry. Readers get the wittiest period piece of the dry years, two journalists drinking in print on the night the taps closed.
in-wicklow-and-west-kerry:
John M. Synge gathered In Wicklow and West Kerry from articles printed in the Manchester Guardian and the Shanachie. The volume, issued in 1912 after his death, joins two Irish journeys. Wicklow, south of Dublin, supplies the first set of sketches. West Kerry, on the Atlantic edge, supplies the second.

Synge walks with vagrants who have tramped the Wicklow roads for generations. He writes of the oppression of the hills, the people of the glens, and a fair day crowd. A landlord's garden and the valley of Glencree receive quieter studies. His prose listens closely to peasant speech and storytelling. Readers meet an Ireland of workhouses, small farms, and stubborn character, recorded by a playwright with an ear for how people actually talk.
jeff-briggs-s-love-story:
Bret Harte opened Jeff Briggs's Love Story on a storm night at Eldridge's Crossing, where Jeff Briggs keeps the ramshackle Half-way House. Wind and rain batter the loose shutters while the landlord reads himself to sleep in his attic, until a gaunt woman in a plaid shawl taps at his door. The visitor brings the past with her, and with it the love story of the title, told back through Jeff's rough California years.

Harte frames the tale as a confidence made in bad weather: how a stage-stop keeper loved, lost, and kept the memory. His California of inns, crossings, and sudden guests supplies the weather and the people. It is a quieter Harte piece, built on voice and retrospect rather than gold-camp incident.
jewish-history-an-essay-in-the-philosoph:
Simon Dubnow's Jewish History is an essay on the philosophy of history, by a leading Russian-Jewish historian. The sample carries the preface written for its German translation. That preface calls Dubnow's place in Russian-Jewish writing almost dominant. It praises his studies of Polish-Russian Jews and of Hasidism as work of lasting weight.

The preface stresses how Dubnow writes, not only what he covers. It joins strict scholarly care with warm feeling and clear, shaped prose. Dubnow held that dullness is no duty of scholarship, and that dry writing faults the writer, not the subject. His aim was to give each fact its place in the line of growth, linking Jewish history with mankind's history.
jim-cummings-or-the-great-adams-express-:
Jim Cummings, or The Great Adams Express Robbery, is a detective tale by A. Frank Pinkerton. It appeared as volume one of the Pinkerton Detective Series, issued monthly from Chicago in March 1887. The book carries a portrait of the notorious Jim Cummings. It also prints scenes tied to the great robbery of its title.

Chapter one opens in a back room behind a Chicago coal office on West Lake Street. Three men sit around a pine table with curtains drawn and a blanket nailed over the door. Maps, railroad time-tables, and pens cover the table. One big man practices writing the name J. B. Barrett again and again. The forged letter and the plan, the chapter heading promises, are taking shape.
kincaid-s-battery:
Kincaid's Battery is George Washington Cable's novel of New Orleans in the Civil War, published in 1908. Alonzo Kimball illustrated it, and Cable inscribes it to E.C.S.C. Thirteen chapters run from Carrollton Gardens to The General's Standard. The general's choice and battery manoeuvres set the military frame early.

One killed and the fight for the standard raise the cost of the battery's honor. Flora, Anna, Constance, and Kincaid each carry chapters named for their turns. Charlie races for Anna, and Anna and Adolphe meet at the corner. A duel, a recall, and the naming of Kincaid's battery close the contents. Cable, the Louisiana novelist, writes of Creole New Orleans divided by war and bound by its codes of honor.
king-alfred-of-england-makers-of-history:
King Alfred of England is Jacob Abbott's biography of Alfred the Great, in his Makers of History series. Harper and Brothers entered the book in 1849. Abbott's preface states the series' aim: a clear and connected narrative of each subject's life. He adds moral lessons drawn from the story, in a direct and simple style.

Abbott believed such lives could interest mature minds as much as young readers. Alfred's story gives him rich matter: a king who fought the Danes and fostered learning. The series made great lives into schoolroom and family reading across America. This volume presents Alfred as scholar, warrior, and lawgiver in Abbott's plain, steady manner. It served generations of young readers as their first Alfred.
laddie-a-true-blue-story:
Gene Stratton-Porter's novel Laddie calls itself a true blue story. She dedicated it to Leander Elliot Stratton. Its motto says the way to be happy is to be good.

A character list opens the book, led by Laddie himself. Chapters move from Little Sister and a first day of school to weddings and Christmas. A Pryor family mystery threads through the later chapters. Stratton-Porter sets the tale in a warm rural home. Faith, family love, and honest work guide its young hero through trouble. A princess, a pie, and a homing pigeon appear in chapter titles. Such touches keep the family story light between its trials.
little-memoirs-of-the-nineteenth-century:
George Paston published these brief memoirs in 1902. Paston was the pen name of Emily Morse Symonds. The preface chooses minor celebrities of the nineteenth century. Their experiences illustrate literary and artistic life especially.

Paston favors figures not yet overwhelmed by minor biographers. Two foreigners join the group for an outsider's verdict. Pückler-Muskau and N. P. Willis observed English manners freshly. Nearly all subjects were born in the late eighteenth century. All heroes and heroines but one were born after 1775. A previous volume treated the eighteenth century the same way.
lovey-mary:
Lovey Mary is a novel by Alice Hegan Rice, published in 1903. Rice had just won fame with Mrs. Wiggs of the Cabbage Patch. Her dedication thanks her husband Cale Young Rice for his secret of plucking roses. The story returns to the Cabbage Patch, a poor city settlement.

Lovey Mary is an orphan girl with a warm, stubborn heart. Chapters bring a runaway couple, a Labor Day, and a Christmas play. The cactus plant of the first chapter blooms by the last. Rice writes of poor neighbors with humor and deep kindness. The book mixes tears and laughter in her beloved style.
manual-for-noncommissioned-officers-and-:
The Manual for Noncommissioned Officers and Privates of Infantry dates from 1917. The War Department issued it as Document Number 574. It was approved at Washington on April 14, 1917, days after America entered the war. Engineer and Coast Artillery companies also used it for infantry training.

Chapter one lays down military discipline and courtesy. Sections cover the oath of enlistment, obedience, and loyalty. Saluting gets its own rules, spelled out in fine detail. Drill, guard duty, and camp life fill the chapters after. The manual put one standard into every soldier's hands. It shows the citizen army of 1917 learning its trade.
maria-chapdelaine-a-tale-of-the-lake-st-:
Maria Chapdelaine is Louis Hémon's tale of the Lake St. John country. W. H. Blake translated it, and Macmillan printed it at New York in 1921. Edition after edition followed through 1922, a sure sign of success. The first chapter names Peribonka, the village of Maria's home.

The Chapdelaines farm a clearing cut from the wild northern forest. François passes by, and vows are made under the northern sky. Maria must choose between the land's hard call and an easier life. Snow, church bells, and backbreaking work fill her seasons. Hémon wrote French Canada's most beloved novel of the soil. Its plain, strong beauty has never faded.
mary-prince-history:
Mary Prince dictated The History of Mary Prince in London in 1831. She was the first enslaved Black woman to publish a life narrative in Britain. Anti-slavery allies printed her words while her case stirred public debate.

Prince tells of slavery in Bermuda and Antigua: salt ponds, beatings, and masters who blocked her marriage and her freedom. She came to England as a servant and refused to return to bondage. Her plain account of pain and labor shocked British readers. The book struck a real blow for abolition in the last years before emancipation in the colonies.
mary-slessor-of-calabar-pioneer-missiona:
W. P. Livingstone wrote Mary Slessor of Calabar: Pioneer Missionary. His first note sets out the kind of life he means to tell. Slessor, he says, broke rules and followed ideals, not mere routine.

She meant to write her own tale, but died before she could. Livingstone built the book from her letters and many other sources. He praises her self denial, her courage, and her power over fierce folk. Yet he notes her shyness, her fears, and her plain, childlike faith. He warns that no sketch can hold her full, mixed nature. That frank note makes the praise that follows ring more true.
mcclellan-own-story:
George McClellan, the Union general who built the Army of the Potomac, died before finishing his memoir. McClellan's Own Story appeared in 1887, set in order by his literary executor. It is his defense of his Civil War command.

McClellan tells of the Peninsula campaign, Antietam, and his removal by Lincoln. He insists that Washington starved him of men and misread the enemy. Critics have long disputed his claims, which is part of the book's interest. Few Civil War memoirs show so clearly how a general argues his case to history. His widow saw the unfinished work through the press after his death.
men-of-invention-and-industry:
Samuel Smiles wrote these biographical sketches of British inventors and engineers. Each chapter takes up one maker or one trade. Subjects include shipbuilder Phineas Pett and John Harrison, inventor of the marine chronometer. Other chapters cover the screw propeller, the silk trade, and steam printing.

Smiles tells each life as a lesson in patience, thrift, and steady work. He follows printers like Koenig and Clowes as they mechanized the book trade. A closing section looks at industry in Ireland, including coach operator Charles Bianconi. The book captures Victorian faith that character, more than genius, drives invention.
michael-brother-of-jerry:
Jack London published this dog novel in 1917, as a companion to Jerry of the Islands. Its hero is Michael, an Irish terrier and Jerry's brother. London opens with a long foreword about trained animals. He says he learned early to look behind every animal act for the cruelty that produced it.

The foreword argues that deliberate cruelty reaches its worst form in the training ring. London lists the horrors he witnessed in slums, prisons, and battlefields, yet ranks stage training as colder. The novel then follows Michael through the world of ships and show business. It asks readers to see performing animals as victims, not amusements.
mistress-and-maid-a-household-story:
Dinah Maria Mulock Craik published this household story under the name Miss Muloch. This Richmond edition appeared in 1864. The tale opens as the three Leaf sisters debate a revolution: hiring a servant. Their new maid is a tall, awkward girl of fifteen, daughter of a widowed washerwoman named Mrs. Hand.

The sisters have long done everything themselves. Hilary, the youngest, teaches school, cooks dinner, and scrubs floors, ruining her pretty hands. Selina is often ill, and Leaf is aging. Craik, who wrote John Halifax, Gentleman, turns domestic service into a study of class, duty, and sisterly sacrifice.
mosaics-of-grecian-history:
Marcius Willson and Robert Pierpont Willson wrote this history of Greece for general readers. Their preface declares its object: a trustworthy history within moderate compass, and an interesting one. They attack the standard school manuals, mere abridgments and outlines. Outlines, they argue, invert the natural order of learning and make history drudgery.

People actually read legends, romances, poems, and biographies, the Willsons note. Shakespeare's plays, they claim, taught the public more English history than all formal tomes. They quote Macaulay approving a touch of fiction's exaggeration in history. Their mosaic pieces Greek cities, wars, and philosophers into vivid fragments a beginner can enjoy.
mother-a-story:
Kathleen Norris opens this story in a village schoolroom during a storm. Margaret Paget has taught there nearly four years, since her seventeenth birthday. Snow has turned to rain, and muddy streams run through the schoolhouse yard. Margaret knows every feature of the big bare room by heart.

Norris dedicates the book with a poem about bringing tales to a mother's knees. The title promises the theme: a woman's life given to mothering. Margaret's years at the window, in all weathers, frame a story of patience and sacrifice. Norris became one of America's most popular novelists of domestic life, and this early book shows why.
mouser-cat-s-story:
Amy Prentice wrote this children's story, illustrated by J. Watson Davis with thirty-five pictures. A color frontispiece shows Mrs. Mouser Cat carrying a mouse to Aunt Amy. The frame opens on a stormy day. Aunt Amy, kept idle by illness, sits lonely by the window, sure no animal friend will visit in such weather.

Then Mrs. Mouser Cat speaks from the doorway, for the first time ever. She scolds Aunt Amy for not caring whether Mrs. Man makes the pickles properly. Aunt Amy, astonished, finds a new storyteller. Prentice's animal tales let each creature narrate its own life, and the cat takes her turn here.
mr-world-and-miss-church-member-a-twenti:
W. S. Harris, a minister, wrote this allegory in twenty-five chapters. Its title pairs Mr. World with Miss Church-Member. Harris says critics read the draft and helped polish it. Paul Krafft of New York drew the pictures.

The tale works like a modern Pilgrim's Progress. Mr. World courts the church member and lures her toward ease. Worldly fashion and pleasure test her faith step by step. Harris aims the lesson at churchgoers of his own day. He feared new morals were pulling believers from strict paths. The book states its moral truths in story form, plainly and with zeal.
nasa-tm-19650017032-a-wind-tunnel-invest:
Robert T Taylor and William J Alford Jr at Langley tested small models of two famous aircraft together in December 1959. One model was the X-15 rocket plane, at one-fortieth scale. The other was its B-52 carrier aircraft. In real flights, the B-52 carried the X-15 aloft before release.

Taylor and Alford measured the carry loads between the pair. They also measured how each aircraft disturbed the air for the other. That mutual interference affects loads at the moment of release. Tunnel data on models let the team study a risky moment safely, before any crew flew it for real.
nasa-tm-19660014308-saturn-i-summary:
A narrative summary of the Saturn I launch vehicle fills this volume, from its start in 1958 through 1965. It is told as a story, not a data report. The prologue opens with the old dream of space travel, noting a fictional Moon voyage written by the year 160. Flying chariots, wings, and rides with angels fill the early pages, before real rockets enter.

Then the account turns to Saturn I itself, with its development and mission highlights. A photograph of the fifth Saturn I rising opens the surviving sample. Program summaries like this one were written for a broad audience. They preserve how the Saturn team told its own story while the larger Saturn V was still being built.
nasa-tm-19670008944-the-atmosphere-of-me:
S. I. Rasool, S. H. Gross, and W. E. McGovern wrote this paper on the atmosphere of Mercury in January 1966. Rasool and McGovern worked at New York University and NASA's Goddard Institute for Space Studies in New York. Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun, and whether it holds any air at all was then an open question.

The review moves from early visual observations of the planet to recent radar measurements. It weighs the evidence for an atmosphere from polarimetric and spectroscopic studies. Temperature measurements from infrared and microwave work come next. A central problem follows: Mercury's weak gravity lets gases escape thermally, and the solar wind strips more away. Closing sections build models of the atmosphere's thermal structure, from the lower layers up through the thermosphere and exosphere.
nasa-tm-19670009385-the-capillary-instab:
N. K. Nayyar and a colleague, both visiting NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center from the University of Delhi in India, study a liquid jet in this paper. The jet carries an electric current along its axis. Their question is how stable such a jet is against the pinching forces that break jets into drops.

They investigate the instability for varicose deformations, the bulging mode of the jet. Their analysis includes the Hall current in Ohm's law. Including it, they find, makes the jet less stable, though with a small frequency of oscillation. The result bears on liquid-metal flows proposed for space power systems.
nasa-tm-19680016463-exploring-in-aerospa:
Exploring in Aerospace Rocketry records a Lewis Research Center program for select high school students, run in 1966 and 1967 under advisor James F. Connors. Director Abe Silverstein started the Lewis Aerospace Explorer Post in December 1965. Principals at seven local high schools picked boys, ages fifteen to nineteen, who showed skill and interest in math and science.

The post took students out of the classroom and into the real world of aerospace engineering. Its stated aims were career guidance and fresh drive toward technical and professional work in the field. Sessions showed the young men the skills, planning, and teamwork behind a successful mission. The volume preserves how NASA introduced itself to a future generation of engineers.
nasa-tm-19680024835-on-the-thermal-radio:
Yu. N. Vetukhnovskaya and A. D. Kuzmin, of the P. N. Lebedev Physical Institute in Moscow, wrote this study of Mercury's thermal radio emission. Issued in Russian in 1967 and translated in June 1968, it reads the planet's heat through radio telescopes. The measured glow, called brightness temperature, varies with sunlight phase and with the wavelength observed.

The authors argue such readings can reveal Mercury's temperature pattern and the heat and electrical traits of its surface soil. Night side readings in infrared light carry special weight, they note. Because Mercury's sunlight far exceeds the Moon's and swings widely, lunar theory cannot simply be copied. The paper therefore builds Mercury's own thermal model and compares theory with experiment.
nasa-tm-19690026544-the-magnetic-structu:
Norman F. Ness, of Goddard Space Flight Center's Laboratory for Space Sciences, wrote this August 1969 paper, X-616-69-334. He summarizes present understanding of the magnetic structure of interplanetary space. Since 1962, spacecraft had measured the region between Venus's orbit and beyond Earth's. They confirmed a continuous flow of plasma from the Sun, the solar wind that Parker had predicted.

A very weak magnetic field of solar origin threads that plasma, Ness explains. It generally keeps a direct connection back to the Sun. At Earth's distance the field averages only about six gamma, a whisper beside Earth's own field. Wind ions stream outward near four hundred kilometers per second on average, a few particles in every cubic centimeter.
nasa-tm-19700030148-flat-conductor-cable:
James R. Carden of the Manufacturing Engineering Laboratory wrote this report in October 1970. It comes from the Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama. It covers flat conductor cable built for limited rotary or straight-line motion, the kind of cable that must flex again and again inside moving equipment.

Carden reports the cable's mechanical properties first: tensile strength, bending torque, and flexing endurance. A stiffness comparison then sets the flat cable against ordinary round wire cables. Later sections apply the cable to straight-line motion, including a rolling loop arrangement for drawers. The figures throughout let a designer judge whether the flat form would survive the motion a job demands.
nasa-tm-19710007015-experimental-verific:
NASA issued this preprint on an experimental check of the theory of weak turbulence. It reads a sequence of diffuse plasma resonances that were observed in space. Plasma is the charged gas that fills much of the space around Earth, and its faint resonances carry clues to its hidden motions.

Two space probes, the Alouette 2 and ISIS-A satellites, recorded the resonances in orbit. The author explains them through waves and particles acting on each other in a weakly turbulent plasma. One part of that picture is a wave instability tied to electrons circling in a magnetic field. He then compares the observed center frequencies with the values the theory requires. The resonances that lasted longest, he notes, match the states most favorable to that instability.
nasa-tm-19720018359-transonic-transport-:
Louis J Williams of the Office of Aeronautics and Space Technology summarized this transport study in May 1972, as NASA TM X-62,156. Williams worked in the Advanced Concepts and Missions Division at Moffett Field. The study asked what faster cruise speeds would buy future airliners. Higher speed promises a market edge over rivals. It also raises each aircraft's productivity, since one jet makes more trips. The designs targeted service entry in 1980.

All the aircraft studied were transcontinental swept wing designs. None was allowed to boom the ground with sonic shock. Each carried two hundred passengers over a twenty seven hundred nautical mile range. No cargo was carried in the study designs. Results compare the speed gains against their costs. The summary runs to forty six pages.
nature-s-serial-story:
Edward Payson Roe called his book Nature's Serial Story, and his preface tells why. A tired brain worker once told him life had begun to drag and lose its zest. Roe answers that such weariness seldom hits a person who has fallen in love with nature.

Mr and Mrs Clifford in the story are not wholly made up, Roe says. An old man in the tale loved his garden and fruit trees past eighty years. An invalid found comfort in flowers that Roe says he did not stretch. The story aims to draw readers outdoors, where each spring brings a fresh chapter.
on-heroes-hero-worship-and-the-heroic-in: Thomas Carlyle's 1841 lectures on great men: Odin, Muhammad, Dante, Shakespeare, Cromwell, Napoleon. Arguing that history is shaped by heroes, Carlyle thunders through biography as moral epic. Overblown and magnificent, the book shaped Victorian ideas of greatness and coined the phrase "hero-worship."
once-aboard-the-lugger-the-history-of-ge:
Arthur Stuart-Menteth Hutchinson wrote this novel of George and Mary. The contents divide the tale into three books. Book one treats George, his melancholy, and a hospital. A heroine makes a magnificent arrival late in book one. Book two turns to Mary's memory and mind.

Book three mixes love and war in its chapters. Bridges, letters, and dinners at Palace Gardens appear. Hutchinson jokes that some chapters may be skipped. It calls the tale a salt-sprayed romance aboard a lugger. Tender humor and sea air fill the story.
ontario-teachers-manuals-history:
Ontario's Department of Education issued this history teaching manual. Copp Clark published it in Toronto, copyrighted in 1915. The minister of education authorized the book for teachers. It opens with the public and separate school course. Chapter one treats the aims and stages of study.

Chapter two gives general methods for teaching history. Chapter three treats correlation with other school subjects. Special topics include current events, local material, and civics. Chapter five gives illustrative lessons for each form. A devices section closes the practical guidance. The manual helped Ontario teachers plan history lessons well.
our-lady-saint-mary:
J. G. H. Barry's Our Lady Saint Mary, published in 1922 and dedicated to the League of the Blessed Virgin, is an Anglo-Catholic book of devotion to the Virgin Mary. An epigraph from Origen heads it: would that I might be called a fool by the unbelieving for believing such things. The contents follow Mary's whole story. The Annunciation and Visitation come first. Cana, Holy Week, and the Crucifixion follow. The Resurrection, the Ascension, and the descent of the Holy Spirit close her earthly story. The Assumption and the Coronation end the book.

Before the life comes doctrine: the book's first part takes up loyalty and the meaning of worship, opening with the Church's collect rejoicing in Mary's joys. Barry writes for believers who keep her feasts, and the life is told as a sequence of mysteries to be contemplated rather than argued.
parisians-in-the-country:
Honoré de Balzac wrote the two works bound together in Parisians in the Country. The first, The Illustrious Gaudissart, dates from 1832, near the height of his powers. The second, The Muse of the Department, came more than ten years later. An editor's introduction compares the two pieces and traces Gaudissart through Balzac's other novels.

Gaudissart is a travelling salesman, full of talk and confidence, whom country villagers manage to outwit. The Muse of the Department turns to provincial literary ambition and gives a long, careful portrait of the man of letters Lousteau. Together the pair show Balzac moving between Paris and the provinces, his two great territories.
peggy-from-kerry: The sample we host shows only the front matter of Peggy from Kerry, the title page, copyright page, and the start of the contents, with no chapter text visible. The title page names Mrs. L. T. Meade and illustrator Martin Lewis, and Hurst and Company published the book in New York with copyright dated 1912. The frontispiece shows two girls, Molly and Jessie, stealing into a room to look at the sleeping Peggy.
pipe-and-pouch-the-smoker-s-own-book-of-:
Joseph Knight compiled Pipe and Pouch, subtitled The Smoker's Own Book of Poetry, in Boston in 1895. He dedicated the anthology to his friend and fellow-smoker Walter Montgomery Jackson. He gathered poems all turning on pipes, tobacco, and the pleasures of smoking.

Knight's preface admits this is an age of anthologies. He argues that broad collections have met with favor, since they serve both the busy man and the student of literature. Here the range is narrow on purpose: one subject, many poets. The volume offers smokers a shelf of verse matched to their habit. It is chosen for companionship rather than for study.
pipes-o-pan-at-zekesbury:
James Whitcomb Riley published Pipes O'Pan at Zekesbury in Indianapolis in 1895. He dedicated it to his brother John A. Riley, with memories of the old home. Riley was Indiana's beloved dialect poet, and Zekesbury is his invented Hoosier village.

The book opens with At Zekesbury and then a long run of Down Around the River poems. They include Romancin', Has She Forgotten, A' Old Played-Out Song, The Lost Path, Babyhood, The Days Gone By, and Mrs. Miller. Many titles are spelled in country dialect. The subjects are home, courtship, childhood, and loss. Readers who know Riley's homespun voice will find it here in a full village setting.
plays-acting-and-music-a-book-of-theory:
Arthur Symons wrote Plays, Acting and Music: A Book of Theory, published in London in 1909. Symons was a critic of drama, music, and dance. The book is dedicated to Maurice Maeterlinck, in friendship and admiration, as its front pages state.

Essays in the first part judge great stage figures of the day. Symons writes on Sarah Bernhardt, Coquelin in the plays of Molière, and Sir Henry Irving, among others. One essay takes up Nietzsche on tragedy, and the book opens with a piece called An Apology for Puppets. Later essays turn to drama itself, with pieces on Tolstoi and on trained and untrained actors.
podcast-dannyjones-nCbtQCikARY:
