The opening lingers on French-named voyageur families whose hands opened the North for generations.
the-weapons-of-mystery: Joseph Hocking's name heads this record as author of The Weapons of Mystery. No title page, contents, or chapter of any novel follows in what is preserved here. Instead the pages carry a publisher's list of Hocking titles with brief praise attached. Lest We Forget is noted as over a hundred thousand copies sold. His novel Ishmael Pengelly is called his most successful work, with the same sales figure given. All Men are Liars and The Scarlet Woman close the list. The story itself is absent.
the-works-of-lord-byron-vol-1-poetry:
Ernest Hartley Coleridge edited Poetry volume one of Byron's works for an 1898 illustrated edition. His preface explains how the text was established. It rests on John Murray's six-volume edition of 1831. That edition followed printings Byron revised during his lifetime. Editors also collated manuscripts that Thomas Moore had used. Variorum readings emerged from those comparisons.

Later editions added fresh collations with original manuscripts. Emendations and new variants entered the text over time. Coleridge presents this history to justify his text. Readers learn how carefully Byron's poems were edited after his death. The preface suits students who care about textual accuracy.
the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-12-mod: Modern history fills volume twelve of The World's Greatest Books, edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton, shown here by its contents list. Prescott's conquests of Mexico and Peru represent America. Macaulay and Clarendon cover England's past. Bagehot's English Constitution also appears. Voltaire, Tocqueville, and Mignet write on France. The condensed histories themselves are absent from the pages present in this record.
the-wreck-of-the-golden-mary:
A sea captain introduces himself at the start of The Wreck of the Golden Mary. He was apprenticed to the sea at twelve years old. Rough weather, literal and figurative, has filled his life since. He prides himself on learning widely despite little schooling. A man who knows only one subject, he says, is nearly the most tiresome sort. The tale comes from an 1894 edition of Christmas stories.

He insists he does not usually talk about himself. These remarks, he explains, simply introduce who and what he is. His name begins William George, and the sea is his trade. Readers can expect a sailor's plain-spoken shipwreck narrative. Experience, not book learning, gives the telling its authority.
the-young-enchanted-a-romantic-story: Hugh Walpole's The Young Enchanted, copyrighted in 1921 by George H. Doran, is shown through dedication pages only. Walpole dedicates the romantic story to his friend Lauritz Melchior. Through him, he extends the dedication to friends in Denmark. A motto from Walt Whitman follows about decillions of years. No chapter or scene of the novel appears in the pages present in this record.
three-plays-the-fiddler-s-house-the-land:
Padraic Colum published Three Plays at Boston with Little, Brown in 1916, collecting The Fiddler's House, The Land, and Thomas Muskerry. He called them three Irish plays and dedicated them to Thomas Hughes Kelly. His author's note explains their origins in the Irish National Theatre.

Colum wrote for a small, barely furnished stage and an audience hungry for national character. The Land celebrates tenant ownership after the Land Act of 1903 and questions why the young emigrate. Family authority conflicts with individual freedom across all three plays. Readers get compact Irish drama about soil, art, and leaving home.
torquemada-and-the-spanish-inquisition-a: Rafael Sabatini's history of Torquemada and the Spanish Inquisition, dated 1913, is introduced here by publisher's advertisements for his romances. The Strolling Saint, The Lion's Skin, The Justice of the Duke, and Bardelys the Magnificent are praised in quoted newspaper lines. The Pall Mall Gazette calls Sabatini unmatched among historical romance writers. A histories heading begins after the romance list, naming this work, then breaks off. The advertisements are what is present here, so Sabatini's history of the Inquisition itself does not appear.
tudela-itinerary:
Benjamin of Tudela, a Jewish traveler from Navarre, journeyed across the known world in the years around 1160. His Itinerary, in Marcus Adler's translation, reports what he found from Spain to Baghdad and beyond. It is the medieval world's most important travel narrative of its kind.

Benjamin counts Jewish communities in city after city, noting their scholars, trades, and numbers. He also describes Rome, Constantinople, Jerusalem, and Baghdad with a merchant's eye for wealth and power. Tales of distant lands, some fabulous, close the route home. Historians mine the book for facts found nowhere else. Adler's notes trace his route and test his claims against other sources.
types-of-weltschmerz-in-german-poetry: Wilhelm Alfred Braun's Types of Weltschmerz in German Poetry, a Columbia University essay of 1905 reprinted in 1966, opens with a note by Calvin Thomas. The note calls it a modest contribution to the natural history of Weltschmerz, the world-weariness the title names. The contents begin with an introduction, then chapters on Holderlin and Lenau. Only the note and start of the contents are present here, so Braun's analyses themselves do not appear.
umbrellas-and-their-history: William Sangster's Umbrellas and Their History carries a Latin motto meaning a defense against rains. The contents promise the ancient history of the umbrella, the umbrella in England, a story of the parachute, and a chapter on the umbrella's regeneration. Chapter one begins by asking whether the present practical age can believe what follows. Only the title page, contents, and opening lines are present here, so Sangster's history itself does not appear.
uncle-titus-and-his-visit-to-the-country:
Johanna Spyri's Uncle Titus and His Visit to the Country, translated from the German by Louise Brooks, was published at Boston in 1886. The subtitle calls it a story for children and for those who love children. Its contents promise days under the lindens, life on the other side of the hedge, and before and after the flood.

Chapter one watches the afternoon promenaders under the lindens of Karlsruhe. Two newcomers draw every eye: a man so ill he can only move slowly, and his companion, whose care in walking beside him touches the watchers. Charades, a frightful deed, and long-wished-for happiness wait in the chapters ahead.
unconscious-memory: Samuel Butler's Unconscious Memory appears in a 1910 Fifield edition, entirely reset, with an introduction by Marcus Hartog of Cork. Two long quotations face the title page. One is the Edinburgh Review's brutal 1803 dismissal of Dr. Young's lecture on light. The other tells how Brougham's attack quenched Young's wave theory for fifteen years before Fresnel revived it. Only the title page and these motto extracts are present here, so Butler's essay itself does not appear.
us-an-old-fashioned-story: Mrs Molesworth wrote Us, an old fashioned story for children, issued by Macmillan at London in 1899 with pictures by Walter Crane. The pages here give the title page and the first part of the contents only, so the story itself does not appear. Early chapters promise how the children came to be called Us, then bread and milk, queer visitors, and babes in a wood. The frontispiece shows a dog named Toby with his nose in a bowl, to his great content.
voltaire-s-philosophical-dictionary:
Voltaire's Philosophical Dictionary opens with a preface on how to read it. The book does not demand steady reading, the preface says; open it anywhere and you will find matter for thought. The most useful books are those readers half compose themselves, stretching the germ of an idea, fixing what seems weak or wrong by their own reflection.

Only enlightened people, Voltaire grants, can truly read such a book. The common man does not read; he works six days a week and goes to the inn on the seventh, so no one need fear truths hidden from the people. The alphabet that follows draws on worthy works not within most readers' reach. Every honest man, the preface ends, should try to be a philosopher, without pluming himself on the title.
washington-up-from-slavery:
Booker Washington published Up from Slavery in 1901, and it became the most influential Black memoir of its era. Born enslaved in Virginia, Washington taught himself to read after emancipation. At twenty-five he founded the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama.

He tells of working in salt furnaces and coal mines to reach Hampton Institute. At Tuskegee he built a school from almost nothing, brick by brick, with student labor. His Atlanta speech of 1895, urging work and patience, made him a national figure. Critics then and since have debated his bargain with segregation, but the book's reach is beyond doubt.
watch-work-wait-or-the-orphan-s-victory:
Sarah A. Myers wrote Watch, Work, Wait, or The Orphan's Victory. T. Nelson and Sons issued it at London in 1862. A note at the front calls the book a plain record of the hardships and lures a poor orphan boy went through a few years earlier. It teaches, the note says, that a child needs God's help through life's battle. It shows that a child may grow into a fine character amid heavy trials and great evils.

The author pledges that the incidents are real. Some of them are stranger than fiction, yet facts and not fancies. The frontispiece shows William at his mother's grave, sketching the little square where his loved ones sleep. Chapter one, William's First Grief, opens in a village on the Hudson river. Readers follow a bereaved boy through work, want, and temptation, toward the victory of the title.
we-girls-a-home-story:
Mrs. A. D. T. Whitney, author of Faith Gartney's Girlhood, wrote We Girls, a home story, issued at Boston with dates of 1870 and 1890. Her contents promise twelve chapters of household life. The story begins, amphibious days, and betwixt and between come first. Halloween, winter nights and winter days, and Ruth's responsibility follow. Barbara's buzz and emergencies close the list. The frontispiece shows hands binding rings.

Chapter one owns the method at once: it begins right in the middle, since a story must begin somewhere. The town lies down below the hill. It stretches in a hollow till it runs against another hill, and climbs a little way before it can stop, just as it does on the narrator's side. From that ground the tale settles into one family's kitchen and parlor. Sisters learn work, patience, and each other there.
welsh-lyrics-of-the-nineteenth-century: Only the title page and contents are present here, so the poems themselves do not appear. Edmund O. Jones chose and translated the pieces, printed in London and Bangor in 1896. The contents group short Welsh poems by poet. Alun has four pieces, one on a fisherman's wife and one on Tintern Abbey. Ieuan Glan Geirionydd, Glasynys, Ioan Emlyn, and Trebor Mai also appear. Caledfryn has a poem on the cuckoo, and Gwilym Marles closes the early list.
when-the-yule-log-burns-a-christmas-stor: Nothing past the title page and contents is present here for Leona Dalrymple's When the Yule Log Burns, a Christmas story printed in 1916. The contents divide the tale into two parts. Part one, in which a yule log is lit, has chapters named Kindlings, Wishing Sparks, By the Fire, and Embers. Part two lights the new log with embers of the old. Its chapters run from The Fire Again to The Log at Twilight. A picture note describes a doctor's house in snow.
when-wilderness-was-king-a-tale-of-the-i: The pages here stop at edition notices and a contents list for Randall Parrish's When Wilderness Was King, so his tale does not appear. Parrish set the story in the Illinois country. Burt printed it in New York, with the first edition dated March 26, 1904. Six more editions followed by December 1905. The contents open with a message from the West and a call of duty. Later chapters name Captain Wells of Fort Wayne, old Fort Dearborn, and a lane of peril.
why-worry:
George Lincoln Walton, a consulting neurologist at Massachusetts General Hospital, wrote Why Worry? A Chinese saying heads the book: the stork's legs are long, the duck's are short, and neither can be changed. Walton gives the book to the family and friends whose patience his war on worry tried. His preface offers no apology for one more book on the theme.

Worry, Walton says, will not yield to mere resolve. He hopes plain cases and common sense tips will turn the reader's mind to healthier paths. His goal is not to make busy men idle thinkers. He wants them to work better by dropping undue care. The book treats worry as a habit that can be retrained.
wild-flowers-or-pastoral-and-local-poetr:
Robert Bloomfield, author of The Farmer's Boy, published Wild Flowers, or Pastoral and Local Poetry, in London in 1806. The contents list ballads and tales with rural names: Abner and the Widow Jones, The Horkey, and The Broken Crutch. Other pieces praise love of the country and a spot called Shooter's Hill.

The first ballad opens with a carter set on courting the Widow Jones the next day, road rough or smooth. His old horse Bayard, he fears, faces the hounds if younger horses take the stable room. Bloomfield writes of farm folk in plain, warm verse. Work, courtship, and loss fill his local tales.
wild-wales-its-people-language-and-scene: The front pages here hold an edition note and a picture list for George Borrow's Wild Wales, with none of Borrow's travel text present. Murray printed the book in London, first in 1862. The note, dated January 1901, says this edition was checked against the first to keep Borrow's spellings of names exact. A Welsh verse from Taliesin heads the title page, on keeping a language while losing a land. The pictures, drawn by A. S. Hartrick, include Llangollen and the wilds of Snowdon.
woman-and-her-saviour-in-persia-by-a-ret:
A returned missionary compiled this account of Christian work among women in Persia. The preface centres on Miss Fiske and her fifteen years of labour there. Friends asked her to publish the facts herself. She could not, so the writer gathered her letters and talks instead. Material also came from others who knew the work firsthand.

The account focuses on the female seminary at Oroomiah and on Nestorian Christians. Revival stories appear as side sketches rather than the main thread. The writer shaped each topic fully rather than follow strict date order. Readers get mission history told through women's schooling and faith.
women-of-the-country: Gertrude Bone wrote these sketches of country women, published in London in 1913 with a frontispiece by Muirhead Bone. Pages present here hold a long list of companion volumes in the Roadmender series, the title page, and a chapter heading. No chapter prose appears in these pages. The series list names works by Michael Fairless, Edward Thomas, and others, which sets the quiet, rural mood Bone's sketches likely share.
youth-and-egolatry: Pio Baroja wrote these essays on himself and his ideas, rendered from Spanish by Jacob S. Fassett, Jr. and Frances L. Phillips. Pages present here hold a contents list with an introduction by H. L. Mencken, but no essay text. Listed pieces cover egotism, religion, music, Wagner, and folk song. A second part turns to Baroja as writer, his youthful works, anarchism, and longing for change. The essays themselves do not appear in these pages.
zuleika-dobson-or-an-oxford-love-story:
Max Beerbohm wrote this comic novel about Zuleika Dobson and Oxford. His 1922 note settles her name's sound first. Friends in London said it wrong after the first edition, he complains. Readers should say Zu-leek-a, as Joseph thought of his wife. Chapter one then opens at Oxford station. Undergraduates in tweed and flannel wait idly in afternoon sunshine for a train.

The Warden of Judas stands apart, a pillar of tradition in silk hat and white shirt front. A furious engine curves in under smoke. Zuleika arrives with it, unknown to the waiting men. Readers get a polished satire of Oxford worship and hopeless love.
